title: Multi-Modal Computer- and Robot-Assisted Navigation in Spinal Surgery
abstract: Spinal disorders affect over 619 million people worldwide and are a leading cause of disability. In cases of severe pathology—such as spinal deformities, instability, or degenerative disc disease—surgical fusion is considered as the mainstay of therapy to restore spinal alignment and relieve chronic pain. A cornerstone of this procedure is the precise placement of pedicle screws (PSP), which demands millimeter accurate surgical execution to avoid neurological, vascular, or mechanical complications. Despite advances in computer-assisted navigation (CAN) and robot-assisted guidance (RG), current systems remain constrained by their reliance on single-modality data—typically optical tracking and intraoperative imaging—which makes them vulnerable to registration errors, anatomical shifts, and workflow deviations, particularly in minimally invasive settings. They also lack the flexibility to adapt to intraoperative surgical difficulties such as unexpected bleeding, tissue swelling, or altered exposure, which can compromise anatomical context and reduce the accuracy of navigation. Furthermore, these technologies still introduce additional costs and prolong surgical time due to required setup procedures, repeated imaging, and the need for highly specialized, additional personnel—factors that limit their broader clinical adoption, especially in resource-constrained environments. In contrast, surgeons dynamically construct an internal model of the surgical environment by integrating diverse sensory cues: visual inspection, tactile feedback, auditory signals, and procedural experience. This thesis is driven by the hypothesis that multi-modal navigation—integrating visual and non-visual sensing with learning-based inference—can overcome the rigidity and limitations of existing systems and enable safer, more adaptive, and radiation-free surgical guidance. To lay the foundation for this work, Chapter 2 presents a comprehensive review of intraoperative sensing and tissue classification techniques in orthopedics and neurosurgery. The review analyzes 60 studies across modalities, classification goals, algorithms, and validation methods, highlighting common limitations such as over-reliance on phantom models and lack of multi-sensor integration. Chapter 3 addresses the first research direction: non-visual sensing. A vibro-acoustic sensing framework was developed by integrating accelerometers and microphones. Using a fusion model, the system achieved 98.0% breach detection accuracy in ex-vivo porcine vertebrae, leveraging optical tracking for automated ground-truth labeling. This validates the feasibility of real-time cortical breach detection using auditory cues—emulating the natural sensory strategies used by surgeons. Chapters 4 and 5 focus on the second direction: the advancement of visual sensing for vertebral localization and reconstruction. Chapter 4 introduces a transformer-based 3D shape completion model that reconstructs vertebral anatomy from sparse stereo-vision point clouds. It achieved a mean Chamfer distance of 5.39 mm, an F-score of 0.85, and a surface signal-to-noise ratio of 22.9 dB against ground-truth CT in cadaveric testing. Chapter 5 presents a robotic ultrasound system for radiation-free bone surface reconstruction, combining force-controlled scanning with a deep-learning segmentation pipeline. The system achieved mean surface errors of 1.28 mm in phantoms and 1.74 mm in human cadavers, demonstrating potential for real-time vertebral mapping in percutaneous procedures. Chapter 6 addresses the final research direction: registration-free navigation. It evaluates whether the shape-completed vertebrae from intraoperative RGB-D data can be used to enable fully automatic pedicle screw planning directly. The system proposed candidate trajectories based solely on intraoperative reconstructions and achieved 100% Grade A screws in cadaveric validation—comparable to CT-based methods. Collectively, these contributions form a coherent multi-modal navigation framework that integrates nonvisual cues, visual reconstruction, and machine learning to bypass traditional registration and intraoperative imaging. By mirroring the surgeon’s perceptual strategies, this approach improves adaptability, enhances safety, and supports radiation-free guidance—paving the way toward broader clinical use in both open and minimally invasive spinal surgery.

title: MP68-18 CONSOLE-INTEGRATED REAL-TIME THREE-DIMENSIONAL (3D) PHYSICAL MODEL NAVIGATION FOR ROBOTIC PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY IN PATIENT WITH HIGHLY COMPLEX RENAL TUMORS (RENAL NEPHROMETRY SCORE≥7): PROSPECTIVE CASE-MATCHED STUDY
abstract: You have accessJournal of UrologyKidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy VI (MP68)1 Apr 2020MP68-18 CONSOLE-INTEGRATED REAL-TIME THREE-DIMENSIONAL (3D) PHYSICAL MODEL NAVIGATION FOR ROBOTIC PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY IN PATIENT WITH HIGHLY COMPLEX RENAL TUMORS (RENAL NEPHROMETRY SCORE≥7): PROSPECTIVE CASE-MATCHED STUDY Jung Kwon Kim*, Hakmin Lee, Jong Jin Oh, Sangchul Lee, Seong Jin Jeong, Sung Kyu Hong, Sang Eun Lee, and Seok-Soo Byun, Seongnam-si Jung Kwon Kim*Jung Kwon Kim* More articles by this author , Hakmin LeeHakmin Lee More articles by this author , Jong Jin OhJong Jin Oh More articles by this author , Sangchul LeeSangchul Lee More articles by this author , Seong Jin JeongSeong Jin Jeong More articles by this author , Sung Kyu HongSung Kyu Hong More articles by this author , Sang Eun LeeSang Eun Lee More articles by this author , and Seok-Soo Byun, Seongnam-siSeok-Soo Byun, Seongnam-si More articles by this author View All Author Informationhttps://doi.org/10.1097/JU.0000000000000948.018AboutPDF ToolsAdd to favoritesDownload CitationsTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints ShareFacebookLinked InTwitterEmail Abstract INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVE: Three-dimensional (3D) images can be used to facilitate patient education, surgical planning, as well as both a research and marketing tool in field of surgery. In current study, we tried to evaluate the effectiveness of 3D physical model for robotic partial nephrectomy (RPN) in patient with highly complex renal tumors (RENAL nephrometry score [RNS] ≥ 7) METHODS: A total of 80 patients who underwent RPN were included in current prospective case-matched study [case group (n = 40, application of 3D physical model during RPN) vs. matching group (n = 40), Figure 1]. RPN performed by single surgeon (SSB) who has experience of over 500 cases of RPN. RPN procedure consisted of 6 steps: (1) vessel preparation for clamping; (2) tumor detection and dissection; (3) robotic ultrasound; (4) tumor resection; (5) calyx repair and hemostasis; (6) renorrhaphy. RESULTS: Both groups were well-balanced in all baseline characteristics. Mean and median RNS were 9.54 and 10, respectively. Total agreement rate in RNS was 92.5% (37/40). Mean and median console time and warm ischemic time (WIT) were 71.51 / 69.67 (min) and 23.1 / 23.5 (min), respectively. In comparative analysis of each step time including console time and WIT, we found the significant differences in console time, vessel preparation time, detection and dissection time, and calyx repair and hemostasis time between the two groups (all, p < 0.05). On multivariate logistic regression analysis, tumor radius (p < 0.001) and application of 3D physical model (p = 0.009) were identified as significant predictors of console time ≤ 70 (min). In subgroup analysis according to the each component, we also found some effectiveness of 3D physical model (Figure 2). CONCLUSIONS: We found the effectiveness of 3D physical models for RPN in specific patient groups with highly complex tumors. title: Intrinsically Passive Control for Ultrasound-guided Robotic Scanning of the Breast
abstract: Automated breast ultrasound imaging systems provide the ability to combine the high anatomical detail of preoperative imaging with real-time intraoperative imaging. Ultrasound imaging involves interaction between the transducer and the patient, which requires a compliant behaviour of the robot in manipulating the transducer. We present an energy-based control strategy augmented with a visual servoing algorithm to improve the image quality online. An impedance controller is extended with energy- and power-based safety metrics to adjust the dynamic behavior of the robot and with energy tanks to ensure passivity. The quality of the ultrasound images is represented by a confidence map that is computed online, following a model of ultrasound propagation in soft tissue. Experiments were conducted with the 7 degree-of-freedom KUKA LBRMed articulated robot. First, a port-Hamiltonian model of the robotwas created to design and test the controller in simulation. Second, the controllerwas transferred to the robot controller for experimental validation of the proposed control strategy. Simulational and experimental results have validated the controller design in interaction with the environment. Experiments with an ultrasound phantom have demonstrated that the visual servoing algorithm corrects the probe pose in case of (partial) contact loss between the transducer and the skin surface. This significantly increases the global image quality of the 3D image of the breast. Our approach has resulted in a very promising control strategy for autonomous ultrasound scanning that can be integrated in an automated breast biopsy procedure.

title: Multimodal Cross-Attention Fusion of B-Mode Ultrasound and Strain Elastography for Tumor Segmentation in Robotics-Assisted Surgery
abstract: Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery offers high precision and dexterity, opening up new possibilities for intraoperative imaging to improve tumor localization. B-mode ultrasound provides real-time anatomical views, while strain elastography (SE) adds tissue stiffness information. Used together, they provide complementary cues that help increase the accuracy of tumor localization by improving boundary detection. We present a robotics-integrated framework for autonomous ultrasound scanning and multimodal tumor segmentation. The system utilizes the da Vinci® Classic surgical robot with the da Vinci® Research Kit (dVRK) and a custom ultrasound transducer. It simultaneously acquires paired B-mode and SE images from silicone phantoms and ex vivo porcine livers. Our architecture extends the conventional U-Net by integrating dual encoders with cross-attention and selective fusion. Cross-attention allows one modality to refine the features of the other, while selective fusion balances their contributions. We performed experiments on a multimodal dataset to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Results indicate that our approach outperforms unimodal baselines and standard fusion methods across both segmentation and classification metrics. These findings suggest that multimodal cross-attention and selective fusion can improve tumor segmentation in ultrasound imaging. Ultimately, the goal is to use such advances to support intraoperative guidance for robot-assisted liver surgery.

title: V05-01 3D AUGMENTED REALITY-GUIDED ROBOTIC-ASSISTED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: REVEALING THE CONCEALED
abstract: You have accessJournal of UrologyCME1 May 2022V05-01 3D AUGMENTED REALITY-GUIDED ROBOTIC-ASSISTED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: REVEALING THE CONCEALED Alberto Piana, Gallioli Andrea, Pietro Diana, Angelo Territo, Josep Maria Gaya, Pavel Gavrilov, Óscar Rodriguez Faba, Jordi Huguet, Lluis Guirado, Carme Facundo, Riccardo Campi, Andrea Bellin, Daniele Amparore, Sergio Serni, Joan Palou, and Alberto Breda Alberto PianaAlberto Piana More articles by this author , Gallioli AndreaGallioli Andrea More articles by this author , Pietro DianaPietro Diana More articles by this author , Angelo TerritoAngelo Territo More articles by this author , Josep Maria GayaJosep Maria Gaya More articles by this author , Pavel GavrilovPavel Gavrilov More articles by this author , Óscar Rodriguez FabaÓscar Rodriguez Faba More articles by this author , Jordi HuguetJordi Huguet More articles by this author , Lluis GuiradoLluis Guirado More articles by this author , Carme FacundoCarme Facundo More articles by this author , Riccardo CampiRiccardo Campi More articles by this author , Andrea BellinAndrea Bellin More articles by this author , Daniele AmparoreDaniele Amparore More articles by this author , Sergio SerniSergio Serni More articles by this author , Joan PalouJoan Palou More articles by this author , and Alberto BredaAlberto Breda More articles by this author View All Author Informationhttps://doi.org/10.1097/JU.0000000000002579.01AboutPDF ToolsAdd to favoritesDownload CitationsTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints ShareFacebookLinked InTwitterEmail Abstract INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVE: Robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) has long shown solid results as a minimally invasive alternative to the standard open approach (OKT) for living donor and promising results for deceased donor. However, RAKT is still limited in those cases where the recipient’s iliac vessels present atherosclerotic plaques, frequently found in elder patients and in those subjected to long-term hemodialysis. Unlike OKT, where the surgeon can palpate the arterial plaques, in minimally-invasive surgery the haptic feedback is missing making the vascular clamping and arteriotomy unsafe. To overcome this limitation, 3-Dimensional (3D) imaging virtual reconstruction was employed using the Augmented Reality (AR) to intraoperatively locate the plaques, driving the surgeon during the crucial steps of KT. METHODS: Our study was conducted according to IDEAL model for surgical innovation. 3D printed and virtual models were obtained from high-accuracy conventional CT scan imaging and superimposed on the vessels during RAKT using the Da Vinci console software. RESULTS: In the IDEAL phase 0, 3D virtual models were obtained from patients with artery plaques, printed and compared to the vascular anatomy of the patient during 2 OKTs by manual palpation. In phase 1, the 3D virtual models of patients without plaques were superimposed during a combined open-robotic KT and 2 RAKTs. Anatomical fidelity was assessed by measuring and comparing the virtual model to the real vessels. Then, we employed the 3D AR on a clinical case without plaques during the vascular clamping and arteriotomy phases to gain insight of anatomy modification during vessel dissection. The correspondence of 3D virtual models with the real anatomy of patients with plaques was tested by scanning the iliac arteries with a robotic ultrasound (US) probe in 10 patients undergoing robotic-assisted iliac lymph-node dissection for prostate cancer. Finally, after US confirmation, the 3D-AR accurately enabled the surgeon to place the clamp and perform the arteriotomy safely in a clinical case with arterial plaques. CONCLUSIONS: The employment of 3D-AR allowed to overcome one of the main limitations of RAKT, setting the foundation to expand its indications to patients with advanced atheromatic vascular disease. title: Point-of-care ultrasound training in infectious diseases: Educational models, challenges, and multi-sectoral roles
abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has become an essential diagnostic and procedural adjunct in infectious disease practice, providing real-time bedside evaluation that improves patient outcomes. Despite its clinical relevance, broad implementation faces educational challenges, including limited access to hands-on training, inconsistent curricular integration, and lack of standardized certification pathways across all stages of medical education. This review frames POCUS education as a longitudinal, progressive pathway starting with foundational exposure in undergraduate medical curricula and advancing through competency-based postgraduate training, continuing professional development, and formal credentialing. Key educational frameworks such as G.O.O.S.E. and I-AIM structure the acquisition of both technical imaging skills and clinical integration, fostering critical ultrasound competence. Various stakeholders contribute to this continuum: medical schools form the foundational base; private sector programs fill training gaps using innovative educational approaches including immersive workshops, simulation, blended learning, and small-group pathology-focused sessions; and scientific societies provide leadership by defining standards, supporting collaborative research, and advocating for formalized training and certification. These innovative training modalities enable flexible, practical skill acquisition tailored to evolving clinical needs and diverse practice environments, accelerating learners' progression toward competent, autonomous ultrasound use. Such approaches are especially valuable in resource-limited settings or where traditional academic resources are constrained. Sustained multisectoral collaboration among academic institutions, private educators, scientific societies, and regulatory bodies is vital to ensure accessible, effective, and equitable POCUS training worldwide. By outlining this comprehensive educational roadmap and recognizing ongoing innovations, this review aims to guide the integration of POCUS into infectious disease care, ultimately improving global patient outcomes.

title: Advanced Functional Soft Miniature Robotic Systems for Biomedical Applications
abstract: Wireless soft miniature robots, representative of miniature medical devices (MMDs), can access hard-to-reach regions with minimal invasion, such as areas deep inside gastrointestinal tracts and distal vascular lumens, enabling safe tissue interaction and biomedical functions like drug delivery and embolization. While previous studies have demonstrated designs for multi-modal locomotion and proof-of-concept medical applications, critical gaps persist in translating these capabilities to complex physiological environments. Key challenges include insufficient understanding of robot-tissue interactions, limited functionality-driven robot design, suboptimal control algorithms for dynamic scenarios, and the lack of robust navigation systems under medical imaging. This dissertation aims to address these limitations by developing miniature robotic systems that integrate novel functional robot designs, mechanics-informed control strategies, and medical imaging-guided navigation frameworks. By synergizing task-oriented robot design, real-time tracking, and robust control, this work advances the deployment of miniature robots in anatomically complex and clinically relevant scenarios. The first part of the dissertation introduces a minimally invasive method for sensing physiological properties of gastrointestinal (GI) tissues using wireless miniature soft robots. Unlike conventional implanted sensors and medical-imaging-based methods, this approach utilizes external magnetic fields to precisely control robot-tissue interactions to recover advanced deep-tissue properties via a magnetic-mechanical model and robot shape analysis under X-ray imaging. The millimeter-scale robots, integrating pH-responsive and bioadhesive patches, present multimodal locomotion across tissue barriers and enable sensing of adhesion, pH, and viscoelasticity with static (buckling-based) and dynamic (undulating) shape changes, validated through comprehensive experiments on synthetic materials and ex vivo tissues. With the unprecedented capability of sensing tissue physiological properties with minimal invasion and high resolution deep inside animals, this technology can potentially enable critical applications in basic biomechanics research and clinical practice. While the first study focuses on a single-sheet magnetic robot in GI tracts, the second part investigates multiple stent-shaped magnetic robots in blood vessels. Despite differences in design, workspace, and robot number, both studies emphasize analysis of robot–tissue interactions to advance minimally invasive interventions. Deploying multiple robots can enhance the efficacy and multifunctionality of these procedures; however, multirobot deployment in physiologically relevant three-dimensional (3D) tubular structures is limited by the lack of effective mechanisms for independently controlling magnetic soft robots. To address this, the proposed framework leverages shape-adaptive robot design and heterogeneous resistance from robot-lumen interactions. A magnetic-mechanical model defines influence and actuation regions, guiding a magnetic path-planning algorithm for individual robot navigation. Under X-ray medical imaging, multiple robots are independently controlled within multilayered 3D lumen networks to perform tasks like multilocation cargo delivery and flow diversion. This approach offers a scalable solution for multirobot actuation in complex biomedical environments. The translation of these MMDs to clinical settings requires seamless integration of medical imaging and robotic control. The third part addresses the challenge of automated robot navigation over extended distances within noisy, low-contrast B-mode ultrasound images. Ultrasound imaging is advantageous due to its non-ionizing nature, portability, and low latency. However, its limited field of view and complex imaging scenes make continuous robot localization difficult, rendering manual probe adjustments labor-intensive and impractical. Thus, a robotic navigation system is developed that combines synthetic data-enhanced deep learning for robust robot detection and automated robotic ultrasound probe control. Object detection models are trained on synthetically generated data and real data of synthetic materials, mitigating data scarcity and labeling burdens. Integrated with a 7-DOF robotic arm, the system autonomously adjusts the ultrasound probe to maintain continuous visualization during magnetic actuation. Demonstrated navigation through tortuous lumens highlights the potential of this approach for real-time, ultrasound-guided interventions in complex biological environments. For deep tissue access and clear visualization, X-ray fluoroscopy is clinically essential, providing high-resolution near real-time imaging; however, its use in dynamic, cluttered settings remains labor-intensive due to manual MMD identification and precise tool manipulation. Furthermore, the scarcity of labeled clinical data for MMDs further limits learning-based approaches. The fourth part proposes MicroSyn-X, a framework for synthesizing high-fidelity, pixel-accurate, domain-randomized X-ray images of MMDs in customizable anatomical scenes. This end-to-end approach overcomes data scarcity and eliminates manual labeling, enabling direct training of computer vision models for robust MMD localization under low-contrast, noisy, and occluded imaging scenarios. Integrated into a teleoperated robotic system, MicroSyn-X-trained models enable vision-based closed-loop control for precise MMD navigation. The system's effectiveness is validated through real-time navigation of soft and liquid robots in diverse \emph{ex vivo} and dynamic \emph{in vivo} environments, demonstrating robustness in physiologically relevant contexts. The open-sourcing of the first X-ray MMD dataset facilitates benchmarking and democratizes development. Bridging the data gap and enabling precise real-time control, this work advances the feasibility of robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery under clinical X-ray imaging, marking a critical step toward next-generation precision interventions.

title: Surgical Robot Learning from Human Demonstrations
abstract: This thesis investigates how robotic surgical systems can efficiently acquire and generalize manipulation skills through Learning from Demonstration (LfD), even under severe data scarcity and uncertainty. Inspired by the apprenticeship model of surgical training—“see one, do one, teach one”—we explore how robots can learn surgical task execution from expert demonstrations and gradually extend this capability to less curated and non-surgical data sources. Our goal is to develop a scalable and generalizable learning paradigm that bridges the gap between limited expert surgical data and abundant human activity data.We first study autonomous ultrasound scanning as a structured exemplar of high-quality demonstration learning. By leveraging consistent and noise-free expert demonstrations, we develop a precise motion learning and control framework that enables reliable scanning behavior under controlled conditions. This stage establishes the foundation of demonstration-based robotic learning in surgical contexts.Building upon this, we address the challenge of imperfect and variable demonstrations that naturally arise in real-world surgical settings. We introduce a probabilistic learning framework based on a Donut mixture model and RANSAC-based outlier rejection to extract robust motion intent from heterogeneous and partially erroneous demonstrations. This framework demonstrates how surgical robots can maintain stable learning performance despite noisy or inconsistent data, thus relaxing the dependency on ideal demonstrations.Finally, we extend the paradigm beyond surgical data by exploring the feasibility of learning from human Activities of Daily Living (ADL). We propose a cross-domain transfer learning framework based on successor feature learning and generalized policy improvement (GPI), which captures transferable coordination and manipulation patterns from large-scale human activity datasets. These representations are then adapted to surgical task domains, enabling data-efficient policy transfer without additional expert supervision.Through this progressive exploration—from perfect surgical demonstrations to imperfect and cross-domain human data—this thesis presents a unified framework for scalable, data-efficient, and generalizable robotic surgical skill acquisition. The proposed methods collectively demonstrate a pathway toward autonomous surgical systems that can learn safely and effectively from diverse human demonstrations, advancing the long-term goal of data-driven surgical autonomy.

title: Suivi des vaisseaux sanguins en temps réel à partir d’images ultrasonores mode-B et reconstruction 3D : application à la caractérisation des sténoses artérielles
abstract: La maladie des artères périphériques (MAP) se manifeste par une réduction (sténose) de la lumière de l’artère des membres inférieurs. Elle est causée par l’athérosclérose, une accumulation de cellules spumeuses, de graisse, de calcium et de débris cellulaires dans la paroi artérielle, généralement dans les bifurcations et les ramifications. Par ailleurs, la MAP peut être causée par d`autres facteurs associés comme l’inflammation, une malformation anatomique et dans de rares cas, au niveau des artères iliaques et fémorales, par la dysplasie fibromusculaire. L’imagerie ultrasonore est le premier moyen de diagnostic de la MAP. La littérature clinique rapporte qu’au niveau de l’artère fémorale, l’écho-Doppler montre une sensibilité de 80 à 98 % et une spécificité de 89 à 99 % à détecter une sténose supérieure à 50 %. Cependant, l’écho-Doppler ne permet pas une cartographie de l’ensemble des artères des membres inférieurs. D’autre part, la reconstruction 3D à partir des images échographiques 2D des artères atteintes de la MAP est fortement opérateur dépendant à cause de la grande variabilité des mesures pendant l’examen par les cliniciens. Pour planifier une intervention chirurgicale, les cliniciens utilisent la tomodensitométrie (CTA), l’angiographie par résonance magnétique (MRA) et l’angiographie par soustraction numérique (DSA). Il est vrai que ces modalités sont très performantes. La CTA montre une grande précision dans la détection et l’évaluation des sténoses supérieures à 50 % avec une sensibilité de 92 à 97 % et une spécificité entre 93 et 97 %. Par contre, elle est ionisante (rayon x) et invasive à cause du produit de contraste, qui peut causer des néphropathies. La MRA avec injection de contraste (CE MRA) est maintenant la plus utilisée. Elle offre une sensibilité de 92 à 99.5 % et une spécificité entre 64 et 99 %. Cependant, elle sous-estime les sténoses et peut aussi causer une néphropathie dans de rares cas. De plus les patients avec stents, implants métalliques ou bien claustrophobes sont exclus de ce type d`examen. La DSA est très performante mais s`avère invasive et ionisante. Aujourd’hui, l’imagerie ultrasonore (3D US) s’est généralisée surtout en obstétrique et échocardiographie. En angiographie il est possible de calculer le volume de la plaque grâce à l’imagerie ultrasonore 3D, ce qui permet un suivi de l’évolution de la plaque athéromateuse au niveau des vaisseaux. L’imagerie intravasculaire ultrasonore (IVUS) est une technique qui mesure ce volume. Cependant, elle est invasive, dispendieuse et risquée. Des études in vivo ont montré qu’avec l’imagerie 3D-US on est capable de quantifier la plaque au niveau de la carotide et de caractériser la géométrie 3D de l'anastomose dans les artères périphériques. Par contre, ces systèmes ne fonctionnent que sur de courtes distances. Par conséquent, ils ne sont pas adaptés pour l’examen de l’artère fémorale, à cause de sa longueur et de sa forme tortueuse. L’intérêt pour la robotique médicale date des années 70. Depuis, plusieurs robots médicaux ont été proposés pour la chirurgie, la thérapie et le diagnostic. Dans le cas du diagnostic artériel, seuls deux prototypes sont proposés, mais non commercialisés. Hippocrate est le premier robot de type maitre/esclave conçu pour des examens des petits segments d’artères (carotide). Il est composé d’un bras à 6 degrés de liberté (ddl) suspendu au-dessus du patient sur un socle rigide. À partir de ce prototype, un contrôleur automatisant les déplacements du robot par rétroaction des images échographiques a été conçu et testé sur des fantômes. Le deuxième est le robot de la Colombie Britannique conçu pour les examens à distance de la carotide. Le mouvement de la sonde est asservi par rétroaction des images US. Les travaux publiés avec les deux robots se limitent à la carotide. Afin d’examiner un long segment d’artère, un système robotique US a été conçu dans notre laboratoire. Le système possède deux modes de fonctionnement, le mode teach/replay (voir annexe 3) et le mode commande libre par l’utilisateur. Dans ce dernier mode, l’utilisateur peut implémenter des programmes personnalisés comme ceux utilisés dans ce projet afin de contrôler les mouvements du robot. Le but de ce projet est de démontrer les performances de ce système robotique dans des conditions proches au contexte clinique avec le mode commande libre par l’utilisateur. Deux objectifs étaient visés: (1) évaluer in vitro le suivi automatique et la reconstruction 3D en temps réel d’une artère en utilisant trois fantômes ayant des géométries réalistes. (2) évaluer in vivo la capacité de ce système d'imagerie robotique pour la cartographie 3D en temps réel d'une artère fémorale normale. Pour le premier objectif, la reconstruction 3D US a été comparée avec les fichiers CAD (computer-aided-design) des fantômes. De plus, pour le troisième fantôme, la reconstruction 3D US a été comparée avec sa reconstruction CTA, considéré comme examen de référence pour évaluer la MAP. Cinq chapitres composent ce mémoire. Dans le premier chapitre, la MAP sera expliquée, puis dans les deuxième et troisième chapitres, l’imagerie 3D ultrasonore et la robotique médicale seront développées. Le quatrième chapitre sera consacré à la présentation d’un article intitulé " A robotic ultrasound scanner for automatic vessel tracking and three-dimensional reconstruction of B-mode images" qui résume les résultats obtenus dans ce projet de maîtrise. Une discussion générale conclura ce mémoire. L’article intitulé " A 3D ultrasound imaging robotic system to detect and quantify lower limb arterial stenoses: in vivo feasibility " de Marie-Ange Janvier et al dans l’annexe 3, permettra également au lecteur de mieux comprendre notre système robotisé. Ma contribution dans cet article était l’acquisition des images mode B, la reconstruction 3D et l’analyse des résultats pour le patient sain.

title: Artificial intelligence in cardiac imaging: the future is now
abstract: Chiara Bucciarelli-Ducci, consultant cardiologist and imaging specialist at the Royal Brompton and Harefield Hospitals, London, UK, gives an overview of the current dynamics around artificial intelligence (AI) in cardiac imaging, originally presented at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Spring Summit and Cardiovascular Round Table (Figure 1). Chiara Bucciarelli-Ducci, consultant cardiologist and imaging specialist at the Royal Brompton and Harefield Hospitals, London, UK How would you characterize the present landscape regarding AI in cardiac imaging? Currently AI occupies a lot of space in healthcare generally, from use in diagnoses and patient management to data analysis and storage of clinical records. Developments in AI powered hardware and software have far-reaching consequences for every modality of imaging—cardiac included. It’s a dynamic area and many developments have come as a surprise to me. Some seem futuristic but are currently in use at hospitals in the United States and China and will be coming to Europe soon. There is also a new language which we all must learn to understand the differences between terms like machine learning and deep learning. What value can AI bring to cardiac imaging? Being able to use AI for the identification of unrecognized patterns of diseases at the preclinical stage is exciting and a potential game changer in the patient journey. It will enable personalized care, allow us to tailor that care to individual patients and refine risk assessment. On a practical level using AI to complete laborious tasks such as image segmentation will free up time, whilst also increasing precision and accuracy particularly of less experienced operators. A comprehensive review published in the European Heart Journal gives a broad overview of all the important aspects of AI in cardiovascular imaging.1 It covers everything from patient selection to AI-guided acquisition, segmentation, analysis, and integration with other clinical data. It also looks at how AI can enable personalized care and guide interventions. When you consider what AI can do across the entire cardiovascular imaging pathway, the scope is very wide. How are hardware developments enhancing imaging? We’re seeing new equipment that enables guided examination set-up, touchless patient sensing, automatic and fast Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (CMR) planning and scanning, and even remote CMR capabilities. Robot Assisted Ultrasound examination—or RAUS—was originally developed in China during the COVID 19 pandemic to serve rural communities without access to specialists.2 It uses a hub-and-spoke model with a physician sitting in a central location guiding a robot performing echocardiography on a remote patient. It’s connected through cloud computing and is already being used clinically to diagnose cardiac abnormalities. Other AI-powered hardware innovations include guided set-up systems for echocardiography and CMR, plus one-touch technology for Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) where you position the patient in the scanner, push a button, and the entire scanning protocol runs automatically. Of course, you still need a radiographer for troubleshooting, but this ‘one-click MRI’ has been in clinical use for two years at major US institutions where they've scanned over 2000 patients with no complications, good image quality and ∼30% reduction in scanning time, thus greater efficiency and throughput. Portable imaging is another exciting area St Thomas’ Hospital in London has deployed a portable MRI scanner in their emergency department—this is used for brain imaging at present. We are also seeing smaller computed tomography (CT) scanners being developed that can fit in an office or outpatient clinic setting instead of a full hospital set-up. What about software? There are some impressive deep learning algorithms that improve image quality—making images clearer and sharper even when patients move or in cases of atrial fibrillation. These algorithms can compensate for missing data through what's called accelerated CMR image reconstruction, so you get good image quality with great resolution and speed, which is the ideal combination. Other AI algorithms allow us to do deep phenotyping of the heart, particularly through T1 and T2 mapping sequences—providing another level of tissue characterization of the heart that allows us to distinguish between different diseases based on diverse magnetic properties and abnormalities in the myocardium. We're rewriting the pathophysiology of disease just by understanding these different properties and creating what are essentially new imaging biomarkers, clinically, every day. CMR fingerprinting is in the clinical validation stage and provides a literal fingerprint of the myocardium in a single acquisition that captures all the different properties of the heart. We can also now do quantitative perfusion with CMR, which is a major advance. Another exciting development on the horizon is the digital twin—a twin model of a specific patient to test different strategies and treatments to see what will work best for an individual patient. What are researchers currently saying about AI? Many of the studies that myself and my colleagues have been participating in have shown how AI can perform complex tasks much quicker than experts. It generally takes around 13 minutes for a cardiologist to interpret a CMR scan, but thanks to machine learning algorithms, AI can deliver a similar analysis in four seconds—nearly 190 times faster.3 This is more efficient, cheaper, and can cut waiting lists. We also did a study on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy where ten experts were asked to measure maximum wall thickness twice, one month apart. The results were quite humbling as they demonstrated how the machine learning tool was more consistent than the experts in assigning diagnoses of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with less variability. Why is AI integration essential in cardiovascular imaging? It offers solutions to inequality of care by making these capabilities available to more patients. Chatbot applications can enable patient interaction, education, preparation for imaging, and follow-up, as well as managing appointments and notifications. These applications can capture interactions between doctors and patients and transfer that information directly into clinical records. Requests for imaging are increasing drastically—and dealing with such a huge volume, it's impossible to deliver quality care unless we accelerate and automate these processes. What are some of the challenges ahead? As well as the ethical, social, and political challenges surrounding the use of AI, hardware and software is expensive although should be cost-effective over time. The main challenges include clinical validation and regulatory approval, training doctors on both the advantages and limitations of AI solutions, and the fact that AI and machine learning need big datasets that aren't always available. It’s also important to remember that AI augments and enhances physician skills rather than replacing them and to keep in mind that it creates significant value for stakeholders in our current value-based health system. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders in Sonographers—A Unique Perspective and a Call for Change, as Conveyed Via a Letter to the Office of the Directorate of Enforcement Programs of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. Includes a Letter Response From the Directorate of Enforcement
abstract: October 10, 2023 U.S. Department of Labor –OSHA Directorate of Enforcement Programs (DEP) 200 Constitution Avenue, N.W. Room N3119 Washington, D.C., 20210, USA Dear Sir or Madam, We would like to formally request that the Directorate of Enforcement Programs reinvestigate the status of work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) for sonographers and consider a hazard alert addressed to US hospitals and clinics, and the makers of ultrasound equipment. The rate of injury for sonographers continues to be one of the highest of all medical professions. Our personal experiences as radiologists over the last 30-plus years have allowed us to bear witness firsthand to the ongoing devastating effects of scanning-related injury in these medical professionals. Sonographers are integral members of the medical profession, who obtain diagnostic medical images of patients' abdominal, cardiac, obstetric, gynecologic, small parts, vascular, breast, and musculoskeletal anatomy. As of 2023, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates there are 84,900 diagnostic medical sonographers and 58,400 cardiovascular sonographers and technicians.1 Musculoskeletal injuries among sonographers result in significant workplace absenteeism; 1 of every 5 sonographers will experience a career-ending musculoskeletal injury.2 Occupational injuries are almost inevitable for a majority of sonographers.3 SONOGRAPHERS AND WMSDS To obtain ultrasound images, a sonographer pushes a transducer (probe) against the patient's body, as she or he examines the images on a display monitor. Optimal viewing angles for image acquisition require varied hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder positions.4 With the nonscanning hand, the sonographer makes image optimization adjustments and annotations using the control panel. When scanning obese patients, excessive force and strain combined with awkward body and hand positioning are often required to obtain diagnostic images.5 Surveys indicate that two-thirds to 90% of sonographers experience pain while they are scanning.5–8 The most common locations of WMSDs are the shoulder, neck, wrist, and hands. Common symptoms include aching, stiffness, sharp pain, weakness, tingling, and numbness. In young sonographers, early in their careers, WMSD symptoms may be temporary and diminish with rest at the end of the workday. Over time, symptoms can become unremitting, leading to permanent injury requiring medical and/or surgical intervention.2 The onset of WMSDs symptoms can occur as early as 6 months from the start of employment (15% incidence), increasing to 45% after 3 years, and as high as 72% after 10 years of employment.7 APPLIED FORCES REQUIRED WHILE SCANNING Scanning requires long periods of static shoulder abduction and outward rotation, combined with static loading of the muscles needed to push the transducer against the body wall. This results in mechanical compression of portions of the rotator cuff against the bony structures of the shoulder girdle, decreased perfusion of blood to the muscles and tendons, and microtrauma to the muscle fibers. Awkward postures, repetition, and sustained or forceful gripping are risk factors for the hand/wrist and elbow injury.9 Studies have quantified postural and muscular loads required for scanning. Trask and Village (2007) showed sonographers held the transducer with an average grip force of 4 kg (8.8 lb), with peak forces measuring around 27.6 kg (60.8 lb). Prior studies have shown that gross grasp (fist motion) greater than 4.5 kg is a risk factor for developing musculoskeletal injury at the hand and wrist.10 Dhyania et al (2017) measured the sonographer axial force applied through the probe while scanning the abdomens of volunteers with variable body mass index (BMI). The measured force varied from 1.2 N to 36.5 N (0.27 to 8.2 lb) with a mean axial force of 8.2 N (1.8 lb). The mean maximum force applied for subjects with high BMI was 25.3 N (5.7 lb), which was significantly higher than the force applied for subjects with normal BMI, which was 17.4 N (3.9 lb). The force utilized was directly related to the subject's BMI, and not to sonographer experience. Given the rapidly rising prevalence of obesity in adults and children in our society, the average forces applied by all sonographers are significant and increasing.11 Most recent demographic data (2018) reveal that 42.4% of American adults and 18.5% of American children meet the criteria for obesity.12,13 SONOGRAPHER WMSDS ARE A RECOGNIZED, PERSISTENT PROBLEM In hundreds of reviews and studies over 3 decades, there has been a broad acknowledgment of the significant problem of WMSDs in sonographers. In 1985, occupational hazards for sonographers were first reported by Craig et al, which prompted the performance of an increasing number of studies to better quantify the prevalence of work-related injuries among sonographers.14 In 1999, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, in conjunction with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, issued a paper regarding WMSDs in sonography.15 This was published after a requested National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health Hazard Evaluation at a specific medical institution.16 The paper advised methods to reduce WMSDs, which included room design and equipment recommendations, ergonomics training for the sonographer, and attention to workload scheduling by management, with consideration for a maximum number of scheduled exams for sonographers.15 In 2004, OSHA and the Society of Diagnostic Medical Sonography formed an Alliance to work collaboratively to provide organization members and others in the medical community with information, guidance, and access to ergonomic training. These organizations agreed to conclude the Alliance as of October 26, 2008.17 In 2016, The Industry Standards for the Prevention of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WRMSD) in Sonography was developed as an updated work product of a 2016 Consensus Conference involving 26 sonography-related professional organizations, accreditation bodies, and manufacturers. The collaborative effort produced a detailed resource guide designed to reduce the incidence of WMSDs among sonographers.18 In January of 2023, the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine published Practice Principles for Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders Among Ultrasound Professionals. This was another collaborative effort with several different medical specialties, all of which use ultrasound. The document reflects an expansion upon the above-mentioned 2016 Industry Standards for the Prevention of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders in Sonography (WRMSDs) and provides support guidance for quality improvement for preventing and reducing injury rates. This includes detailed guidelines on personal controls, administrative controls, workplace culture, and ergonomic strategies tailored to specific types of ultrasound exams. Scheduling recommendations include defining a minimum time allotment for different types of ultrasound exams.2 RISING DEMAND FOR ULTRASOUND EXAMS EXACERBATE WMSDS Worldwide, the number of ultrasound examinations performed has exponentially increased because ultrasound is a relatively inexpensive means of cross-sectional imaging that is noninvasive and does not use radiation.2 Technological advances in computation power, algorithms, and computer externalization of scan conversion, have resulted in enhanced image reconstruction and display, and have extended the range and utility of ultrasound studies. Sonographers can detect smaller and subtler lesions, and evaluate for previously indiscernible anatomic disorders. Unfortunately, there is a negative byproduct to these advances. The faster processing of images translates to more “efficient” use of sonographer time, with more time available for scanning and less recovery time between patients. With the ability to detect more complex disorders among complex patients, ultrasound studies are longer and more demanding. Greater use of ultrasound-guided biopsy and ablation procedures has become especially taxing, sometimes requiring hours of fixed-position scanning.3 More scanning time means greater exposure to injurious stresses and less time between patients means less time for damaged muscle fibers to repair.19 When patients are medically fragile, ultrasound imaging can be performed portably, unlike magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) imaging. This results in a steady demand for this service. Portable studies often require sonographers to scan in awkward postures due to the amount of intensive care equipment limiting room space. Therefore, portable studies further exacerbate WMSDs.3 ECONOMIC COSTS AND SONOGRAPHER SHORTAGES Challenges facing many imaging departments center around having a stable, experienced workforce. Worker injury can have an emotional impact on the individual worker and a large impact on the department's worker morale, and the quality of patient care.20 Besides the human costs of injury, there are also economic costs that have affected every ultrasound workplace. The cost of hiring temporary staff replacements is between (US) $130,000 and $166,000 per year. The estimated average cost to find, hire, and train a new sonographer is (US) $10,500. If an ultrasound examination room is unused because of worker injury, the lost revenue to the department approaches (US) $4500 per day.3 WRMDs cost employers up to $120 billion yearly in direct and indirect costs through workers' compensation or lost work time.9 Given the combined growth in imaging demand and worker shortage, ultrasound users are being asked to increase productivity. This can lead to insufficient rest periods, further increasing sonographers' exposure to the risk of injury.9 Unfortunately, despite the best efforts of ultrasound education programs to keep up with demand, there is a shortage of ultrasound technicians. Currently, there are 143,400 medical and cardiovascular sonographers and technicians. US. employment demand for these technicians is projected to grow 11% from 2023 to 2033, much faster than the average for all occupations.21 SOLUTIONS THAT MAY MITIGATE THIS CRISIS Develop Assistive Technology Current mitigation strategies have failed. Many of the repeatedly proposed or reiterated solutions to reduce WMSDs fail to address the inherent problems with how ultrasound technology is designed and used. Manufacturer ergonomic improvements in the control panel design, transducer technology, AI-supported processing of images to reduce scan times, and smart device compatibility are laudable. However, in the end, these are cosmetic and do not address the main cause of musculoskeletal injury. As currently performed, ultrasound scanning requires repetitive and awkward movements and positions. These are essentially unavoidable for the sonographer, as long as the sonographer needs to be connected to the patient and the equipment simultaneously.4 An exception is the automated breast ultrasound machine. This machine's transducer moves automatically over the breast. This takes the sonographer's hand out of direct imaging and has been commercially available now for several years (although sonographer injuries were not the primary impetus for development). This type of equipment has been, thus far, applied only to breast imaging, due to the opportunities afforded by the specific anatomy involved. However, this equipment does have some imaging trade-offs.22 It has been adopted in some practices, but traditional hand-held ultrasound scanning remains the norm for breast imaging in the majority of practices in the US. Wireless transducers have been recently developed by manufacturers that would remove cord drag but do not alleviate aforementioned grip and pushing forces required.3 Development of new assistive technology to significantly off-load the sonographer forces needed to obtain medical images would be the most effective means of reducing WMSDs. One manufacturer has recently developed a ‘deep abdominal transducer,’ which allows for reduced required axial force to visualize the anatomy at greater depths.23 This is a step in the right direction. There has been some research by academic labs into assistive ergonomic design solutions, such as special gloves, splints, and 2-handle transducers. Research into robotic ultrasound has been conducted for remote or physical distance scanning during Covid3 and for reducing sonographer-required forces at the bedside.24 That said, no experimental system has yet been able to replicate the precise range of motion and level of transducer control by the sonographer's hand. A recent comprehensive review of past design research efforts to reduce sonographer WMSDs has indicated potential avenues that could be pursued.3 Clearly, an industry-wide response is needed. We are confident that a solution can be found for this crisis. In the field of surgery, for example, resources were spent to develop revolutionary robot-assisted surgery systems, which can mimic the functionality of the human wrist and hand movements allowing surgeons to perform complex movements with precision.25 These devices have been made to scale, and between 2012 and 2022, the proportion of surgical procedures in the US performed using robotic technology rose from 0% to 22%.26 Besides this technology allowing more complex operations to be less invasive, there are also ergonomic benefits to the surgeons.27 The failure to effectively address ergonomic injuries with ultrasound scanning likely reflects the lack of economic impetus. As long as sonographers are considered expendable, the human cost has not been a compelling reason to innovate. Ultrasound equipment manufacturers have not seen the need to address this crisis yet. Investment in redesign and development would be needed to alter the current standard machine/human interface design. Despite the worker injury entailed with using standard ultrasound equipment, ultrasound equipment sales continue to show robust growth. With North America as the leading market, global ultrasound equipment market size is estimated at $9.86 billion in 2024. It is projected to grow with a compound annual growth rate of 8.4% from 2025 to 2034 to a market size worth $22.09 billion by 2034.28 Manufacturers of ultrasound equipment must be made to assume some responsibility for the ergonomic crisis. Measure and Limit Injury Risk Exposure A comprehensive survey study, performed in China, demonstrated that scanning hours per day, number of patients per day, and years of experience were positively associated with the occurrence and frequency of experiencing WMSDs among sonographers. Their study revealed that it is essential to reduce the number of scanning hours and patients per day, schedule regular rest breaks and microbreaks during the work day, and encourage the performance of regular physical activity during leisure time.29 Virtually all reviews on ways to reduce WMSDs of sonographers recommend reducing scan time and increasing rest breaks. Roll et al (2014) reported that the average number of examinations performed per day by each sonographer was between 9 and 11.30 Research reports that sonographers performing more than 100 studies per month are at risk for developing musculoskeletal disorders.31 If sonographers scan an average of 10 patients per day, then over a month, excluding weekends and on-call periods, sonographers would scan approximately 230 patients, equivalent to more than twice the safe amount.4 In a recent publication, the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine recommended a minimum time allotment for common types of ultrasound exams with the intent to reduce the pace of work.2 It is known that sonographers, under time pressure, often take shortcuts without respect for their own safety, choosing not to readjust rooms or equipment for optimal ergonomic positioning.4 Overuse of medical imaging has been a well-known concern for years, and despite campaigns to educate and reduce referrals, there has been continued growth in CT, MRI, and ultrasound imaging.32 Ultrasound is often seen as a risk-free alternative to CT and MRI because it involves no radiation and patients tolerate the exam fairly well. However, rarely are the risks to the sonographer considered. Decreasing the availability of ultrasound exams will likely increase the retention of sonographers lost through injury or burnout. Some radiology departments, including ours, have decreased the availability of nighttime ultrasound exams to reduce sonographer sleep deprivation and improve retention. Attempting to reduce the number of daytime ultrasound exams, however, is more challenging in the face of annual growth in demand and unlikely to be embraced by hospitals and clinics. Recognizing that ultrasound scanning is inherently hazardous, and monitoring sonographer musculoskeletal stress exposure would allow standards and limits to be instituted. When sonographers reach a predefined risk limit, an enforced break could be mandated.3 CONCLUSIONS Sadly, sonographers are medical professionals who often sacrifice their well-being to contribute to the well-being of others. Losing experienced, qualified sonographers to WMSDs is a price the health industry should not be willing to pay.19 Mitigation strategies over the last 30-plus years have been failures. A fundamental change in scanning is past due. The associated human and economic costs are too significant. Another 30 years of repetitive articles reporting what everyone in the industry already knows is unacceptable. We strongly recommend DEP reinvestigate this persistent rate of WMSDs among sonographers. Based on the General Duty Clause, Section 5(a)(1) of the OSH Act, DEP could conduct new investigations into practices and issue citations; develop occupational exposure standards for sonography, and issue a nationwide hazard alert addressed to US hospitals and clinics, and ultrasound equipment manufacturers. A nationwide goal to reduce WMSDs among sonographers by a defined amount by a defined date should be set. Hospitals and clinics would likely have to choose to reduce sonographer scanning time (while concurrently using ‘best available’ ergonomic practices) until assistive technology becomes available. Once an economic cost becomes as urgent as the human cost, hospitals and clinics would likely pressure manufacturers to make design improvements. Manufacturers need to put resources into developing effective, scalable technology that significantly offloads the forces borne by the sonographers performing their daily work. Sincerely, Emily Lewis, MD, and Mark Kliewer, MD, Professor Emeriti Dept. of Radiology, University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health, Madison, Wisconsin

title: The Use of Remote Presence Robotic Tele-Presentation in Rural and Remote Canada: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Objective: One potential solution to limited health care in rural and remote regions is remote presence robotic tele-presentation to allow health care providers to care for patients in their home community via a robotic interface. We synthesized evidence regarding the use of remote presence robotic tele-presentation in rural and/or remote Canadian health settings. Methods: Medline, PubMed, and Embase were searched up to August 2023. Remote presence robotic tele-presentation refers to any robotic device used for the purpose of presenting and/or collecting patient information. Primary research was included if the patient was located in remote and/or rural Canada, featured remote presence robotic tele-presentation, and assessed patient, family, or clinician satisfaction, patient transport to nearby regional or urban center, health care costs, clinical outcomes, infrastructure outcomes, adverse events, or telementoring. Results: Six studies were included. Patients, nurses, and physicians all reported high levels of satisfaction when using the remote presence robotic tele-presentation. Fifty to sixty-three percent of patients were managed in their home community and did not require transfer to another center. Remote presence robotic sonography resulted in adequate imaging in 81% of first trimester ultrasound limited exams but was less useful for second trimester complete obstetric ultrasounds (20% adequate imaging). Two of eight laparoscopic colorectal surgeries had to be converted to open surgeries. Telerobotic ultrasound clinics resulted in a diagnosis in 70% of cases. Conclusions: Evidence suggests remote presence robotic tele-presentation is a safe and cost-effective approach to providing care in distant communities and can prevent some transfers and evacuations to tertiary hospitals.

title: 3D Reconstruction of the Kidney and Lesions from 2D Ultrasound Images Using Robotic Ultrasound Diagnostic System.
abstract: This study presents an innovative approach based on the Robotic Ultrasound Diagnostic System (RUDS) for 3D reconstruction of organs and lesions from sequential 2D ultrasound slices. The RUDS comprises four main components: the Organ Tracking Robot (OTR) for multi-angle probe scanning, the Phantom Posture Robot (PPR) for optimizing probe contact with the abdomen, the Robotic Bed (RB), and the Robotic Supporting Arm (RSA). Leveraging the high flexibility and degrees of freedom in probe manipulation, the OTR controls probe rotation to capture and process continuous 2D slices, enabling precise 3D reconstruction of the kidney and associated lesions. By adjusting scanning speed and contact angles and analyzing spatial relationships within the 3D models, RUDS demonstrates superior accuracy in 3D modeling, supporting preoperative planning in High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) and minimizing risks to non-tumor tissue.Clinical Relevance- This enables precise 3D reconstruction of kidneys and lesions from 2D ultrasound images, supporting HIFU planning and enhancing ultrasound diagnostic accuracy.

title: How robotic platforms have expanded the boundaries of minimally invasive surgery: a narrative review.
abstract: Robotic surgery has evolved from a technological adjunct into a major platform for extending the reach of minimally invasive surgery (MIS). In contrast to conventional laparoscopy, robotic systems offer three-dimensional magnified visualization, wristed instrumentation, tremor filtration, improved ergonomics, and greater precision in narrow anatomical spaces. These features have supported wider adoption of technically demanding minimally invasive procedures that are difficult to reproduce consistently with straight-stick laparoscopy alone. This narrative review examines how robotic platforms have expanded MIS across urology, gynecology, colorectal surgery, thoracic surgery, and upper gastrointestinal surgery. Current evidence suggests that robotic surgery often reduces conversion to open surgery, blood loss, and length of hospital stay in complex procedures, although operative time is frequently longer and superiority over laparoscopy is not universal. The review also discusses the barriers that continue to limit broader expansion, including capital and maintenance costs, learning curves, absent or limited haptic feedback, unequal access, and heterogeneity in the evidence base. Finally, it considers emerging directions, including artificial intelligence, image guidance, robotic ultrasound integration, and haptic innovation. Robotic surgery should therefore be understood not as a wholesale replacement for laparoscopy, but as a selective enabler of advanced MIS when anatomical and technical constraints expose the limitations of conventional approaches.

title: Standardizing Virtual Healthcare Deployment: Insights From the Implementation of Telerobotic Ultrasound to Bridge Healthcare Inequities in Rural and Remote Communities Across Canada.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the integration of virtual care into healthcare systems, presenting a unique opportunity to address healthcare inequities in rural and remote communities, particularly those that are Indigenous. This commentary outlines critical steps and best practices for deploying virtual care in underserved regions, drawing on over a decade of experience in Saskatchewan. Key recommendations include creating detailed community profiles, assessing digital literacy, and using standardized readiness tools to evaluate infrastructure and clinical needs. A weighted prioritization framework ensures efficient resource allocation, while partnerships with Indigenous-led institutions, such as SIIT, equip local healthcare assistants to support virtual care delivery. Examples from successful telerobotic ultrasonography deployments in the rural and remote communities of Saskatchewan highlight the potential of virtual care to improve healthcare access, outcomes, and sustainability. By tailoring interventions to community-specific contexts and involving local stakeholders, virtual care can bridge health disparities and serve as a replicable model for similar settings worldwide.

title: 3D Reconstruction and Visualization of Tissue Structure and Elasticity Using Robot-Assisted Ultrasound and Shear Wave Elastography Imaging<sup/>.
abstract: Tissue elasticity is a critical component of medical diagnostics, serving as a key indicator for tumor detection and pain assessment. Moreover, understanding tissue stiffness is essential for the precise fitting of prostheses. Conventional imaging techniques such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Computed Tomography (CT), besides being costly, fall short in accurately measuring tissue stiffness, highlighting the need of innovative approaches like shear wave elastography (SWE). The three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction for SWE images has the potential to provide a simplified visual interpretation of tissue properties. However, the acquisition of high-quality, meaningful images and an accurate 3D reconstruction necessitates the precise positioning of the transducer and the controlled application of pressure. Robotic assistance offers a solution to these challenges by ensuring repeatability and enabling detailed 3D imaging, thereby further improving the understanding of tissue structure. Building up on our prior work with conventional ultrasound (US), this study advances our methodology by adding SWE in an experiment conducted on a multi-layered silicone phantom. This not only provides an overview of the phantom's structure but also illustrates the stiffness distribution across the phantom. Additionally, the study includes a comparison with clinical CT imaging, demonstrating the benefits of 3D US and SWE. Overall, this research demonstrates the viability of incorporating SWE into robot-assisted systems and the reconstruction of 3D SWE data. These findings lay the foundation for future advancements in tissue characterization.Clinical Relevance- Precise 3D visualization of tissue structure and elasticity improves diagnostic accuracy for conditions such as tumors and chronic diseases. In addition, this technique has the potential to enhance the customization of prostheses, thereby improving patient quality of life.

title: 3D Image Reconstruction Using Force-Controlled Robot-Assisted Ultrasound Scanning.
abstract: Ultrasound (US) is a valuable tool for imaging anatomical structures and tissue characteristics due to its noninvasive nature, real-time imaging capabilities, and wide accessibility. Accurate positioning and defined application of pressure with the US probe play a significant role in US imaging. Robot-assisted US imaging can address these issues and additionally facilitate three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of US images, providing a deeper understanding of tissue structures. Therefore, this paper focuses on the fundamental step of acquiring US images and reconstructing US volumes through the integration of a US system with a collaborative robot. The paper demonstrates that force-controlled images can be acquired with high accuracy and that 3D images can be accurately reconstructed to closely match real-world measurements. The utilization of the DICOM standard enhances the performance of robot-assisted 3D reconstruction in this preliminary phase by enabling image extraction and pose data embedding. Furthermore, tissue elasticity is a critical factor in various medical applications, and accurate measurement of tissue stiffness is essential for prosthesis fitting, requiring innovative approaches such as shear wave elastography (SWE) in addition to conventional US imaging. Therefore, this paper also lays the groundwork for future efforts in 3D reconstruction of SWE images with the aim of refining tissue modeling for prosthetic fitting and diagnostics.

title: What Ranges of Probe Pressure Are Applied During Ultrasound Examinations? A Systematic Review.
abstract:
The number of US exams has nearly doubled in the last ten years. Many researchers point out the probe pressure force influence on image quality and other aspects of examination. This review aims to identify the range of applied probe pressure during US examinations and gather information on probe compression force values during various US examinations (examination types, body regions, etc.).

Methods

A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted using IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed/MEDLINE. Studies with quantitative data on probe pressure during US by human operators or RUSs (robotic ultrasound systems) were included.

Results

From the 26 included studies, force ranges varied up to 34.5 N for abdominal exams. Robotic systems applied slightly higher maximum forces (34.5 N) than human operators (30 N). Most studies reported positive impacts of force monitoring on image quality and diagnostic precision, with no adverse effects on patient comfort.

Conclusions

The evidence collectively emphasizes the critical role of applied pressure in US. The nonuniformity of the reviewed studies does not allow for identifying a clearly defined range of probe pressure forces or force monitoring protocols. Integrating RUS and standardized pressure protocols could improve diagnostic consistency and accuracy.

title: Feasibility of Robot-Assisted Ultrasound Imaging with Force Feedback for Assessment of Thyroid Diseases.
abstract: Medical ultrasound is extensively used to define tissue textures and to characterize lesions, and it is the modality of choice for detection and follow-up assessment of thyroid diseases. Classical medical ultrasound procedures are performed manually by an occupational operator with a hand-held ultrasound probe. These procedures require high physical and cognitive burden and yield clinical results that are highly operator-dependent, therefore frequently diminishing trust in ultrasound imaging data accuracy in repetitive assessment. A robotic ultrasound procedure, on the other hand, is an emerging paradigm integrating a robotic arm with an ultrasound probe. It achieves an automated or semi-automated ultrasound scanning by controlling the scanning trajectory, region of interest, and the contact force. Therefore, the scanning becomes more informative and comparable in subsequent examinations over a long-time span. In this work, we present a technique for allowing operators to reproduce reliably comparable ultrasound images with the combination of predefined trajectory execution and real-time force feedback control. The platform utilized features a 7-axis robotic arm capable of 6-DoF force-torque sensing and a linear-array ultrasound probe. The measured forces and torques affecting the probe are used to adaptively modify the predefined trajectory during autonomously performed examinations and probe-phantom interaction force accuracy is evaluated. In parallel, by processing and combining ultrasound B-Mode images with probe spatial information, structural features can be extracted from the scanning volume through a 3D scan. The validation was performed on a tissue-mimicking phantom containing thyroid features, and we successfully demonstrated high image registration accuracy between multiple trials.

title: Ultrasound-guided robotic surgical procedures: a systematic review.
abstract:
Introduction

Ultrasound has been nicknamed "the surgeon's stethoscope". The advantages of laparoscopic ultrasound beyond a substitute for the sense of touch are considerable, especially for robotic surgery. Being able to see through parenchyma and into vascular structures enables to avoid unnecessary dissection by providing a thorough assessment at every stage without the need for contrast media or ionising radiation. The limitations of restricted angulation and access within the abdominal cavity during laparoscopy can be overcome by robotic handling of miniaturised ultrasound probes and the use of various and specific frequencies will meet tissue- and organ-specific characteristics. The aim of this systematic review was to assess the reported applications of intraoperative ultrasound-guided robotic surgery and to outline future perspectives.

Methods

The study adhered to the PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to October 2023. Manuscripts reporting data on ultrasound-guided robotic procedures were included in the qualitative analysis.

Results

20 studies met the inclusion criteria. The majority (53%) were related to the field of general surgery during liver, pancreas, spleen, gallbladder/bile duct, vascular and rectal surgery. This was followed by other fields of oncological surgery (42%) including urology, lung surgery, and retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy for metastases. Among the studies, ten (53%) focused on locating tumoral lesions and defining resection margins, four (15%) were designed to test the feasibility of robotic ultrasound-guided surgery, while two (10.5%) aimed to compare robotic and laparoscopic ultrasound probes. Additionally two studies (10.5%) evaluated the robotic drop-in probe one (5%) assessed the hepatic tissue consistency and another one (5%) aimed to visualize the blood flow in the splenic artery.

Conclusion

The advantages of robotic instrumentation, including ergonomics, dexterity, and precision of movements, are of relevance for robotic intraoperative ultrasound (RIOUS). The present systematic review demonstrates the virtue of RIOUS to support surgeons and potentially reduce minimally invasive procedure times.

title: Optimizing Configurations for 7-DoF Robotic Ultrasound Guidance in Radiotherapy of the Prostate.
abstract: Robotic ultrasound guidance is promising for tracking of organ motion during radiotherapy treatments, but the radio-opaque robot and probe interfere with beam delivery. The effect on treatment plan quality can be mitigated by the use of a robot arm with kinematic redundancy, such that the robot is able to elude delivered beams during treatment by changing its configuration. However, these changes require robot motion close to the patient, lead to an increased treatment time, and require coordination with the beam delivery. We propose an optimization workflow which integrates the problem of selecting suitable robot configurations into a linear-programming-based workflow for treatment plan optimization. Starting with a large set of candidate configurations, a minimal subset is determined which provides equivalent plan quality. Our results show that, typically, six configurations are sufficient for this purpose. Furthermore, we show that optimal configurations can be reused for dose planning of subsequent patients.

title: Autonomous Scanning Target Localization for Robotic Lung Ultrasound Imaging.
abstract: Under the ceaseless global COVID-19 pandemic, lung ultrasound (LUS) is the emerging way for effective diagnosis and severeness evaluation of respiratory diseases. However, close physical contact is unavoidable in conventional clinical ultrasound, increasing the infection risk for health-care workers. Hence, a scanning approach involving minimal physical contact between an operator and a patient is vital to maximize the safety of clinical ultrasound procedures. A robotic ultrasound platform can satisfy this need by remotely manipulating the ultrasound probe with a robotic arm. This paper proposes a robotic LUS system that incorporates the automatic identification and execution of the ultrasound probe placement pose without manual input. An RGB-D camera is utilized to recognize the scanning targets on the patient through a learning-based human pose estimation algorithm and solve for the landing pose to attach the probe vertically to the tissue surface; A position/force controller is designed to handle intraoperative probe pose adjustment for maintaining the contact force. We evaluated the scanning area localization accuracy, motion execution accuracy, and ultrasound image acquisition capability using an upper torso mannequin and a realistic lung ultrasound phantom with healthy and COVID-19-infected lung anatomy. Results demonstrated the overall scanning target localization accuracy of 19.67 ± 4.92 mm and the probe landing pose estimation accuracy of 6.92 ± 2.75 mm in translation, 10.35 ± 2.97 deg in rotation. The contact force-controlled robotic scanning allowed the successful ultrasound image collection, capturing pathological landmarks.

title: Basic performance of domestic surgical robot and the safety and effectiveness of integrated energy equipment.
abstract:
Objectives

Surgical robot system has broken the limitation of traditional surgery and shown excellent performance in surgery, and has been widely used in minimally invasive treatment in most areas of surgery. This study aims to verify the basic performance of the domestic surgical robot system and the safety and effectiveness of the integrated bipolar electrocoagulation and ultrasonic knife.

Methods

The basic performance of the domestic surgical robot system was evaluated by completing the square knot and surgical knot, vertical and horizontal perforation and right ring perforation and suture, as well as picking up beans. Compared with laparoscopy, the safety and effectiveness of the domestic surgical robot after integrated interconnection bipolar electrocoagulation and ultrasonic scalpel were evaluated by detecting the vascular closure performance and the degree of histopathological damage in animals.

Results

Compared with freehand knotting, domestic robot knotting speed and circumference were slightly worse, but better than laparoscopic knotting. There was no statistical significance in the tension difference of the surgical knots among the 3 methods (P>0.05), but the tension of the square knots made by the freehand and the domestic surgical robot was greater than that of the laparoscopy (P<0.05). The space required for both the left and right forceps heads of knots was smaller than that of laparoscopy (P<0.001), which successfully completed the 4 quadrant suture tasks, and the time of picking up beans was significantly less than that of laparoscopy (P<0.05). There was no significant difference in the temperature of the liver tissue after the bipolar electrocoagulation between the interconnected domestic surgical robot and the laparoscopy (P>0.05), and the acute thermal injury was observed under the light microscope. The temperature of the liver tissue treated by the domestic robotic ultrasound knife was higher than that of the laparoscopic ultrasound knife (P<0.05).

Conclusions

Domestic surgical robots are obviously superior to laparoscopy in suturing, knotting, and moving objects, and domestic surgical robots' interconnect bipolar electrocoagulation and ultrasonic knife have achieved success in animal experiments, and hemostasis is considered to be safe and effective.
