title: Obstetric issues admixed with some gynecology
abstract: Copenhagen and the 38th NFOG congress are just around the corner, as always a major event to look forward to among obstetricians and gynecologists in the Nordic countries. The NFOG congress addresses needs of both the generalist and the sub-specialist, offering a broad range of lectures and workshops that should provide good professional updating. It is not so large as some other international conferences where one may be hard pressed to decide which of the multitude of concurrent sessions to select. The EBCOG congresses are in some ways similar, but within Europe it would be highly desirable to have that Pan-European meeting alternating in years with the more regional venues like NFOG. Congresses such as these, and more focused sub-speciality meetings, provide major means of keeping abreast with new developments and have long been recognized as part of continuing professional education. Copenhagen in the middle of June is sure to be both professionally and socially good. This largely obstetrical issue commences with the first of two overview articles by Minna Tikkanen from Helsinki, Finland (pp. 732–740) on placental abruption. This is a subject where new understanding and information has been added in recent years, but many questions, not least with regard to etiology, prediction and prevention, remain. Randomized or prospective studies in this field are hardly applicable. Audit and observational studies must provide the data needed. The consequences are still as serious as they have always been for the baby, while we have, at least in high- and middle-income countries, managed to do better in saving the mothers from serious injury and death. For this topic, an overview with search for best evidence as a basis is of much value, as done in this well written article. The same is true for the other overview in this month's issue, on pre-malignant disorders in the vulval skin by Annelinde Terlou and colleagues in Amsterdam and Rotterdam in The Netherlands (pp. 741–748). This provides the reader with an excellent update, not least on etiology and the relation of these lesions to human papilloma viruses. For practising clinicians and researchers careful reading should be rewarding alike, also with a view to understand the basis for rational therapy which can be offered to women with these distressing conditions. On pages 757–761 Hiroshi Miura and colleagues from Akita in Japan provide interesting data on time-related changes of the cervix as a means of predicting onset of term labor. The practicability of using ultrasound to assess the cervix rather than digital examination and the Bishop score is questionable, but it may be the applicability of this type of information to preterm labor that matters. That needs better study. Transvaginal ultrasound has been a revolution in relation to management of threatened preterm delivery and cervical incompetence, but it may not be universally realized that cervical size and length can vary considerably between women and over time in pregnancy. The cervix is in spite of its sphincter-like function an organ undergoing dynamic change as pregnancy progresses. Using a universal cut-off value for all women may not be the optimal approach. The large study on indirect causes of maternal mortality from the Netherlands (Joke Schutte and colleagues from several Dutch centers, pp. 762–768) is a reminder of the serious consequences associated with childbirth at a more advanced age, in part through assisted reproduction techniques. It also calls attention to the increased vulnerability of immigrant women, who form an increasing proportion of delivering women in northwestern Europe. Services may not be equipped to meet the added demands that this entails. Throughout Europe and in many other countries around the world, there are news of dramatic cuts in public expenditure. That this will affect health services is inevitable and it is becoming imperative to firstly take care not to create problems and high cost for society by offering assisted reproduction to women who face such added risks and secondly to reconsider the way resources are allocated, in order to protect vulnerable groups better. Saving by reducing manpower is a tempting first solution by politicians and in some countries cuts in trainee posts are being seen. That is short-sighted and serious given the central role that obstetrics and gynecology has in relation to reproductive health. A related article is also provided by Per Bergsjö and colleagues from Oslo and Bergen in Norway and Moshi in Tanzania on pp. 789–793, showing that reporting issues matter in relation to maternal mortality. New information in the Lancet in April that maternal mortality may be on the decline in the world and that half of it is now confined to a few low income countries in Asia and Africa, is encouraging news (1, 2), but is all of it reliable? That no reduction was seen in some high income countries, including some of the Nordic countries, is despite low actual numbers a cause for concern (2), perhaps related to the indirect causes for maternal calamities referred to above. At the same time it is sobering to note the finding of Britt-Ingjerd Nesheim and colleagues in Oslo, Norway (pp. 813–816) that so-called low-risk units with facilities for operative delivery do not lead to lower cesarean section rates. This necessitates re-evaluation of policies with regard to centralization and decentralization of maternity services in high-income countries. Low-risk units have their justifications as pointed out in this article, but how should they be constructed, who should be selected for delivery there and how? The short report on pp. 835–839 by Jan Persson and colleagues from Lund, Sweden, is a rather long one. This is on purpose to allow proper publication of an article that has points of interest both to pathology mechanism and the usefulness of modern robotic surgery, a rapidly evolving field in gynecology. The considerations that come into consideration for managing and minimizing the risks for intra-operative bleeding and dissection of tissues are worth noting. We found the French article on the effects of Google on breastfeeding rates among a Chinese subpopulation in Paris after the melamine milk scandal highly interesting (Jeremy Seror and colleagues, pp. 823–827). We even decided to publish Chinese characters (Table 2, p. 825), may be for the first time in this journal. Early intervention with weight-control programs for obese women may be beneficial (pp. 840–843). Active compared to expectant management after PPROM at 34–36 weeks has advantages with regard to development of infection, but is offset by more neonatal problems (pp. 776–781).

abstract: Organ preservation after total neoadjuvant therapy in high risk locally advanced rectal cancer: A single tertiary care cancer centre experience Navya Virginia, Deepak Damodaran MVR CCRI, Kozhikode, Kerala, India Background: Total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) for high risk locally advanced rectal cancers has evolved through RAPIDO, OPRA, CAO/ARO/AIO 12 trials. With pCR rates exceeding 25% following neoadjuvant therapy, a “Watch and wait” (W&W) strategy was first described by Habr Gama et al in 2004 involving documentation of cCR followed by stringent locoregional surveillance. OnCoRe project (2016) showed that >60% of watch and wait patients could avoid major surgery and 25% could avoid stoma at 3 years, all without oncological compromise. Materials and Methods: Retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database of cases of TNT was done from May 2020 to September 2023. Our protocol for TNT in high risk locally advanced mid and distal rectal cancer was SCRT followed by 9 cycles FOLFOX or 6 cycles CAPEOX. All underwent an interim MRI and clinical examination at 10th week, if suggestive of iCR or progression, the patient would undergo TME surgery and if cCR or nCR would complete chemotherapy. On completion of TNT, clinical examination and MRI is done and cases are triaged to W&W for cCR, TAE for nCR and TME for iCR. Surveillance is done with clinical examination every month for the first 6 months,2 monthly for next 6 months and 3 monthly for next year and MRI with rectoscopy at 3rd,6th,12th,18th and 24th month. During surveillance, for local regrowth patients would undergo TAE/ TME surgery. Results: 85 cases of TNT were analysed; mean age was 57 (31 73 years) with a median follow up of 18 months (1 to 36 months). 42 cases had cCR. 5 cases had nCR and underwent TAE. Therefore 47 cases had organ preservation and were kept in W&W strategy, of which 10 had TME after local regrowth. There were 30 cases of iCR and had TME. 6 patients with iCR defaulted post chemotherapy and 2 had disease progression at laparotomy. Organ preservation rate following TNT was 55%. Chemo induced toxicity was observed in 5 cases requiring drug omission/ dose reduction. Conclusion: Organ Preservation by W & W strategy is a feasible approach in carefully selected patients with good response following TNT. Patient compliance to strict surveillance is mandatory and timely surgical intervention is needed for local recurrence. Seven year experience of minimally invasive lateral pelvic lymph node dissection (LPND) in rectal cancers and comparison of laparoscopic and robotic surgery Tejas Vispute, Nishant Yadav, Nivedita, Yogesh Bansod, Sanjay Singh, Ankit Sharma, Mufaddal Kazi, Ashwin Desouza, Avanish Saklani Tata Memorial Center, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India Introduction: Treatment of rectal cancer is complex involving multidisciplinary approach. Total mesorectal excision is mainstay of surgical treatment along with lateral pelvic lymph node dissection in selected cases. Minimally invasive lateral pelvic lymph node dissection for rectal cancer in technically challenging procedure with definite learning curve. This study compares surgical outcomes following lateral pelvic lymph node dissection using Robotic DaVinci Xi platform (RLPND) vs laparoscopy platform (LLPND). Methods: It is a retrospective study from prospectively maintained database from Aug 2015 to July 2023. Surgical outcomes were compared using appropriate statistical methods in SPSS? version 25. Some studies have shown advantage of robotic platform with better nodal yield along with ease operation. Results: From August 2015 to Sept 2023, we operated 182 cases of LPLND. 146 were laparoscopic and 35 robotic. 26 PLNDs were done for total pelvic exenteration (1 robotic and 25 laparoscopic). 37% underwent APR, followed by 18% LAR an 15% pelvic exenteration, 14% underwent ISR Mean age was 46 years and mean BMI was 23.3. Mean distance from anal verge was 3.3 cm. Median blood loss was 150 ml which was similar in both groups. 35% underwent Left and right PLND each and 30% had bilateral PLND. Mean hospital stay was 9.5 days in whole cohort. 87% were adenocarcinoma of rectum followed by melanoma 8% and 5% cases were of other histology like NET, GIST, SCC. 42% were pathologically N0 followed by 36% N1 and 15% N2 in whole group. 34% were pN1 in laparoscopy group and 45% in robotic. 16.6% were N2 in lap group and 11% in robotic group. 56% were pN+ in lap group and 57% in robotic group. CRM positivity for primary was 3.7% (5 cases) in lap group and 5.7% (2 cases) in robotic. PLN + were in 30% in lap group and 23% in robotic. Average nodal yield was 8.3 nodes in entire cohort. 8.5 nodes in lap group and 7.7 in robotic group. Pelvic collection was seen in 12% after LLPND and 18% after RLPND (P = 0.02). Average total positive nodes in laparoscopic was 0.57 and 0.5 in robotic with no statistical difference. Conclusion: If performed in high volume laparoscopy center, laparoscopy and robotic is equal in terms of surgical and oncological outcomes for lateral pelvic lymph node dissection in rectal cancer. CRS with HIPEC in colorectal peritoneal metastasis: A clinical retrospective observational study from a tertiary cancer care centre Divyam Goel, M. D. Ray, Ravi Venugopal All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, India Background: NCCN guidelines state that complete cytoreductive surgery (CRS) and/or intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) can be considered in experienced centers for select patients with limited peritoneal metastases, for whom CC 0 resection can be achieved. While a mutlicentre RCT – PRODIGE 7 – showed CRS with HIPEC was associated with increased postoperative morbidity without significant survival benefit. We present a single institutional experience of 53 patients of colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastasis, who underwent CRS with HIPEC at our centre, in terms of perioperative outcomes and survival benefit. Methods: We did retrospective analysis of patients with colorectal peritoneal metastatic (CRC PM) disease registered under peritoneal surface malignancy (PSM) clinic who underwent CRS with HIPEC between the period of 2014 and 2020. Patients with synchronous peritoneal disease were selected. Patients with extraperitoneal disease were excluded from the study. Selected patients were retrospectively analysed for perioperative morbidity, mortality and survival outcomes. Results: A total number of 53 patients were found to have synchronous CRC PM and underwent CRS with HIPEC during this study period. All patients were discussed by multidisciplinary team and were planned to receive perioperative chemotherapy. 10 patients (18.8%) received chemotherapy prior to surgery. 43 patients (81.2%) were operated upfront and received post-operative adjuvant chemotherapy. Average PCI was 7.7 and rate of optimal CRS was 96.2%. All patients received intraperitoneal mitomycin at 42? C for 60 -90 minutes. 2 patients (3.8%) had severe postoperative morbidity. There was no treatment related mortality. At median follow up period of 34 months, 3 year, 5 year overall survival (OS) and peritoneal recurrence free survival (pRFS) are 78.5%, 41.6% and 27.7%, 16.6% respectively. Median OS and pRFS are 38.8 months and 23 months respectively. Conclusion: Results of our study indicate that in CRC PM disease with low PCI (<10), CRS with HIPEC is a feasible procedure with acceptable perioperative outcomes, OS and pRFS. A protocol based multidisciplinary team approach, optimal patient selection, and surgical expertise is essential for achievement of optimal outcomes. These encouraging results support the need for prospectively designed study to clearly define the role of CRS with HIPEC in CRC PM Disease. title: Complete canal loss after penile inversion vaginoplasty: a call for surgical rethink
abstract: Penile inversion vaginoplasty (PIV) remains the gold standard for gender-affirming genital reconstruction in transgender women. PIV involves a technically complex dissection between the rectum and urinary structures within Denonvilliers’ fascia. The neovaginal canal is typically lined with penile and scrotal skin, and sometimes peritoneum. As epithelial tissues have a propensity to adhere, lifelong dilation is necessary to maintain patency. Vaginal stenosis following PIV can range from mild canal shortening to complete canal loss, although the timing of this remains unclear.1 Vaginal stenosis is common, though definitions vary widely. We aim to distinguish vaginal stenosis, which is typically managed with operative dilation, pelvic floor physical therapy, or Z-plasty, from complete canal loss, which necessitates re-creation of the entire vaginal canal. The literature around complications from PIV rarely distinguishes complete canal loss from vaginal stenosis. A better understanding of when and why complete canal loss occurs may aid in identifying at-risk patients and improving selection, surveillance, and intervention strategies. We present the immediate and delayed incidence of complete canal loss and its primary contributing factor. We retrospectively reviewed all primary PIV cases by a high-volume surgeon (GYN) from January 2018 to March 2025. After IRB approval, we collected demographic, surgical, and follow-up data from the medical record (see Supplementary Methods section). All patients were seen 1 week postoperatively and several times thereafter during the first few months. Canal depth was assessed at each follow-up visit based on self-reported dilator size and depth of insertion, verified by speculum examination. Complete canal compromise was defined as a blind-ending divot at the introitus and an inability to insert a speculum. All outcomes within the study were measured by the same surgeon (GYN). Demographic and surgical characteristics were extracted based on clinical relevance and feasibility. Time-to-event analysis was used to visualize the cumulative incidence of canal compromise. Patients with rectal injury or fistulae (n = 3) were excluded. Patients were censored at the time of last known follow-up. We compared the predictor variables listed between those with and without canal compromise. We used t-tests and Mann–Whitney U-tests for continuous data, and chi-squared tests for categorical variables. All P-values <.05 were considered statistically significant. We report the primary contributing factor for each case of complete canal loss, as identified by the primary surgeon (GYN). To minimize the risk of identifying individual patients, contributing factors are described in general terms. During the study period, 114 PIV were performed. The median age at the time of surgery was 32 (IQR 26-47), and the median years on hormone therapy prior to surgery was 5 (3-7). The majority of surgeries were done robotic-assisted (n = 106, 93%), and of those, 84 (79%) had a peritoneal flap to augment the canal. The median follow-up time was 10 months (IQR 3-20). The median depth of the vaginal canal among those without complete canal loss was 14 cm (IQR 13-15). In univariate analysis, none of the variables collected were significantly associated with complete canal loss (Table S1). Figure S1 shows the cumulative incidence of complete canal loss (n = 9). At 6 months, the risk of complete canal loss was 5% (95% CI, 2-8), and at 12 months, the cumulative risk of complete canal loss was 10% (95% CI, 5-21). Table S2 shows a brief description of the primary contributing factor to complete canal loss. All complete canal losses were due to dilation non-adherence. The most common reason for complete canal loss was dilation fatigue, which is broadly defined as physical and/or psychological exhaustion associated with the need for vaginal dilation, despite adequate healing or pain control. Dilation non-adherence also occurred within the context of psychosocial stressors, such as terminating a relationship or severe depression. One case developed severe hypergranulation within the canal and could no longer dilate. Two patients had undergone operative dilation and scar incision and eventually lost the canal after the first year. We sought to determine the incidence of complete canal loss following PIV. Notably, we observed a cumulative incidence of 5% every 6 months within the first postoperative year—an unexpectedly high rate. While no baseline demographic or clinical factors were significantly associated with canal loss, the most frequently cited contributor was dilation fatigue. We propose that dilation fatigue is a distinct phenomenon, separate from but potentially related to pain with dilation.2 Additional qualitative observations suggested that unaddressed poor mental health and unstable relationship dynamics may also increase risk. These findings underscore the ongoing challenge of accurately assessing readiness for PIV and for some patients, zero-depth vaginoplasty may represent a safer alternative. PIV requires months of diligent vaginal dilation postoperatively. Among a sample of patients who recently underwent gender affirming vaginoplasty, 21% stated that dilation was the “greatest challenge” after surgery.2 Factors associated with difficulty with dilation include pain, pelvic floor muscle spasms, wound healing issues, etc. Inadequate canal dissection may also cause dilation to be challenging. Risk factors for difficulty with dilation have been described, which include Medicare insurance status, unemployment, hyperlipidemia, HIV, psychiatric diagnosis besides gender dysphoria, and primary peritoneal vaginoplasty.3 Many of the same factors were tested in the current study, and we could not replicate these findings. “Difficulties with dilation” and complete canal loss may not represent the same construct. Many patients in our study who experienced complete canal loss did not cite pain as a primary reason for non-adherence. Rather, they appeared unprepared for the extent to which dilation would dominate their daily lives. Other nonpain-related factors that have been associated with not dilating include younger age, sexual orientation, and mental illness.4 We propose that dilation fatigue represents a distinct construct, potentially related to pain, but more closely associated with the demanding, time-intense nature of postoperative dilation protocols. Standardized definitions are lacking for several important biopsychosocial constructs following PIV, including dilation fatigue. Accurately measuring this construct may allow for further prevention and intervention strategies. Additionally, ongoing behavioral health monitoring after surgery may help identify at-risk patients. One case in the present series was due to severe pelvic pain, which inhibited dilation. Her pain was refractory to medications, pelvic floor physical therapy, and pelvic floor Botox injections. Ultimately, the patient stopped dilating completely due to pain and lost the canal within the first year after surgery. Mild to moderate pelvic pain with dilation after PIV occurs frequently due to pelvic floor dysfunction. Pre-operative and postoperative pelvic floor physical therapy can greatly aid with dilation. In the early postoperative period, other causes of pain with dilation should be excluded including wound infections and dehiscence. Monitoring frequently for the development of pelvic pain after PIV may identify patients at risk for complete canal loss. The generalizability of our findings is limited by the absence of a standardized, study dilation protocol and by potential selection bias inherent to a single-institution, retrospective study. The majority of patients were completed robotic-assisted, which may not represent other vaginoplasty centers. Dilation fatigue does not currently have a standardized definition. We acknowledge the possibility of unmeasured confounding, including other mental health diagnoses or substance use as these are not uniformly collected within the EHR. The study may not be powered to detect differences among those with and without canal compromise. As gender-affirming surgery evolves, understanding patient goals and readiness will be essential to guide care. None declared. None declared.

abstract: 13th edition Jane C. Rothrock, ed Mosby, 2007, 1280 pages $93.95 hardcover If a perioperative professional could chose only one reference, this book would be the one. Alexander's has been a standard perioperative reference for more than 60 years, and the 13th edition incorporates exciting additions in a refreshed form. Foundations of Practice, Surgical Interventions, and Special Considerations. Best Practices, Research Highlights, Sample Plans of Care, and Patient and Family Education. Relevant illustrations, photographs and charts are scattered throughout each chapter and the references at the end of each chapter are current and purposeful. The clinical chapters include the Surgical Pharmacology, Patient Safety, and History Box features found in prior editions of the book. The History Box features in chapter seven detail surgical progress during the past two decades, from the introduction of laparoscopic surgery in 1987 to the advent of robotics in 1991. Kay Ball, RN, BSN, MSA, CNOR, FAAN, the author of this chapter, shares her expertise in all aspects of endoscopic minimally invasive surgery and her knowledge of various surgical energies, such as lasers, electrosurgery, ultrasonic devices, hydrodissection, and cryosurgery. The specific surgical procedures highlighted in each specialty chapter present procedural considerations, such as patient positioning and instrumentation, coupled with the step-by-step surgical procedures, from skin marking to dressing application. Even the most seasoned perioperative professional will find a refresher on a particular procedure, position, or closure technique. The authors address key health care industry concerns, such as the consistent integration of patient and family education and comprehensive discharge planning. They also address emergency preparedness and bioterrorism from the perspectives of patient and environmental safety, infection prevention and control in the perioperative setting, and trauma surgery. Two online supplemental tracks are available, one for students and the other for instructors. These include narrated animations, printable patient and family education tables, and surgical pharmacology tables. In less than five minutes, readers can easily register for these online resources as supplements to this exceptional text. It was a privilege to review this perioperative classic. After reading this text, receptive novices will begin to appreciate the sheer wonder of surgery and the tremendous responsibilities that guide most perioperative veterans in each patient encounter. All readers, experienced and new to the profession, will gain a pragmatic education through their study of this book. This book is available from http://www.aornbookstore.org. 11th edition Nancymarie Phillips, ed Mosby, 2007, 1024 pages This book provides a wealth of information that is necessary for any health care team member caring for a surgical patient. The book is especially appropriate for RNs, whether they are beginning their perioperative practice or they have been practicing in the OR for many years. It also would be useful for surgical technology students and for those nurses who are preparing for their certification examinations. As a clinical educator for a Surgical Services Department, I believe that this book would be a valuable tool for new staff member orientation and for continuing education purposes as well. The preface discusses the evolution and history of both the book and its authors and demonstrates how it has been updated over the years and is of value in today's OR. It also outlines all features of the book, including those that are new to this 11th edition. The preface concludes with a brief synopsis of each of the subsequent sections. The overall content of the book is well organized, beginning with perioperative education and the foundations of perioperative patient care. It then progresses through all aspects of surgical knowledge and techniques that are essential to providing optimal patient care. Each chapter includes objectives, an outline, and key terms with definitions pertinent to that chapter. AORN's standards, recommended practices, and guidelines are incorporated throughout the book. Charts, diagrams, and illustrations enhance the written content. This book is well written and beneficial for any novice or expert in perioperative care. As an educator, I found the perioperative flash cards to be especially appealing and useful—a picture truly is worth a thousand words. I will use this book to prepare orientation programs for new employees, and I recommend this book for health care professionals who are considering becoming a part of the perioperative team. This book is available from http://www.aornbookstore.org. Tim Porter-O'Grady and Kathy Mulloch Elsevier, 2007, 656 pages The content of this book brings nursing management and leadership into the twenty-first century by emphasizing the importance of teamwork. The arrangement of the book is more similar to that of a reference book than one that is meant to be read from cover to cover. The book is divided into six units with four or five chapters in each unit. The use of illustrations, notes, and scenarios encourages readers to continue reading. Each chapter concludes with a list of references and suggested readings. The book begins with a unit describing the concept of team development. This includes a review of what makes an effective team, how to manage conflict, and how to evaluate results. The second unit assists readers in building decision-making skills. The discussion regarding leadership styles addresses leaders who are still using the parent-to-child method of leadership instead of using adult-to-adult principles. The authors present excellent information regarding how managers can empower team members. The third unit discusses accountability, both of the manager and staff members. The authors address risk-taking and how leaders can encourage staff members to safely reach out and use new approaches to confront change directly. Unit four builds on the other units and discusses staff member retention. The structure of the organization must promote staff member excellence. This unit also presents the 14 Forces of Magnetism. Magnet accreditation is one of the ways to validate excellent patient care. The leaders ability to sustain staff member excellence by empowering them also is discussed. The fifth unit presents information regarding recruiting the best staff members. Information regarding “selling” the organization to prospective staff candidates is included. The author highlights the interview process and includes “red flags” that indicate when the person being interviewed may not be the right person for the organization. The last unit of the book focuses on the role of the leader in the ever changing world of health care. The first chapter in this section is devoted to “Synthesis: the new role of the leader.” This chapter provides managers with concepts for developing the ability to link their analysis of situations with data integration and incorporate all parts into a whole situation. Even though this may not be a new concept, a manager who has been a leader for a number of years may not be aware of the skills and value of synthesis. This is one of the most important chapters for managers to read and use to develop and maintain successful leadership in their organization. The last chapter discusses the need and benefits of building relationships with employees, patients, and the community. New and seasoned managers will gain knowledge from each chapter and will find the book to be a good resource to assist with issues in the constantly changing health care arena. This book is available from http://www.aorn.bookstore.org.

abstract: Podcast Host: Dr. Andrew Huberman (Stanford Associate Professor - brain development, brain plasticity, and neural regeneration and repair fields) - Podcast Link - Youtube - Lab WebsitePodcast Guest: Dr. Matt MacDougall (Head Neurosurgeon at Neuralink) - LinkedIn profileKey takeaways The brain regulates physiological processes and cognitive functions but can malfunction (Segment 01).Sleep deprivation affects frontal cortex activity and emotion regulation, causing irritability and stress (Segment 02).Neuroplasticity allows the brain to adapt, and psychedelics may enhance it (Segment 03).Neuralink aims to alleviate suffering by enabling digital autonomy through brain implants (Segment 04).The neocortex governs advanced cognitive processes in the human brain (Segment 05).Neuralink is developing a high-bandwidth brain-machine interface for manipulating electronic devices (Segment 06).Neuralink electrodes are primarily for individuals with medical conditions but are safe for use (Segment 07).Bluetooth headphones have a negligible impact on neural function and thermal equilibrium (Segment 08).Neuralink aims to restore connectivity between the motor cortex and body using implants (Segment 09).Neuralink's technology has the potential for telepathy, non-invasive devices, and cognitive enhancement (Segment 10).Video games can be used to enhance proficiency in managing Neuralink devices (Segment 11).Neuralink prioritizes animal welfare and uses pigs for research safety (Segment 12).Head trauma can cause TBI with varying impacts, including disability and mortality (Segment 13).Understanding drug effects on the adolescent brain can improve treatment strategies (Segment 14).The human brain has high plasticity and can overcome deficits (Segment 15).Tesla's eye-tracking system aims to enhance road safety (Segment 16).Summary:This discussion concerns Neuralink, a company that aims to develop innovative technologies to address clinical challenges related to the brain and nervous system. Dr. Matthew MacDougall, the chief neurosurgeon at Neuralink, exemplified the amalgamation of cutting-edge machinery and devices with the human nervous system through a surgical intervention that involved the implantation of a radio receiver in the periphery of his body. The organization utilizes an interdisciplinary approach that amalgamates diverse fields including neuroscience, neurosurgery, robotics, machine learning, computer science, and device development to revolutionize the operation of the human brain. The aim of Neuralink is to enhance brain performance by means of enhancing memory, cognition, and human-machine communication. The technology in question endeavors to tackle movement disorders, including Parkinson's disease and deep brain function disorders, while concurrently augmenting human brain function beyond the innate boundaries of evolution. The experimental research conducted by Dr. MacDougall and his team represents a significant advancement in the field of science, and he will provide a detailed report on their ongoing inquiries.(01): 00:00:00 Dr. Matthew MacDougallDr. Matthew MacDougall serves as the head neurosurgeon at Neuralink, a company that aims to develop innovative technologies to address specific clinical challenges related to the brain and nervous system. Additionally, Neuralink seeks to enhance brain functionality by augmenting memory, cognition, and communication between humans and machines. These ambitious goals are achievable due to the company's unique approach, which combines existing knowledge of brain function from the fields of neuroscience and neurosurgery with robotics, machine learning, computer science, and the development of novel devices. By leveraging these interdisciplinary approaches, Neuralink is poised to revolutionize the way in which the human brain operates. The present discourse aims to elucidate the workings of the brain, with a particular focus on Neuralink's perspective regarding the tractability of challenges associated with brain function disorders. Additionally, the discourse will expound on strategies for enhancing brain functionality. The present discourse delves into the topic of developing the peripheral nervous system. Specifically, Dr. MacDougall has undergone a procedure to implant a radio receiver in the periphery of his body. This intervention was not intended to address any particular clinical issue, but rather to surmount various routine challenges of daily life. Furthermore, it serves as a demonstration of the advantageous potential of integrating innovative machinery and devices with our nervous system, as well as with diverse objects and technologies in our environment. Dr. Matthew MacDougall conducted experiments involving the implantation of devices in individuals, including his own family members. These experiments aimed to address movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease and other deep brain function disorders, as well as to enhance human brain function beyond the limits of natural evolution. The results of these experiments represent a significant advancement in the field of science. Dr. Matthew MacDougall will provide a detailed explanation of the experiments being conducted at Neuralink [1]. References1. A Direct Link Between the Brain & Everyday Technology. The brain is accountable for the regulation of various cognitive functions, such as intelligence, creativity, emotion, and memory, among others. The cranium serves as a protective covering for the brain, which is composed of three primary regions, namely the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem.The human brain has the capacity to process sensory information from five primary modalities, which include vision, olfaction, somatosensation, gustation, and audition, often in a simultaneous manner. The procedure of message assembly holds importance as it confers significance to the conveyed information and aids in its retention in our cognitive faculties. The brain, which is a component of the central nervous system, plays a crucial role in the regulation of cognitive processes such as memory, thought, and speech, as well as motor functions such as the movement of limbs and the proper functioning of bodily organs.The Central Nervous System (CNS) comprises the encephalon and the spinal cord. The composition of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of spinal nerves that bifurcate from the spinal cord and cranial nerves that bifurcate from the brain. The ability of the brain to generate human behavior and sustain life through electrical impulses is a remarkable phenomenon. Upon observing patients with brain tumors, it becomes apparent that discrete functions of the brain can be affected in isolation, highlighting the modular nature of the brain. Despite being connected within the confines of the skull; the brain is composed of functional modules that can exhibit intriguing failure modes. abstract: : 016: Role of stereotactic body radiation therapy in liver metastasis: A pilot study S. Kumar, R. Kapoor, A. Oinam, A. Duseja, N. Kalra Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, India, E-mail: [email protected] Background: Stereotactic external-beam radiation is an increasingly attractive modality for patients with a limited number of unresectable liver metastases because of their non-invasive nature, excellent tolerability & high rates of local control. This trial studies the feasibility & potential utility of SBRT in these patients. Aims: (1) To assess the local response of the liver lesions post- SBRT in terms of number and size of lesions. (2) To evaluate the toxicity to OARs (Liver, Right kidney, Duodenum, spinal cord). Materials and Methods: 15 patients were planned to be enrolled in this study from November 2014-October 2015. This is an interim analysis of the results of 10 patients who have completed the protocol. The inclusion criteria are patients with 1-3 liver metastasis from any solid tumor except germ cell tumor or lymphoma with adequate liver and kidney function with no evidence of progressive disease outside the liver. A planning 4D-CT scan is taken with patient in immobilization device & the GTV is defined on all respiratory phases 0-90). PTV is generated by giving margin of 5mm. Dose prescribed is 36 Gy/3# on alternate days. Before each fraction, a cone-beam CT is taken with the patient in the treatment position with the help of on-board kVCBCT imaging system. Stereotactic repositioning is done. Patients are followed up to assess toxicity, and response is defined by CECT abdomen done at 6 weeks &3 months post-SBRT as per RECIST guideline (v1.1). Results: The median age of the patients was 64 years (range 36-65 years). The median time since primary tumor diagnosis was 6 months (range 1-13 months). No patient had received prior local therapy for liver metastasis. 3 patients had received prior systemic chemotherapy for metastatic disease. The median aggregate Gross tumor volume was 75 ml (range 0.8 ml-95 ml). The median Maximal tumor diameter was 4.4 cms (range 1 cm-6.5 cms) 5 patients had partial response, 3 patients had stable disease and 2 patients had complete response at site of original lesion but developed new lesion elsewhere i.e., Progressive disease. One patients experienced Grade 2 small bowel toxicity, none of the other patients had Grade 2 or higher Hepatic/Gastric/Renal/Small bowel toxicity. Conclusion: This trial examines the feasibility of SBRT to liver metastasis in the Indian setup. It shows excellent tolerability and is a safe & non-invasive therapeutic option for inoperable patients, showing good local control. Bellutagi Karnataka Cancer Therapy and Research Institute, Hubli, Karnataka, India, E-mail: [email protected] Introduction: Skin metastasis from internal malignancies are common in breast, lung cancer & melanomas. we are hereby reporting a rare case of skin metastasis in esophageal cancer. Esophageal malignancies most commonly metastasis to lung, liver & bone. In general skin metastasis from internal organs are rarely seen with an incidence of 0.7%-9%. Metastatic spread to the skin occurs through hematogenous or lymphatic pathway & presents in the form of rapidly growing nodules. On histological examination, a cluster of atypical cells infiltrating the dermis without connection to the adjacent epidermis can be seen. abstract: RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY WITHOUT PRIOR BIOPSY This prospective study[1] aimed to evaluate the feasibility and accuracy of performing radical prostatectomy (RP) without prior prostatic biopsy in patients with high suspicion of prostate cancer (PCa) based on multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mp-MRI) and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography (PET). Fifty patients underwent RP without prior biopsy. The patients were divided into three groups: Group 1 (n = 27), with (i) suspicious digital rectal examination, (ii) prostate-specific antigen ≥10 ng/mL, (iii) Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 4/5 on mp-MRI, and (iv) high suspicion of PCa on PSMA-PET; Group 2 (n = 6) fulfilling criteria i, ii, and iii, but did not undergo PSMA-PET imaging; Group 3 (n = 17) fulfilling at least one clinical (i or ii) and one imaging (iii or iv) criterion. All of the patients were diagnosed with PCa on final histopathology. The study concluded that RP without prior biopsy is safe in diagnosing clinically significant PCa when applying proper preoperative risk stratification involving mp-MRI and PSMA-PET imaging. NOVEL BIOMARKERS TO PREDICT SURVIVAL IN CLEAR CELL RENAL CELL CARCINOMA This study aimed to identify biomarkers to predict the prognosis of patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) using proteomic and transcriptomic data.[2] The researchers measured the concentrations of 92 inflammation-related proteins in cell-free urine supernatant and plasma from 17 patients of ccRCC. They performed a targeted mRNA analysis of genes encoding these proteins using the Cancer Genome Atlas. The results reported four novel biomarkers, with low expression of fibroblast growth factor 21, TWEAK, and CCL7 and high expression of CX 3CL1, distinguishing the severity of prognosis in ccRCC. The researchers developed a nomogram using transcriptomic risk factors and risk groups associated with overall survival (OS) to predict 2-year and 5-year OS across different tumor stages. The decision curve analysis showed that the model was associated with a net benefit improvement compared to the treat all or none strategies. These findings suggest that these novel biomarkers can provide noninvasive prognostic information to guide management strategies for ccRCC patients. HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE TO PREVENT KIDNEY-STONE RECURRENCE In a recent double-blinded RCT, Dhayat et al.[3] estimated hydrochlorothiazide’s (HCT) efficacy in preventing renal stone recurrence. Patients were randomized to receive HCT at 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, or placebo once daily. The primary endpoint was the recurrence of renal calculus. A total of 416 participants were followed for a median of 2.9 years. Stone recurrence occurred in 60/102 (59%) in the placebo group, in 62/105 (59%) in the 12.5 mg HCT group (relative risk [RR] 1.33; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.92–1.93), in 61/108 (56%) in 25 mg group (RR 1.24; 95% CI 0.86–1.79), and 49/101 (49%) in 50 mg group (RR 0.92; 95% CI 0.63–1.36). HCT dosage did not affect the primary endpoint event (P = 0.66). HCT was associated with hypokalemia, gout, new-onset diabetes mellitus, skin allergy, and plasma creatinine levels above 150% of baseline. The authors concluded that HCT at 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, or placebo had similar recurrence rates. TRANSPERINEAL LASER ABLATION OF THE PROSTATE: EFFICACY AND SAFETY IN BPH MANAGEMENT Transperineal laser ablation is a minimally-invasive ejaculation-sparing procedure for BPH treatment. It requires a biplanar transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) and EchoLaser® system consisting of multisource diode lasers with four independent laser sources, operating at 1064 nm wavelength. TRUS-guided 21G Chiba needles are placed under local anesthesia, followed by laser fiber placement and energy delivery. The laser causes hyperthermia, denaturation, and coagulative necrosis of proteins.[4] Seven studies (n = 315) were included in the review, all single-arm and noncomparative. The prostate volume varied across the studies from 30 to 100 ml. All authors reported a significant, durable improvement in functional outcomes and promising efficacy at short to mid-term follow-up. Four authors reported improved postoperative International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) scores, with no negative impact on erectile and ejaculatory functions. All authors reported a good safety profile with 0%–13% complication rates. PELVIC HYPOTHERMIA USING A RECTAL COOLING DEVICE DURING ROBOTIC-ASSISTED RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY TO IMPROVE POTENCY This prospective phase I/II clinical trial by Han et al. evaluated the results of hypothermic robotic-assisted RP (RARP). The research included 20 patients scheduled for RARP who had preoperative IIEF-5 scores of more than 12.[5] An endorectal cooling device was used to induce pelvic hypothermia (BelloCool® System). The nadir neurovascular bundle temperature was 24.9°C (22.4–28.2) and 10.2°C (7.0–13.1) lower than the nadir core body temperature. There was no device-related complication, and bowel function was unaffected during the entire follow-up period. Potency and continence recovery rates were greater in the hypothermia group (n = 20) than in the matched control group (n = 60) at 12-month follow-up (40% vs. 15% [P = 0.03] and 95% vs. 80% [P = 0.17], respectively). The hypothermia group had a quicker rate of potency recovery on the Kaplan–Meier curve. The authors concluded that hypothermic RARP was both safe and practical. PROGNOSIS OF PRIMARY PAPILLARY TA GRADE-3 BLADDER CANCER IN THE NON–MUSCLE-INVASIVE SPECTRUM Ta Grade-3 (G3) nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is a rare diagnosis with an aggressive grade and nonaggressive stage. This retrospective (1990–2018) muti-institutional study compared the prognosis of Ta-G3 bladder tumors with Ta-G2 and T1-G3 tumors.[6] The authors reported that patients with Ta-G3 tumors (7.5% [318/5170]) had a prognosis between the Ta-G2 and T1-G3 tumors in terms of 5-year progression. However, the time to recurrence was similar for all the groups. Patients with Ta-G3 tumors with CIS had a prognosis comparable to those with T1-G3 tumors with CIS. The study endorses revisions in the EAU NMIBC guidelines for improved risk stratification of Ta-G3 tumors, as many patients had a more favorable prognosis than previously believed. BIOMARKERS PREDICTING RESPONSE TO ANTI-PD -1 THERAPY IN METASTATIC CLEAR-CELL RENAL CELL CARCINOMA This retrospective study (n = 198) aimed to identify a combinatorial biomarker that can predict the response of patients with metastatic ccRCC to anti-programmed death (PD-1) therapy.[7] The authors measured the expression of various immune-related genes and calculated immune scores to assess the immune cell infiltration in the tumor microenvironment. The authors identified a combinatorial biomarker comprising four genes (CXCL13, CXCL9, ICOS, and CD274) that could predict the response to anti-PD-1 therapy. Patients with high expression of all four genes had a 77% objective response rate (ORR) compared to 12% in patients with low expression of all four genes. The study also reported that patients with high tumor mutation burden (TMB) and low expression of the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway had better outcomes to anti-PD-1 therapy, with a 73% ORR, compared to 27% in patients with low TMB and high VEGF expression. The study concluded that patients with a high expression of immune-related genes and high immune scores had significantly better outcomes with anti-PD-1 therapy than patients with low expression and scores. ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER: A NECESSARY EVIL? The relationship between erythritol (a commonly used sugar substitute) and cardiovascular events (major adverse cardiovascular events [MACE], including death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and stroke) was evaluated in recent research.[8] The study examined the levels of multiple polyol sweeteners, including erythritol, in patients undergoing cardiac risk assessment (n = 1,157) and found that elevated levels of erythritol were associated with incident MACE risk over 3 years. Further analysis in stable patients (US: n = 2149 and European: n = 833) undergoing elective cardiac evaluation confirmed this association. Finally, a pilot intervention study in healthy volunteers (n = 8) found that erythritol ingestion increased plasma erythritol levels well above the threshold associated with increased platelet reactivity and thrombosis potential. The association was independent of other cardiovascular risk factors such as age, sex, body mass index, smoking status, and physical activity. Limitations included observational study design limiting causality estimation, self-reported assessment of erythritol intake, and inability to distinguish between natural and artificial erythritol. The results warrant long-term safety evaluation of erythritol. Financial support and sponsorship: Nil. Conflicts of interest: There are no conflicts of interest.

title: Dr. Ramesh Chandra: An Icon of Plastic Surgery in India
abstract: Dr. Ramesh Chandra was born on 9 August 1940 at Moga, Punjab, in an affluent Aryasamaji Punjabi Agarwal family. His father was a general physician and mother a God-fearing pious housewife. His parents moved to Khatauli in District Muzaffarnagar in the state of Uttar Pradesh where he completed his primary schooling. After completing primary schooling, Dr. Chandra moved to Meerut at the age of 15 years where he did B.Sc. from the Meerut University. He was interested in pursuing medicine like his father, and at the age of 17 years, he got admission to study medicine at the prestigious King George's Medical University (KGMU), Lucknow, in 1957. Following his graduation in 1962, he completed his M.S. in general surgery and was appointed as a lecturer in the Department of Surgery. After completion of M.S. in plastic surgery from the same institute, he was appointed as a lecturer in the Department of Plastic Surgery under the guidance of his mentor Prof. R.N Sharma and then became a reader in plastic surgery thereafter ([ Fig. 1 ]). Fig. 1 Dr. Ramesh Chandra (09.08.1940–08.07.2021) He traveled to England in 1978 to the world-famous Stoke Mandeville Hospital, Aylesbury, the United Kingdom, under the mentorship of Mr. Bruce Bailey the renowned microsurgeon ([ Fig. 2 ]). During his training, he also cleared the Fellowship of the Royal Colleges of Surgeons (FRCS) examination in the first attempt which was considered an astounding achievement at that time. Fig. 2 Dr. Ramesh Chandra with his mentor Dr. Bruce Bailey and Dr. Desai at the Stoke Mandeville Hospital, the United Kingdom, in 1979. He returned to India and joined the department fresh with new ideas and knowledge and gained a senior position of a professor of plastic surgery. He became the head of the Department of Plastic Surgery in the December of 1981 and the principal and the dean of KGMU from 1998 to 2000. Reminiscing his years devoted to the plastic surgery department, he contributed to gradual and comprehensive building of the department. In those times, the department was nascent and [ Fig 1 ] was limited to just a ground-floor building. During his long two-decade tenure of headship, he was able to mobilize resources and added the first floor, new equipment, instrumentation, new posts, and trained hundreds of plastic surgeons. He worked selflessly for the department all these years and soon with the hard work and good results of surgery, the patient input rapidly increased and the department grew in leaps and bounds under his able mentorship. He appointed faculty members in the department for the continued growth of the department including Dr. S.K. Bhatnagar and Dr. A.K. Singh who themselves excelled in their careers both in the department and the Association of Plastic Surgeons of India. He invited international and national key faculties in the department regularly for knowledge enhancement and for establishing mutually productive professional relationships. He trained hundreds of plastic surgeons who are making their names in far-reaching corners of the country and the world. His contributions were not limited to the department but were spread over in all the fields including academics, teaching, and clinical research. He has to his credit more than 100 scientific publications including papers in scientific journals, theses, book chapters, and books in plastic surgery. Some of his notable contributions include new techniques for cleft lip repair, cleft lip nose repair, and many new flaps for hand reconstruction. The operation of cleft lip was his favorite, and he was an expert craftsman of the technique of lower triangular method of cleft lip repair. His reconstructed lips have remained symmetrical and shapely even after decades of surgery. He devised a new all-encompassing “definition of plastic surgery” which has been acknowledged in the International Textbook of Plastic Surgery by Peter Neligan. He had gifted hands and was a master of stitch craft. His skin sutures appeared like they have been applied by a robot with precision, neatness, and uncanny symmetry. Dr. Chandra contributed a lot to his alma mater while working as faculty in the Department of Plastic Surgery and also as the principal and the dean. He was the president of the Athletic Association of KGMU and contributed to developing sports infrastructure and culture in the university. He was also an officer in charge of the central library and had the opportunity to improve the facilities and created a computer section and other ancillary facilities for students visiting the KGMU central library. During his tenure as the principal of KGMU, the foundation of the state-of-the-art Trauma Centre was laid by the then Prime Minister Sri Atal Behari Vajpayee. He was awarded the prestigious Dr. BC Roy National Award by the President of India for his all-round contribution to plastic surgery ([ Fig. 3 ]). He served his alma mater with full dedication and maintained the past glory of his university. After superannuation from KGMU, he served as an executive counselor of the university. Fig. 3 Dr. Ramesh Chandra receiving the prestigious Dr. B.C. Roy National Award for excellence in plastic surgery from the President of India in 1997. Dr. Chandra also decorated important positions in the Association of Plastic Surgeons of India. He served two terms as an editor of the Indian Journal of Plastic Surgery. He was instrumental in developing the Indian journal in terms of visibility, quality, and always encouraged the submission of articles by younger faculty and residents. He was also elected as the president of the association in 1997 and organized a memorable annual meeting of plastic surgery in Lucknow. Dr. Ramesh Chandra was tall, slim, and very handsome with a pleasing personality, a teetotaller who loved simple home-cooked food and had a disciplined lifestyle. Dr. Chandra maintained a high level of physical fitness and was an avid tennis player. He used to play in the evenings at the verdant grass courts of KGMU. He was truly an icon, a living legend in his times and a father figure of plastic surgery especially in the state of Uttar Pradesh. He was an ideal father, loving son, exceptional husband, helping brother to his siblings, and a generous grandfather. He leaves a rich legacy of second and third generations of doctors and a gene pool of high traditions, moral values and excellence which will continue in his future generations. His wife, Prof. Padam Kumari Agarwal is a much-respected teacher in pathology and served at the KGMU and is known for expertise in the technique of fine-needle aspiration cytology in the state and beyond. His elder son, Dr. Rajiv Agarwal is trained in craniofacial surgery in Dallas and is currently serving as the head of the Department of Plastic Surgery at SGPGI, Lucknow. He received continuous mentorship from his father that resulted in numerous publications and innovations in plastic surgery spanning over more than two decades. His younger son, Dr. Sanjeev Agarwal excelled in orthopaedics, is a book author in orthopaedics, examiner in FRCS orthopaedics, an expert in revision knee arthroplasty, and is working as a consultant at Cardiff University, United Kingdom. His elder daughter-in-law, Dr. Tulika Chandra is credited with building up and managing one of the largest departments of transfusion medicine in the country at KGMU where she is heading the department. His younger daughter-in-law, Dr. Gaurav Jyoti is a leading consultant radiologist in the United Kingdom and specializes in breast radiology. His legacy continues to shine in his five grandchildren among whom three have chosen the field of medicine and are doing well in their careers. One is studying engineering at Oxford, the United Kingdom, and the youngest also aspires to become a doctor. He was gentle, soft-spoken, caring, and abjured prolixity. He remained fit and healthy in the pink of health even till the very last day and passed away peacefully and painlessly after a massive cardiac event. He leaves behind no debts but only credits and a sea of well-wishers with whom he came in contact with in his lifetime. His life and times are truly a learning textbook with numerous pages of hard work, honesty, dedication, commitment, and accomplishment worthy of emulation. No legacy is as rich as honesty— William Shakespeare Publication History Article published online: 28 February 2022 © 2022. Association of Plastic Surgeons of India. title: Assessing the Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Olympic Games
abstract: The Olympic Games have always been at the forefront of adopting new technologies to enhance various aspects of the competition.1 In recent years, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the Olympics has emerged as a transformative force, promising to revolutionize athlete performance, event management, and audience engagement.2 This technological shift is not merely a trend but a significant evolution that reflects broader changes in how sports are practiced, managed, and consumed in the digital age.3 AI technologies offer unprecedented opportunities to optimize various facets of the Olympic Games. From real-time analytics that provide coaches and athletes with invaluable insights to advanced systems that streamline the logistics of organizing such a massive event, AI is poised to redefine the operational landscape of the Olympics.4 The potential benefits are vast, encompassing enhanced performance metrics, improved safety and security measures, and enriched spectator experiences. These advancements align with the Olympic spirit of pushing the boundaries of human potential and innovation.However, the integration of AI into the Olympics also brings forth a set of complex challenges that need to be addressed.5 The rapid pace of AI development has outstripped the ability of existing regulatory frameworks to keep up, leading to a lack of clear guidelines and standards.6 This regulatory gap raises questions about fairness, accountability, and ethical considerations, particularly in the context of performance enhancement and data privacy.7 The deployment of AI technologies must be carefully managed to ensure that they do not undermine the principles of fair competition and respect for individual rights that are central to the Olympic ethos.8The purpose of this research note is to explore and assess the impact of AI on the Olympic Games, encompassing various dimensions such as athlete performance, event management, and audience engagement. As future developments in AI promise to bring about transformative changes in the future of the Games, this research note aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how AI is currently being utilized in the context of the Olympics, stress the benefits of this integration, and detect potential challenges. To achieve the above aim, three objectives underpinning this note are to (1) identify how AI is currently applied in the Olympics and stress the benefits; (2) detect the challenges of integrating AI into the Olympics; and (3) introduce a set of contextual recommendations for better engagement.By examining the benefits and challenges associated with AI integration, this research note seeks to offer insights into how AI can improve athlete training and performance analysis, streamline event logistics and security, and create more personalized and immersive experiences for spectators. Additionally, the research note will address ethical concerns, such as data privacy and algorithmic fairness, to ensure that the deployment of AI in the Olympics aligns with principles of equity and transparency. Ultimately, this research note contributes to the broader discourse on the role of AI in sports and large-scale events, providing valuable recommendations for stakeholders involved in the planning and execution of the Olympic Games.The 2018 Winter Olympics in South Korea prominently showcased the integration of AI. During the Opening Ceremony, humanoid robots were featured, symbolizing the country's technological progress. A total of eighty-five robots were deployed to perform a range of tasks, including providing information and carrying out cleaning duties, thereby demonstrating innovative applications of AI in managing events and enhancing operational efficiency.9 Likewise, the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics were a pivotal moment for the incorporation of AI into the event. When the 2020 Summer Olympic Games took place in Tokyo a year later than planned because of the COVID-19 pandemic, over 11,000 athletes from 200 countries participated in forty-one sports across forty-two venues. In addition to the postponed schedule and absence of spectators due to pandemic restrictions, the Tokyo Olympics stood out from previous games due to the extensive use of AI technologies. These included robots, wearable sensors, machine learning, and the vast amount of data available for analysis and processing to benefit all participants.10AI-powered technologies play a crucial role in boosting athlete performance and enriching the fan experience. Additionally, robots welcome visitors while ensuring social distancing protocols and autonomous vehicles facilitate the transportation of athletes and officials. Notably, AI was used to compose the theme song, and drones delivered impressive visual displays, showcasing AI's creative capabilities. The integration of AI technologies is not only revolutionizing how the Games are conducted but also elevating the overall experience for athletes, organizers, and fans alike. AI is playing an increasingly pivotal role in the Olympic Games, transforming various aspects, from athlete performance and event management to audience engagement. The integration of AI technologies is enhancing the efficiency, accuracy, and overall experience of the Olympics, making it a more dynamic and engaging event for all stakeholders involved.11 On the field, in the stands, or behind the scenes, there are several ways AI makes an impact at the Olympic games.AI technologies are employed to optimize training regimens, refine performance analysis, and minimize injury risks.12 Machine learning algorithms, such as regression models and classification algorithms, analyze large datasets to predict future performance and assess injury risks based on factors like training load and biomechanics. Artificial neural networks (ANNs), including deep learning models and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), optimize training programs and predict injury risks by learning complex patterns from multifactorial data.13 Natural language processing (NLP) techniques, such as sentiment analysis and text mining, interpret athletes’ language in social media posts and medical reports to gauge their mental state and extract relevant injury information.14 Predictive analytics, employing time-series analysis and survival analysis, forecast optimal training loads, recovery times, and rehabilitation plans, ensuring athletes maintain peak performance while minimizing injury risks. This data-driven approach enables coaches and trainers to create personalized training programs to maximize an athlete's strengths and address their weaknesses.15AI-powered video analysis tools dissect an athlete's movements frame by frame, identifying areas for improvement that may not be visible to the naked eye.16 Computer vision and video analysis tools, including motion capture systems and automated video analysis software, allow for detailed examination of athletes’ techniques, enabling coaches to pinpoint areas for improvement and detect movements that may lead to injuries. In sports like gymnastics or diving, AI can evaluate the precision and execution of complex maneuvers, offering detailed feedback to refine techniques.17 Similarly, in track and field events, AI can analyze an athlete's running form and biomechanics, providing insights that lead to more efficient and effective performance.18 In the Tokyo Olympics, AI has enabled physical tests of athletes to detect early signs of fatigue or stress-induced injuries, a predictive tool that sports organizations and Olympic teams could use to keep athletes safe from future injuries.19One of the most impactful applications of AI in the Olympics is enhancing athlete performance. AI-powered wearable devices monitor an athlete's heart rate, oxygen levels, and muscle activity in real time, providing instant feedback and allowing for on-the-fly adjustments to training routines. These wearables track sleep patterns and recovery times, ensuring athletes are in optimal condition for their events.20 Wearable sensors and IoT devices, such as GPS trackers and smart clothing, monitor real-time physiological and biomechanical data and provide insights into performance metrics like heart rate, speed, and muscle activity. These devices also help in identifying early signs of potential injuries by analyzing movement patterns and physical stress.21 As athletes trained for the Tokyo Olympics, their performance data was gathered through sensors, wearables, and cameras. Devices such as sensors embedded in shoes or bike pedals continuously supplied data, aiding athletes and coaches in adjusting to enhance their competitiveness. Artificial intelligence offered valuable information and insights that were previously inaccessible.22Additionally, AI predicts injury risks by analyzing movement and workload patterns, enabling preventive measures. This predictive capability is especially valuable in high-impact sports where injury risks are significant.23 Moreover, AI can assist in mental training by analyzing an athlete's psychological state and providing insights into their mental well-being.24 This enables coaches to address any psychological issues that may be affecting an athlete's performance, ensuring that they are in peak mental condition for competition. These AI-driven tools and methods provide a comprehensive approach to enhancing athletic performance and safeguarding athletes’ health, offering unprecedented insights and precision in sports science. By leveraging these technologies, coaches and athletes can make data-driven decisions that lead to improved outcomes and reduced injury rates, ultimately contributing to the overall success and longevity of athletes’ careers.AI is significantly enhancing the management and organization of the Olympic Games. One of its primary applications in event management lies in logistics and planning. AI algorithms can process vast amounts of data to optimize scheduling, venue selection, and resource allocation.25 AI can determine the best dates and times for events by analyzing historical attendance data, weather patterns, and matching events. This data-driven approach ensures events are planned with maximum efficiency and minimal conflicts, resulting in higher attendance.26 In terms of attendee management, AI-powered systems streamline registration and check-in processes. Facial recognition technology, for instance, allows attendees to check in without physical tickets or identification, reducing wait times and enhancing security by ensuring only registered individuals gain access.27 Additionally, AI chatbots can handle a wide range of customer service inquiries, from answering frequently asked questions to providing real-time updates on event schedules and locations. These chatbots operate 24/7, offering immediate assistance and freeing up human staff to focus on more complex tasks.28Security is another critical area where AI is making significant contributions. AI-driven surveillance systems can monitor large crowds in real time, identifying potential threats through behavior analysis and facial recognition.29 These systems can alert security personnel to suspicious activities, enabling quicker and more effective responses. Moreover, AI can analyze social media and other online platforms for potential security threats, providing an additional layer of protection.30 The integration of AI in event management not only enhances the efficiency and security of the Olympic Games but also ensures a more enjoyable and seamless experience for all attendees. This contributes to the overall success and reputation of the Games, making them a more attractive event for future participants and spectators.AI is transforming audience engagement at the Olympics by offering customized, interactive, and immersive experiences. A major application of AI in this context is personalized content delivery.31 By analyzing user data, such as viewing history, preferences, and behavior, AI algorithms can curate content specifically tailored to individual tastes. Streaming platforms can utilize AI to recommend particular events, highlights, or athlete profiles that match a viewer's interests, thereby increasing user satisfaction and experience.32 In the sphere of live events, AI-driven platforms are revolutionizing how audiences engage with content. AI-powered real-time data analytics can offer fans immediate access to detailed statistics, athlete performance metrics, and game insights.33 This not only enhances the viewing experience but also enables fans to connect more deeply with the event. For instance, during a live track and field event, AI can analyze athlete movements and strategies in real time, providing fans with a deeper understanding of the competition through augmented reality overlays and interactive features.34 Additionally, AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can respond to fan queries, provide and facilitate social a more engaging and interactive instance, track and field are a of viewing events to the AI-driven This at the and is set to be utilized in the the The with artificial intelligence and vision to real-time data to during biomechanical analysis, including metrics such as athlete speed, and or This information is during live and through AI is enhancing audience engagement through immersive technologies like virtual reality and augmented These AI-powered technologies provide fans with and immersive experiences that viewing reality can fans to virtual enabling them to experience the of a live event from the of their augmented reality can offer real-time overlays of athlete statistics, event highlights, and other interactive during a live making the viewing experience more dynamic and AI is pivotal in enhancing social media engagement.
