ToolsAdd to favoritesDownload CitationsTrack Citations ShareFacebookTwitterLinked InEmail Achieving photochromism, photodeformation, and photoinduced room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) simultaneously in a single type of molecule-doped film is a complex and challenging task. Here, we introduce an efficient design strategy that utilizes dicarbonyl as a bridge linking between phenothiazine (PTZ) units, thereby enabling a synergistic multi-photoresponse upon photoactivation. Our study reveals that thin films of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) doped with five PTZ derivatives (DPTZCn: n = 1–5) show photoactivated RTP. Notably, the DPTZC1 variant in PVA film uniquely undergoes photoactivated macroscopic deformation and displays enhanced photoluminescence efficiency compared to its PTZ counterparts (DPTZCn: n = 2–5) in PVA films. Further photophysical analysis indicates that the exceptional performance of DPTZC1 stems from the combined effects of keto-enol tautomerism and matrix rigidification, which also facilitate the generation of photoinduced radicals in DPTZC1 in the PVA film. We investigate the potential bionic applications of the versatile DPTZC1, providing insights into the design of intelligent, photodriven materials based on RTP. Download figure Download PowerPoint Introduction Photoresponsive properties such as photoinduced room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP), photodeformation, and photochromism, have been extensively studied for their potential in areas such as photodriven soft robotics and chemical sensors.1–15 However, integrating these properties within a single type of molecule-doped film remains a rarity, largely due to their different light irradiation response mechanisms. Achieving effective responsiveness requires a deep understanding of the material's microscopic structural changes and photoresponse mechanisms after irradiation. The concept of tautomerism, especially keto-enol tautomerism in dicarbonyl compounds, plays a pivotal role in this context.16,17 Introduced by Laar in 1886, tautomerism has found extensive applications across synthetic, biological chemistry to materials science, underpinning the development of drugs and advanced materials.18–24 For example, the enthalpic and polar properties provided by keto-enol tautomerism in β-diketone compounds enable substrate activation, facilitating reactions to proceed in good yields.25 Similarly, the construction of covalent organic frameworks with keto-enol tautomerism has demonstrated favorable properties, such as enhanced benzylamine adsorption.26 Phenothiazine (PTZ), a highly versatile organic compound, has been used in various fields, including medicine, in vivo imaging, and batteries, and more recently in optoelectronic materials.27–36 For example, Wang et al. achieved dual phosphorescence from phenoxazine- and PTZ-decorated naphthalene, which could be ascribed to two conformationally modulated T1 states.37 Another example by Gao et al. reported that PTZ derivatives can enhance RTP performance due to their quasi-axial and equatorial conformations in different states.38 Moreover, Chen et al. proposed that emission behavior of the triplet state in PTZ-benzophenone derivatives can be modulated through selecting specific geometries of the intramolecular charge transfer states.39 We reason that the combination of PTZ with keto-enol tautomerism might augment RTP and create a synergistic multi-photoresponse in new material systems. In this system, the PTZ units can effectively engage in charge transfer processes, while the keto-enol equilibrium modulates these processes (Scheme 1). This synergy allows for a material system with nuanced responsiveness, capable of reacting to multiple photoresponses such as changes in light, color, and mechanical force. Scheme 1 | Design strategy using dicarbonyl as a linker between two PTZ units and possible mechanism of multiphotoresponse. The small molecule DPTZC1 was uniformly doped into the PVA film and then excited with 365 nm UV. (i) After UV irradiation, enol structures are continuously formed, which exhibit macroscopic deformation. (ii) Radical cations are stabilized through keto-enol tautomerism. (iii) These radical cations can generate hole-electron pairs, possibly with a large number of triplet excitons forming upon their recombination, which offer another possibililty to produce the triplet excitons. PVA contributes to this process by forming numerous hydrogen bonds, which stabilize the triplet excitons. Download figure Download PowerPoint For a proof of concept, we introduced five PTZ derivatives (DPTZCn: n = 1–5), each consisting of two PTZ units connected by a dicarbonyl linker (see Supporting Information Scheme S1). These PTZ derivatives differ in the spacer between the PTZ units. Once doped into a polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) film, all five derivatives exhibited photoactivated RTP. Notably, DPTZC1 exhibited the highest photoluminescence (PL) quantum yield, which can be attributed to the keto-enol tautomerism in its β-diketone linker, accompanied with macroscopic deformation of the film. Moreover, in the DPTZC1-doped PVA film, photoinduced cationic radicals were detected, as evidenced by both electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals and photochromic behavior. These multifunctional characteristics of DPTZC1 enable potential applications in anticounterfeiting and bionics. Experimental Methods General Unless otherwise specified, the reagents used in the experiments were purchased commercially and the purity was of analytical grade. All chemicals were purchased from Sigma Aldrich PTE. LTD. (Singapore) and were not subjected to additional purification. Chromatographically pure toluene was used after anhydrous and oxygen-free treatment with a solvent purification system (VSPS-5; Vigor Technologies (Suzhou) Co. Ltd., Suzhou, China). For all air-sensitive reactions, the Schlenk technique was used in a nitrogen atmosphere. Synthesis for DPTZCn (n = 1–5) PTZ derivatives DPTZCn (n = 1–5) were synthesized through a one-step acylation reaction (see Supporting Information Scheme S1). Synthesis for hybrids PVA solution (3 wt %): Stir PVA (300 mg) in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (10 g) in a 20 mL flask at room temperature for one night until completely dissolved. Polyethylene (PE) solution (3 wt %): Stir PE (300 mg) in toluene (10 g) in a 20 mL flask at 100 °C for 2 h until completely dissolved. Incorporation of DPTZC1 into PVA film (1:10): First, dissolve 6 mg of DPTZC1 in 2 mL of the 3 wt % PVA-DMSO solution (DPTZC1:PVA = 1:10). Next, apply the mixture dropwise onto a glass substrate. After application, peel the DPTZC1-incorporated PVA film off the glass substrate and allow it to dry. Incorporation of DPTZCn (n = 1–5) into PVA film (1:60): First, dissolve 1 mg of DPTZCn in 2 mL of the 3 wt % PVA-DMSO solution (DPTZCn:PVA = 1:60). Next, apply the mixture dropwise onto a glass substrate. After application, peel the DPTZCn in PVA film off the glass substrate and allow it to dry. Incorporation of DPTZC1 in PVA film (1:600): 1 mg of DPTZC1 was first dissolved in 20 mL of a 3 wt % PVA-DMSO solution (DPTZC1:PVA = 1:600), then the mixture was applied dropwise to the glass substrate, after which the DPTZC1 in PVA film was peeled off from the glass substrate and dried. Incorporation of DPTZC1 in PE film (1:60): 1 mg DPTZC1 was first dissolved in 2 mL of a 3 wt % PE-toluene solution (DPTZC1:PE = 1:60), then the mixture was applied dropwise to the glass substrate, after which the DPTZC1 in PE film was peeled off from the glass substrate and dried. Characterization 1H and 13C NMR spectra were recorded using a Bruker Advance spectrometer (Bruker Singapore Pte. Ltd., Singapore; 400 MHz for 1H, 101 MHz for 13C) in chloroform-d (CDCl3), DMSO-d6, and acetone-d6. 1H and 13C NMR spectra were referenced with respect to residual solvent peaks: (1H) chloroform-d, 7.26 ppm, (13C) chloroform-d, 77.16 ppm, (1H) dimethyl sulfoxide-d6, 2.50 ppm, (1H) acetone-d6, 2.05 ppm. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) spectra were recorded with a Shimazu HPLC chromatograph (Shimadzu (Asia Pacific) Pte. Ltd., Singapore) using acetonitrile as solvent. High-resolution mass spectra (HRMS) were measured on an AmaZon X LC-MS (Bruker Singapore Pte. Ltd., Singapore) for electrospray ionization. Melting points were measured using a WRS-1C Melting Point Tester (HINOTEK GROUP LIMITED, Ningbo, China). Ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) absorption spectra were acquired at room temperature using an Agilent Cary 5000 UV–vis–NIR spectrophotometer (Agilent Technologies Singapore (Sales) Pte. Ltd., Singapore). Luminescence spectra were recorded with an Edinburgh FLS1000 spectrofluorometer (Edinburgh Instruments Ltd., Livingston, United Kingdom). Time-dependent phosphorescence spectra and excitation duration-dependent RTP behavior were collected by a QE65 Pro (Ocean Optics Inc., Shanghai, China). Optical photographs of the samples were obtained using an iPhone 12. EPR spectra were recorded on a JEOL JES-FA200 spectrometer (JEOL Asia Pte. Ltd., Singapore). The sample preparation method is described in the General Synthetic Procedure for Hybrids section and the molar ratio of the samples used for testing is 1:60. In addition, the film samples are cut into pieces approximately 8 mm × 20 mm in size for testing. All ground state optimizations were carried out at the density functional theory (DFT) level with Gaussian 16 using the ωB97XD functional and the triplet zeta valence with polarization quality (TZVP) basis set. Vibrational frequency calculations were performed to ensure that the optimized geometries represent the local minima. Excited-state calculations were performed at the time-dependent DFT level using the same functional and basis set as for the ground state geometry optimization. Spin–orbit coupling matrix elements (x) were calculated based on the optimized geometry of the singlet excited state. Optimizations for the triplet excited state were conducted at the ωB97XD/TZVP level. The surface potential energy scan was conducted using the geometry of the optimized triple excited state. Molecular orbitals were visualized using GaussView 6.0. Spin–orbit coupling matrix elements between singlet and triplet excited states were calculated using the ORCA 5.0.3 program. Results and Discussion The molecular structures and purities of these compounds were confirmed by 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy, HPLC, and HRMS (see Supporting Information Figures S1–S11). In addition, the homogeneous dispersion of DPTZCn derivatives in PVA films was determined by powder X-ray diffraction analysis (see Supporting Information Figure S12), and the molecular packing of DPTZCn (n = 1–5) crystals was examined by single crystal X-ray diffraction (see Supporting Information Table S1). The high thermal stabilities of these compounds were demonstrated through thermal gravity analysis, revealing decomposition temperatures (Td) for DPTZCn (n = 1–5) at 213, 273, 285, 295, and 283 °C, respectively (see Supporting Information Figure S13). The UV–vis absorption spectrum and steady PL spectrum of DPTZCn solution were also characterized (see Supporting Information Figures S14 and S15). We firstly investigated the photophysical properties of DPTZC1 and DPTZC2 in PVA films (molar ratio = 1:60). The steady-state PL spectrum of DPTZC1 in PVA films exhibits a structured emission profile with PL maxima at 450 and 520 nm, respectively (Figure 1a), with a recorded PL lifetime of 1.83 ns (see Supporting Information Figure S16). DPTZC2 in PVA films presents a different emission behavior, characterized by a single peak at 425 nm and an extensive emission tail (see Supporting Information Figure S17). Notably, no afterglow was observed for DPTZC1 and DPTZC2 in PVA films upon a short excitation duration using a 5 W UV torch. However, the emission color gradually evolved from blue to yellowish green as the excitation duration increased (Figure 1b,c), resulting in a detectable afterglow (see Supporting Information Figure S18). The RTP intensity of DPTZC1 in the PVA film gradually increased with UV irradiation time, reaching saturation at 3600 s (Figure 1d). This was accompanied by an RTP quantum yield of 4.91% and a phosphorescence lifetime of 23.96 ms (see Supporting Information Table S2). This RTP behavior was ascribed to interactions between triplet excitons and 3O2. Initially, triplet excitons are quenched by 3O2, leading to the occurrence of RTP after the complete consumption of 3O2 (Figure 1e).40 DPTZC2 shows weaker RTP efficiency (0.83%) and shorter lifetime (7.54 ms) compared to DPTZC1 (see Supporting Information Figure S16 and Table S2). DPTZCn (n = 3–5) in PVA films also exhibited photoactivated RTP in PVA films but with lower RTP efficiency compared to DPTZC1. The molecular structure with the cationic radicals exhibits a more planar structure in the PTZ fraction compared to the neutral state. More specifically, the dihedral angle of the two PTZ subunits increases from 130.68/133.16° (DPTZC1) in the neutral molecule to 132.13/174.75° (DPTZC1+•) in the molecule containing the cationic radicals (Figure 2e). This suggests, as in previous studies, that planar conformations with extended π-conjugation are more favorable for radical stabilization.44–46 This stabilization explains the observed differences: DPTZCn (n = 2–5) compounds exhibit neither a color change nor an EPR signal after UV excitation. The enhanced stability of DPTZC1's radical cations would facilitate the hole-electron recombination, thereby providing more possible chance to generate triplet excitons. Consequently, the RTP performance of DPTZC1 in PVA film improves significantly, from nearly 0% before UV irradiation to 4.91% after 6 min of irradiation (see Supporting Information Table S2). title: 말단 장치의 평면 유지가 가능한 로봇 회전 암의 설계
abstract: This study proposes the design method for the robot rotation arm which the end effector that is connected in end of the arm keeps parallel motion even though the robot arm rotates. So far, most robot arm rotates together the end effector when the arm rotates. For this, this study proposes the mechanism that the arm is linked to each 4 parallel link so that rotation is possible by 4 pins, and the rotation arm connects 2 joints of diagonal line direction to a link in each 4 joint for rotation, and designs so that can change length of the link. For verification of design, this study targeted that develop the rotation arm for medical examination that use in ophthalmology. It is important that a medical robot offers comport to patient and design compactly so that medical examination and treatment space may can be defined enough. It is designed so that all drive elements may be positioned on interior of the arm and optimization of design for main parts was carried out in this study for this. The robot arm which is developed in this study manufactured to use by medical phoropter arm, and got good result by an experiment. The robot rotation arm which is proposed in this study is judged to contribute very effectively in case use of a medical robot arm for medical examination and treatment, also the robot arm which the end effector that is connected in the end of the arm needs to keep parallel motion. And, the robot arm which is developed in this study made an application as license.

title: FULL PAPER Simulated crepitus and its reality-based specification using wearable patient dummy
abstract: Physical therapists are trained in manual examination techniques to test the impaired motor functions of patients. In this study,wehave introduced awearable robotic dummyjointtosimulatedisorderedjointresistancesor behaviors tosupport physical therapists in learning such techniques. We developed a discontinuous joint friction model based on a stick-slip phenomenon to simulate knee joint resistances caused by crepitus, a typical symptom accompanied by osteoarthritis. Practicing therapists participated in a reality-based evaluation test and specified acceptable parameter sets to adjust the simulated crepitus for the exoskeletal patient robot. The simulated crepitus and wearable dummy joint are expected to support the training of physical therapists.

title: The impact of the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) on non-EU cardiac surgery training programs
abstract: The European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) has been at the forefront of advancing cardio-thoracic surgery education and training within the European Union (EU). However, the impact of EACTS extends beyond EU borders, significantly benefiting non-EU cardiac and thoracic surgery training programs. This paper aims to underscore the positive impact of EACTS on non-EU residents in training and standardization of their training program relying on high-quality European leaders and teachers. The Ukrainian cardiac surgery training program originates from the Soviet Union program and still harbours some of its traits such as a short training period and the lack of an international academic development. After 6 years of medical school, graduates are required to undergo 3 years of general surgery residency followed by 6 months of ‘specialization’ in cardiac surgery. Given the extremely short training time, most of the residents apply to cardiac surgery centres where they are eligible to undergo training in both general and cardiac surgery simultaneously. In such circumstances, the provision of top-quality educational and training courses, opportunities to participate in research and leadership programs, and the ability to exchange direct experiences with prominent health care EACTS professionals are fundamental for the professional growth of young cardiac surgeons in non-EU programs. EACTS serves as a hub for expertise and best practices in cardiac surgery. Non-EU cardiac surgery training programs can greatly benefit from the vast knowledge offered by the EACTS. One of the most beneficial educational programs is the EACTS Academy, which provides various training courses with several levels of complexity aimed to fulfil the needs for all levels of surgeons (ie from medical students to expert specialists) [1]. By engaging with EACTS Academy, the non-EU residents gain access to educational resources, guidelines, and standardized protocols that enhance the quality of their training. With the beginning of coronavirus disease pandemic, the Academy launched a series of webinars and hybrid courses for the professionals around the world. These projects obtained strong interest among non-EU residents presenting 15–21% of all the participants and continues to rise yearly (Table 1). One example of EACTS engagement with non-EU residents through an online course is the EACTS Case Corner. This virtual course allows the participants to present interesting cases in an interactive format with fellow residents and experts and to review the evidence that supports management decisions. The guidance and experience exchange from high-qualified professionals within EACTS can significantly impact the career path of non-EU trainee members. Non-European Union member participation in European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Academy courses (webinar and in person) from 2021 to 2023 EU: European Union. Non-European Union member participation in European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Academy courses (webinar and in person) from 2021 to 2023 EU: European Union. Through the Francis Fontan Fund (FFF), EACTS provides a platform for international exchange programs and fellowships, which fosters collaboration between young residents and the most prestigious European institutions. The Fund is primarily financially supported by EACTS. However, there are a number of fellowships that are supported with the help of industry partners, who share the interest in the propagation and education of highly specialized skills. The fellowships are grouped into 3 categories: Research, Leadership, and Education across a range of subspecialities in cardio-thoracic surgery (Table 2) [2]. These fellowships assist surgeons in the development of specific, high-level skill sets that are seldom available in their local institutions (e.g. robotic/minimally invasive surgery, complex valve repairs). The FFF offers research fellowships for young investigators eager to engage in high-level research, such as quality outcomes, statistics, and an opportunity to participate in trials and new scientific projects. This educational offering gives an invaluable opportunity for non-EU residents to develop key theoretical knowledge and provides an opportunity to work alongside leading experts and gain exposure to different healthcare systems, approaches, and cultures. Such experiences promote the transfer of knowledge and skills, ultimately enhancing the quality of their cardiac surgery training. Furthermore, it favours networking with leading centres, so perpetuating the initial benefit, and transforming it in an opportunity for future profitable scientific and professional collaborations. The European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Francis Fontan Fellowship available for European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery members in cardio-thoracic surgery (2024) EACTS: European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery; MICS: minimally invasive coronary surgery; MSTCVS: Michigan Society of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery; OPCAB: off-pump coronary artery bypass. One of the most invaluable features of the FFF is continuous support of trainees who may be experiencing uncontrollable difficulties in their education. For example, in 2022 with the beginning of Russian–Ukrainian War, EACTS via FFF launched the ‘Ukrainian Support Fellowship’ aimed to provide unique opportunities for residents from Ukraine whose surgical training program was temporarily suspended due to hostilities and safety considerations. The Fellowship involved 3 months of high-qualified education in perioperative patient care, advanced cardiac surgical skills, access to complex and hybrid cases, wetlab and simulation training, in addition to the opportunity to attend present at the EACTS Annual Meeting. Another example is the FFF and the charitable arm of the STS, the Thoracic Surgery Foundation (TSF), which sponsor a yearly international travelling fellowship in partnership with the Latin American Association of Cardiac and Endovascular Surgery (LACES). This travelling fellowship fosters the continued growth and development of Latin American cardio-thoracic surgeons by providing opportunities to learn the highest standards of cardio-thoracic surgical care in Europe and North America and gain knowledge of novel techniques and innovative technologies. This unique and prestigious fellowship supports advancing Latin American cardio-thoracic surgical care by sharing clinical experiences across the global cardio-thoracic surgery community. Since the introduction of the FFF Fellowships, the number of non-EU awardees has increased every year: in 2018, 18% of the fellows originated from non-EU countries, whereas in 2023–2024 this part accounted 31% (Table 3). Furthermore, EACTS has launched a donation portal for the FFF to allow senior surgeons and philanthropists to aid in the development and education of the next generation of cardio-thoracic surgeons. This is highly beneficial to young trainees/residents from deprived and low-income regions, who seldom have such career-changing experiences. The EACTS Residents’ Committee’s objective is to connect young professionals and trainees to facilitate resident education and identify issues in training. It is one of the most active networks, including both, EU and non-EU resident members, representing the interests of early-career surgeons. In 2023, the Residents’ Committee organized the first National Trainee Summit—an alliance of the cardio-thoracic national representatives across Europe. In this unique occasion residents had the opportunity to discuss the disadvantages and pitfalls of training programs across and beyond Europe providing fundamental steps and ideas on how to evolve and improve cardio-thoracic surgery training among the participating countries. For the non-EU residents, it was an excellent opportunity to be part of European community which fosters mentorship relations, collaborations, and knowledge exchange, enriching the professional development of non-EU trainees. In addition, the collaboration with the Global Thoracic Surgery Residents Association (GTSRA) represents a dynamic alliance focused on advancing the field of cardio-thoracic surgery and supporting the development trainees worldwide. By aligning their missions and objectives, EACTS and GTSRA leverage their collective strengths to address critical issues impacting trainees of all nationalities across the globe. Through strategic communication channels and advocacy efforts, they promote international collaboration in research and training opportunities including fellowship opportunities. EACTS not only played a crucial role in the foundation of LACES and its residents committee but also nowadays strongly supports LACES in its efforts to improve the quality of the training of Latin American surgeons. Currently, experienced leadership members of EACTS with expertise in surgical education work closely with the LACES board of directors and recently established the LACES Academy, which is the educational domain of LACES that aims to improve the quality of training and increase access to high-quality academic and educational resources to Latin American surgeons, mainly by offering online courses. Since 2023, EACTS, together with the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) and LACES, has held an in-person joint Latin American Annual Meeting. This conference offers an accessible way for Latin American surgeons and trainees to attend a high-level scientific conference with talks from renowned international leaders in the cardio-thoracic surgical field. The Latin American conference program also includes a resident’s session and hands-on training events, in addition to plenty of room and opportunities for global networking. As a further step to improve cardio-thoracic surgical education in Latin America, in 2023, LACES published an international survey-based comparative analysis of cardiac surgeons' training and professional practice across Latin America [3]. This publication was co-authored by representatives from EACTS and presents the first comparative analysis of cardiac surgical training and professional practice across Latin America, thus providing the fundamentals for future academic projects of LACES, like, for example, a Latin American board examination. Another long-term involvement of EACTS outside of the EU is the regular attendance at the Hannes Meyer Registrar Symposium in South Africa, which is a 2-day, practical training-focused meeting for registrars, perfusionists and consultants of all cardio-thoracic units of the country. The highlight of the course is a full performance of an operation on the basis of a patient simulator designed to imitate a patient before, during and after cardiopulmonary bypass for open heart surgery. It is a physiologically responsive system designed to be attached to any heart-lung machine circuit either in VA or VV configuration. In this way, technical challenges and complication management can be learned. Very interestingly, interpersonal teamwork, communication, and leadership skills can be practiced by mixing up the groups working in different, unexpected constellations. For almost 2 decades, EACTS senior members attend the course by contributing actively to the practical training supporting not only as faculty, but also informing about EACTS activities, how young surgeons can enhance their careers, and about possibilities of collaboration. EACTS has been instrumental in establishing and promoting standardized training guidelines and curricula within the EU [4–6]. Non-EU cardiac surgery training programs can leverage EACTS resources and guidelines to align their own training programs with international standards. To promote the excellence and facilitate the mobility of the surgeons across and beyond Europe, the utilization of European Board and Cardio-thoracic Surgery (EBCTS) examination might become a mandatory step on the completion of the training in non-EU countries. The MEBCTS (Membership) and FEBCTS (Fellowship) assess the scope of knowledge, clinical judgement and application of the principles and practice of surgery to a standard expected at the end of national training in cardio-thoracic surgery (MEBCTS—level 1) and of an independent practicing surgeon in 1 or more areas of established sub-specialist practice (FEBCTS—level 2). A total of 387 delegates have participated in the level 1 MEBCTS examination with 141(36%) from non-EU countries. Of the total number of countries represented in the examination (58), 24 (50%) were non-EU. For the level 2 FEBCTS examination, a total of 82 delegates have participated with 45 (55%) from non-EU countries. Of the total number of countries represented (23), 10 (43%) were non-EU (Table 4). This reflects the importance of the examination to residents and fellows outside of Europe. Number of European and non-European countries represented and number of participants in the Membership and Fellowship examinations for the European Board of Cardiothoracic Surgery Number of European and non-European countries represented and number of participants in the Membership and Fellowship examinations for the European Board of Cardiothoracic Surgery By adopting these standardized practices, non-EU programs can enhance the quality, consistency, and recognition of their training, ultimately contributing to the global harmonization of cardiac surgery education. EACTS actively promotes research and innovation in cardiac surgery through grants, awards, and research-focused events. To this extent, an annual Innovation Summit has been established, bringing together surgeons, scientists and engineers to share ideas and form collaborations to streamline new innovations into our specialty. Another example is the recent incorporation of the Resident’s Corner in both the European Journal of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery and Interdisciplinary Journal of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery, which aims to promote the excellent academic work performed by resident surgeons. The best resident papers published under this category could win the Resident’s Corner Award, which is revealed at the EACTS Annual Meeting. Non-EU cardiac surgery residents may benefit from such opportunities as it encourages trainees to participate in local and collaborative international research projects, present their work, and access funding opportunities. This exposure to research and innovation fosters a culture of scientific inquiry and evidence-based practice in non-EU programs, with an evident global benefit. The EACTS has achieved remarkable outreach and impact on non-EU cardiac surgery training programs, however, it faces several challenges in maintaining and expanding its initiatives in a multicultural world. Language barriers: One of the significant challenges is language diversity. While English serves as the primary language during the courses, webinars and in-person events, not all non-EU participants may be fluent at it. Despite that, LACES is actively working towards changing of this paradigm, facilitating the education among Latin American trainees who are mostly Spanish or Portuguese native speakers. For instance, in the online courses, the lectures can be given in any of the 3 languages (English, Spanish or Portuguese) with subtitles, where possible. Joint local events with national associations are organized in the official local language (Portuguese/Spanish). During the annual STS/EACTS/LACES Latin American conference, the presentations are delivered in English; however, the interaction with the audience is possible in Spanish and Portuguese. Cost implications: Another challenge is the cost, particularly associated with participation, travel and accommodation expenses. Members from non-EU countries, where incomes may be lower compared to Western Europe, might find it financially burdensome to attend the in-person events. To address this, the EACTS has increased the number of webinars available and announced the cancellation of fees for all webinars, beginning from March 2024. This strategic shift towards online education reduces financial barriers, making high-quality education more accessible for non-EU members. Cultural challenges: Cultural differences across regions pose another challenge within the Association’s activities. EACTS is working diligently to compose guidelines on clinical management and education curricula to standardize and improve the delivery of cardiac surgical assistance across Europe. By promoting the unified practices and guidelines, the EACTS aims to bridge cultural gaps and ensure consistency in training and patient care practices. Despite the number of cornerstones in maintaining the important outreach of EACTS worldwide, it continues to implement the crucial sustainability strategies, providing exceptional educational opportunities far beyond Europe, including diversification of language offerings, expansion of online education, collaboration and partnership with industry sponsors and regional associations, as well as promotion of standardized practices, helping overcome cultural features and ensure harmonization of training across the world. The EACTS has an important impact on non-EU cardiac surgery training programs. Through access to international exchange programs, mentorship, standardized training guidelines, and emphasis on research and innovation, EACTS enhances the quality of training and professional development for non-EU residents and trainees. The involvement and participation in EACTS educational projects demonstrate a benefit for non-EU trainees, promoting collaboration and knowledge sharing, thereby advancing the field of cardiac surgery, and improving patient care on a larger scale. Conflict of interest: none declared. The data underlying this article were provided by EACTS and the Francis Fontan Fund. The data underlying this article will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author.

title: The rise and fall of surgical aggressiveness for known or suspected differentiated thyroid cancer
abstract: “The scientist explains the world by successive approximations.” —Edwin Hubble Sonographically detectable thyroid nodules affect up to one-half of the adult population. Because the underlying malignancy risk is approximately 5%, the first principle in managing thyroid nodules is to avoid unnecessary intervention in the 95% of benign cases (for the moment, let us set aside symptomatic benign enlargement and benign hyperfunction). At the same time, appropriate intervention is of course required in the small fraction of patients who harbor malignant nodules likely to cause morbidity and (rarely) mortality. Many diagnostic interventions, such as fine-needle aspiration biopsies and thyroid resections for indeterminate nodules, arise because of clinical uncertainty: although the risk of an adverse outcome related to a given nodule may be small, this nonzero risk drives clinicians and patients to achieve a state of reassurance. Depending on the balance of the scientific literature, the state of reassurance may be achieved at various average levels of intervention per capita. Over the past several decades, surgical aggressiveness for known or suspected differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) has risen and then fallen in response to a series of important scientific developments. Sir William Osler stated that, “Medicine is a science of uncertainty and an art of probability.” Indeed, the management of thyroid nodules is a distillation of this maxim. Like all decisions, medical decisions are most straightforward at the extremes of probability. The decision to proceed with surgery is easy to make when a malignant diagnosis is close to certain (>95%), and the decision to observe is easy when the risk of malignancy approaches zero (<5%). Decision-making is difficult in the broad realm of intermediate probabilities.1 Since its inception, diagnostic thyroid cytopathology has been characterized by 3 basic categories: malignant, benign, and indeterminate. The indeterminate category is often considered troublesome because of the clinical uncertainty it carries. However, the indeterminate category is the precise reason why thyroid cytopathology is useful at all: its existence permits the diagnostic probabilities associated with the malignant and benign categories to be pushed to the extremes, where patients can confidently undergo surgery or comfortably be observed. In the absence of the indeterminate category, both the malignant and benign categories would be contaminated to an extent that would bring them into the range of intermediate probabilities, thus greatly diminishing patient value. Debates regarding the appropriate extent of initial surgery for low-risk DTC date back several decades.2 A series of events occurring between 1980 and 2012 caused a progressive increase in surgical aggressiveness for known or suspected thyroid cancer (Table 1).3-24 The development of thyroglobulin as a tumor marker provided a useful quantitative indicator of disease status during thyroid cancer surveillance. At the same time, because death from thyroid cancer is rare, thyroglobulin levels and structural recurrences detected on imaging emerged as secondary outcome measures of treatment efficacy. Put another way, the achievement of low thyroglobulin levels became a goal in and of itself. As thyroglobulin assays and ultrasound imaging grew progressively more sensitive, so did the intensity of postoperative scrutiny, driving surgeons toward increasingly aggressive operations. These operations aimed not only to prevent clinical recurrences but also to eliminate subclinical recurrences (even “biochemical-only” recurrences that manifest as isolated, nonzero thyroglobulin levels). A landmark 1994 study by Mazzaferri and Jhiang established total thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine ablation, and the administration of levothyroxine to suppress plasma thyroid-stimulating hormone levels as the standard of care for the initial treatment of DTC.5 This treatment strategy was reinforced by a 2007 analysis of the National Cancer Database demonstrating the superiority of total thyroidectomy over thyroid lobectomy as measured by recurrence rates and survival7 and was reflected in the 2009 Revised American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer.8 From 2009 to 2012, the march toward increased surgical aggressiveness continued, as multiple groups independently reported on the advantages of prophylactic central neck dissection (compartmental removal of central neck nodes in the absence of clinical or sonographic abnormalities) during initial surgery for DTC. This movement was largely motivated by the desire for improved postoperative thyroglobulin levels, which were achieved by the removal of clinically insignificant nodal micrometastases.12 Circa 2012, surgical aggressiveness reached its peak. Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection (and sometimes even prophylactic lateral neck dissection) had become the standard initial operation at many expert centers across the globe, even for small tumors (<2 cm). The broadening application of screening ultrasound examinations, combined with the relatively indiscriminate use of fine-needle aspiration, drove many patients to surgery. These operations included many diagnostic thyroid lobectomies for indeterminate (Bethesda 3 and 4) nodules, most of which ultimately proved unnecessary because of an underlying malignancy risk of approximately 25%. A final and perhaps most disturbing tributary was the increasing discovery of incidental papillary thyroid microcarcinomas on screening ultrasound examinations performed during routine health checkups. This phenomenon was most pronounced in South Korea, where ultrasound screening fueled a 15-fold increase in the diagnosis of thyroid cancer over a 20-year period.16, 19, 25 By 2011, thyroid cancer became the most commonly diagnosed cancer in South Korea. Yet thyroid cancer mortality remained stable in the low single digits, demonstrating that virtually all of the newly discovered cancers posed no threat to human health. Indeed, more than one-half of newly discovered cancers measured <1 cm in diameter, and one-half again of those measured <0.5 cm in diameter. We now know that these very-low-risk tumors can safely be observed in most instances. In an absurd sequela, a multimillion dollar surgical-industrial complex blossomed in South Korea to manage these tumors, with the end result being the large-scale delivery of unnecessary care. Some centers performed thousands of operations annually for papillary thyroid microcarcinomas, and a market-based system evolved to monetize various remote-access and robotic surgical techniques that have largely fizzled elsewhere in the absence of this kind of factitious economic underpinning. None of the above statements are meant to disparage the South Korean health care system in any way, as the same problem was occurring to various degrees in many if not most developed countries. In 2012, Veracyte Inc launched the Afirma gene expression classifier (GEC) for the molecular diagnosis of indeterminate (Bethesda 3 and 4) thyroid nodules, which make up approximately 25% of thyroid cytopathology readings. The machine-learning algorithm used to develop the GEC was designed to prioritize sensitivity at the cost of specificity. In other words, this was designed to be a “rule-out” test. A molecular-benign GEC result was highly reassuring, with a false-negative rate of approximately 5%, which aligned with the false-negative rate of a benign morphologic cytopathology result (once again, we return to easy decision-making at the extremes of probability). However, a molecular-suspicious GEC result was associated with a malignancy risk of approximately 50%. The benign call rate of GEC was approximately 50%, so the principal added value of the test was the avoidance of surgery in the fortunate one-half of patients who had a molecular-benign result. The remaining patients with molecular-suspicious results were stuck in the realm of intermediate probabilities, and most underwent surgery (although perhaps grudgingly). In 2011, Nikiforov and associates developed the first generation of the ThyroSeq molecular test (ThyroSeq; a joint partnership between the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and CBLPath).26 The original 7-gene mutational panel was a low-sensitivity/high-specificity “rule-in” test examining a small number of mutations known to cause cancer. Therefore, its value was limited in a population with a low prevalence of malignancy and, as a result, the test was not marketed. With the addition of new genetic alterations, the sensitivity of ThyroSeq version 2 increased to 90%, paving the way to broad application within the United States in 2015.27 The advent of molecular profiling simultaneously heralded and contributed to the fall of surgical aggressiveness for known or suspected DTC. Three additional drivers were the recognition of overdiagnosis, the expansion of thyroid lobectomy as definitive treatment for low-risk DTC, and the acceptance of surveillance as a management strategy for very-low-risk tumors. Overdiagnosis is defined as the incidental discovery of “illness” that is almost certain not to cause poor health or decreased life expectancy. Overdiagnosis is a product of screening. Although screening has the potential to improve human health in certain specific conditions, overdiagnosis carries the risk of burdening patients with unnecessary diagnostic tests, treatments, and worry. The first article to call attention to the overdiagnosis of thyroid cancers was published in 2006.6 However, because the report was somewhat isolated in its message, it ended up being a shot across the bow: surgical aggressiveness continued to increase for several years before a critical mass of literature, including that documenting the South Korean experience, accumulated. In a notable reversal of fortune, a re-analysis of the National Cancer Database in 2014 demonstrated equivalency between lobectomy and total thyroidectomy in the surgical treatment of papillary thyroid cancers from 1.0 to 4.0 cm in size.15 This pivot was attributed to longer follow-up and improved adjustment for patient comorbidities and tumor characteristics. However, because of the formidable number of assumptions and the amount of statistical wizardry used to analyze large administrative databases, supplementary evidence from large institutional experiences played an important role in bringing about the liberalized use of lobectomy.28 In 2015, Oda et al from the Kuma Hospital in Japan first described active surveillance as a primary management strategy for very-low-risk papillary thyroid carcinomas.17 This was a logical response to the epidemic of overdiagnosis occurring globally but perhaps most acutely in Northeast Asia. In short order, active surveillance made a jump across the Atlantic.29 The 2015 American Thyroid Association management guidelines for adult patients with thyroid nodules and differentiated thyroid cancer incorporated molecular profiling for indeterminate (Bethesda 3 and 4) nodules, the liberalization of lobectomy for intrathyroidal DTC measuring 1.0 to 4.0 cm, and the use of active surveillance for very-low-risk papillary thyroid carcinomas.18 From 2016 to the present, further declines in surgical aggressiveness have been driven by the creation of the new term noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP), publication of the eighth American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging System for Differentiated Thyroid Cancer, and the release of a second generation of improved molecular tests for indeterminate nodules (Table 1). What do the large-scale trends enumerated above portend for the future of surgery for known or suspected DTC? First, molecular profiling will likely become routine for Bethesda category 3, 4, 5, and 6 nodules. Although, currently, molecular profiling is principally used for diagnostic purposes, it will increasingly be used for prognostic information, to guide initial management (extent of surgery and use of radioactive iodine) in cases of known malignancy. Second, the importance of thyroglobulin in guiding the subsequent management of DTC will likely diminish. In patients who have undergone lobectomy for DTC, the signal of a rising thyroglobulin level attributable to recurrent tumor will likely be small compared with the noise generated by the intact thyroid lobe. This may be just as well because, in our integrated practice, we are already letting go of zero thyroglobulin levels as a goal to be achieved at any cost, and we are now reluctant to allow nonzero thyroglobulin levels to trigger any intervention in the absence of an associated structural finding. Finally, the acceptance of active surveillance as a management strategy for low-risk DTC will have a series of knock-on effects. If we are willing to observe a known DTC, certainly we should be willing to observe an indeterminate nodule, so long as its ultrasound features remain favorable. Truer yet if molecular profiling has revealed an indeterminate nodule not to harbor high-risk mutations such as BRAF V600E or mutational combinations such as BRAF plus TERT and RAS plus TERT. And what about small, nonthreatening recurrences of DTC? Likewise, those will increasingly be managed with active surveillance. Some have described the rise and fall of surgical aggressiveness for DTC as a swinging pendulum. Personally, I find this description to be dispiriting because it suggests that there has been no net progress over time. Hopefully, oscillations in surgical aggressiveness will diminish in amplitude as we asymptotically approach an optimal management strategy through successive approximations. I thank Dalena Nguyen for her help with article preparation. No specific funding was disclosed. The author made no disclosures. Michael W. Yeh is a Professor of Surgery and Medicine at the UCLA David Geffen School of Medicine. After completing his education at Stanford University and Harvard Medical School, he pursued surgical training at the University of California San Francisco and the Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney, Australia. Dr. Yeh currently serves as Chief of Endocrine Surgery, Medical Director of the Endocrine Center Integrated Practice Unit, and Medical Director of Optimal Care at UCLA Health.

title: CORR Insights®: What Factors Are Associated With Postoperative Ischiofemoral Impingement After Bernese Periacetabular Osteotomy in Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip?
abstract: Where Are We Now? Ischiofemoral impingement (IFI) is an underrecognized source of hip pain, especially among recipients of offset-altering or center of rotation-altering hip procedures [2, 7, 12]. This entity was originally described among patients who have had THA in whom excessive medialization of the hip’s center of rotation or reduced offset led to a decreased distance between the lateral aspect of the ischium and the lesser trochanter of the femur, resulting in subsequent impingement [7]. Similarly, IFI can follow periacetabular osteotomy and even occur in a native joint that is anatomically predisposed to this problem [4, 7, 8]. In this issue of Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research®, Huang et al. [5] investigated the link between preoperative and intraoperative determinants and the risk of IFI after Bernese periacetabular osteotomy for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), which to this point has not been well characterized. Periacetabular osteotomy changes the orientation of the acetabulum to redistribute load on the articular cartilage, to decrease the risk of progression to osteoarthritis in patients with hip dysplasia [6, 11, 13]. However, redirection of the acetabulum cannot change the shape of the acetabulum or its total surface area. We do know, from a recent investigation by Fowler et al. [1] using reference-standard CT measurements, that periacetabular osteotomy has been associated with an average medialization of 4 mm ± 3 mm. The extent of medialization was even more pronounced among patients with a lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) of ≤ 15° (in whom the mean medialization was 6 mm ± 3 mm), a cohort that constitutes most of the patients in the investigation by Huang et al. [5] (LCEA < 20° was an inclusion criterion). However, while seemingly intuitive, the association between the extent of medialization after periacetabular osteotomy and the occurrence of IFI had not been extensively described before Huang et al.’s timely study. In addition to the substantial proportion of patients who had some degree of IFI (26%), the factors associated with IFI described by Huang et al. could be categorized into nonmodifiable and modifiable. Nonmodifiable associated factors include increasing the neck-shaft angle and a positive coxa profunda sign; the latter has a negative correlation with IFI. Conversely, medialization of the hip’s center of rotation was the sole surgeon-modifiable associated factor that could influence the development of IFI. Notably, the 1.9-mm cutoff for safe medialization, as described by the authors [5], may be a relatively conservative estimate. If viewed in the context of the average 6-mm medialization reported by Fowler et al. [1], a substantial proportion of patients undergoing periacetabular osteotomy can—and will—exhibit some degree of IFI. Based on Huang et al.’s [5] discoveries, surgeons should not ignore posterior hip or gluteal pain or discomfort after periacetabular osteotomy. This pain could originate from hip arthritis, but also could be due to IFI. A proper investigation and clinical assessment can help the surgeon in defining the source of pain and the right management. Where Do We Need To Go? The study by Huang et al. [5] provides several avenues for further investigation. Although the authors demonstrated that medialization and the neck-shaft angle are associated with the development of IFI, baseline femoral offset is yet to be explored. Furthermore, additional variables that were considered exclusion criteria in the present investigation may need further elaboration, including the effect of a concurrent femoral osteotomy, wider ranges of LCEAs, and most importantly, cutoffs of medialization in periacetabular osteotomies performed in patients without DDH. The criteria for diagnosing IFI remain relatively controversial [3, 7]. IFI is a relatively new topic, and the diagnosis starts with a clinical examination that can be supported by MRI findings and clinical tests. Therefore, compared with femoroacetabular impingement, hip pain owing to impingement between the acetabulum and posteroinferior structures around the hip is much less characterized and may require additional objective parameters [7]. Although Huang et al. [5] used well-defined criteria to diagnose IFI (such as symptoms, MRI findings, and diagnostic ischiofemoral injection), the risk of overdiagnosing or under-diagnosing this condition and its subsequent clinical relevance is yet to be determined. IFI could have existed preoperatively, and establishing a causal relationship between the periacetabular osteotomy technique or anatomic patterns and IFI remains elusive. Moreover, the long-term effect of this spectrum of impingement and the risk of progression to osteoarthritis remain unclear. The position of the lower limb and rotation during activity can increase or decrease the risk of impingement; therefore, preoperative and postoperative activity levels, type of lifestyle, expectations, and demands might also modify symptomatology and subsequent clinical relevance. How Do We Get There? To span this knowledge gap, we need to improve the parameters we use to designate outcomes, in this case, IFI. We also need to conduct adequately powered, prospective, and potentially randomized clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of preoperative planning and intraoperative interventions to mitigate the incidence of IFI, explore additional granular patient and surgical determinants that may influence periacetabular osteotomy outcomes, and gauge outcomes based on patient-specific expectations and activity levels at longer follow-up intervals. The latter may warrant follow-up for the development of IFI-related complications in addition to evaluating joint-specific and general-health patient-reported outcomes. Further research is needed to define more objective clinical and radiologic criteria for diagnosing IFI. This would require comparative studies aiming to validate the currently used diagnostic criteria. Further correlation between such criteria and objective preoperative and postoperative MRI, ultrasound, and clinical parameters while accounting for activity levels and underlying native and/or iatrogenic anatomic variations may be warranted. Leveraging scoring systems such as the Hip Sports Activity Scale may aid in adjusting for activity level. Preoperative advanced imaging-based planning may prove critical in avoiding IFI after periacetabular osteotomy. Surgeon awareness of the patient’s specific anatomy and the subsequently acceptable limits of medialization, acetabular orientation, and concurrent femoral osteotomies is paramount to mitigating the risk of IFI. Although controversial, the use of intraoperative navigation for complex procedures can be investigated to potentially improve intraoperative accuracy, especially in patients with higher complexity [5, 9]. Periacetabular osteotomy is frequently a complex surgery for patients [10]. As such, evaluating the effect of details such as concurrent femoral osteotomies, femoral offset, hip ROM, soft tissue status, and activity level is warranted in future studies to attain a true understanding of patient-specific risk factors. Furthermore, diagnoses other than DDH should be accounted for. Characterizing the roles of such potential modifiers is critical to offering a patient-specific intervention. Currently, technology may be limited, but the rapid evolution of robotics and artificial intelligence in orthopaedics may improve the precision of periacetabular osteotomy. Finally, using patient-reported outcome measures will offer insight into patient satisfaction and perception of improvement to avoid the pitfall of treating radiographic findings, rather than individuals.

title: Target focus capture system based on enhancement learning and impedance variable structure control
abstract: Abstract For the robotic detecting and grasping of the digestive tract, a cyber-physical system of focus capturing based on a physician's vision and the high-performance robot impedance control method are proposed in this study. The structure of the cyber-physical system for the focus information is given, which includes the physician, the network, the robot, and the digestive tract. The structure is controlled remotely by physicians through a 5G network, and is divided into two layers. The upper layer is mainly for physicians to capture the target of digestive tract focus through enhancement learning, and send instructions to the lower layer robot impedance control set and joint controller through space conversion and 5G network. In this way, the lower layer robot joint can quickly find the target of the digestive tract focus according to the instruction. At the same time, the optimal performance of target capturing, target trajectory processing of Akima, and time-varying nonlinear mapping between robot workspace and joint space are discussed. Finally, the Target Focus Capture system based on enhancement learning and new variable structure impedance control is first proposed for the Doctor-Robot system, and the simulation results show that the remote control method is feasible. In addition, it can be used for reference in COVID-19 prevention and control. At the same time, it is of great help to the examination and operation of unskilled professional physicians.

title: Highlights from the 2017 meeting of the Society for Neural Control of Movement (Dublin, Ireland)
abstract: Over 450 researchers, clinicians, and students attended the 27th annual meeting for the Society for the Neural Control of Movement held in Dublin, Ireland (May 1–5th, 2017). A satellite meeting focused on ‘The Roles of Proprioception and Vision in Perception and Action’, while during the main meeting topics ranged from learning sensorimotor maps from scratch to presynaptic inhibition for sensorimotor control to vestibular reflex pathways. Approaches ranged from behavioral assays to single neuron recordings to neural manifolds. Model systems ranged from fruit flies to mice to primates. There was a wide range of interests represented this year (Fig. 1). Here, we present a brief summary of the meeting, highlighting talks that generated extended discussion and posters that featured a novel approach or question. We focus on three themes that emerged across many sessions: learning, motor control of hand movements and holding still, and the advantages of a neural population activity perspective. This year's NCM began with a satellite session centered on sensory control of movement, which covered proprioception, vision, the combination of proprioception and vision, and the clinical application of basic knowledge on these topics in a variety of disorders. Jonathan Cole (Bournemouth University, England) and Fabrice Sarlegna (Aix-Marseille University, France) talked about the importance of proprioception using the dramatic example of deafferented patients. Cole presented a number of studies he did with Ian Waterman, a patient who lost all proprioception and touch below level C3, but still had intact motor function (Cole, 1995). He also retained temperature, pain, and fatigue sensation. Remarkably, Mr. Waterman soon realized that he could control his limbs based on vision, learning to walk and hold heavy objects in the absence of proprioceptive or tactile feedback. He can even perform such challenging tasks as matching the force exerted with both hands, in the presence of visual feedback (Cole & Sedgwick, 1992). He can also perceive weight differences, most likely by detecting the level of muscle fatigue. An alternative explanation, which Cole and his collaborators have not been able to rule out, is that he is detecting changes in central drive. Interestingly, Waterman is better at purely visually guided motor tasks than control subjects. For example, he outperformed controls during a mirror drawing task, probably because he did not suffer from incongruent visual and proprioceptive input (Miall & Cole, 2007). Besides residual sensation and visual feedback, he seems to rely heavily on cognitive strategies for moving and interacting with the environment. Accordingly, his ability to perform rhythmic movements degrades when asked to simultaneously perform another attention-demanding task (Lajoie et al., 1996). Cole's talk highlighted how the study of deafferented patients is a very powerful way to examine the role of sensory pathways in motor control and motor learning. Additional proof of the integral role of sensory pathways in motor learning was presented by Sarlegna. He focused his talk on motor learning in deafferented patients. It had been shown previously that visual feedback is not necessary to learn new dynamics in a force field task (Franklin et al., 2007), but Sarlegna asked whether proprioceptive feedback is needed (Sarlegna et al., 2010). Participants sat on a rotating platform and were required to reach to visual targets while a novel Coriolis force perturbed their movements. The deafferented patient learned the task as well as controls, showing similar time course and magnitude of adaptation. This shows that proprioceptive input helps improve movement quality, but is not critical for sensorimotor adaptation. Indeed, proprioception may even be detrimental in the case of incongruent feedback, as shown by Cole. There still remain open questions about how different sensory pathways interact during motor learning. Simon Gandevia (Prince of Wales Medical Research Institute, Australia) continued the discussion of the role of sensory input for the control of movement. First, he summarized how the perceived position of the wrist during anesthesia and ischemia changes depending on the voluntary command (Gandevia et al., 2006). Then, he introduced the mechanisms underlying different proprioceptive illusions. He described how for the popular rubber hand illusion, anesthetizing cutaneous receptors from different combinations of fingers does not eliminate the sense of ownership: vision and proprioception suffice (Walsh et al., 2011). Gandevia also presented a new ‘plastic finger illusion’ that allowed his group to study the role of proprioception and touch without vision (Héroux et al., 2013). They use a screen to remove visual input, and couple the subject's index finger to an artificial finger positioned above it. With this illusion, they confirmed previous results from other groups showing that vision is not necessary for body ownership. They also found that congruent afferent muscle signals (between the two hands) give a strong feeling of body ownership. This feeling of ownership became stronger once touch and joint receptors were anesthetized, possibly because they decreased incongruent feedback. Importantly, this result indicates that one channel of somatic information (e.g., vision or touch) is enough for embodiment, in contrast to classic illusions that manipulate the correlation between sensory modalities. Therefore, the combination of different sensory modalities with regard to body ownership is more flexible than traditionally thought, and there remain open questions about how a feeling of limb ownership is generated by the brain. Continuing with the theme of the interaction between sensory modalities, several talks discussed the role of different visual pathways in guiding reaching and grasping movements, and how vision and proprioception are integrated. Stephen Scott (Queen's University, Canada) presented a series of studies aimed at understanding the relative contributions of visual and proprioceptive inputs from the perspective of optimal feedback control. He recorded EMG activity while subjects performed a reaching task in a virtual reality environment with their arm supported by a robotic exoskeleton. Some trials included a random mechanical perturbation of the arm. He focused on the EMG activity evoked by this perturbation. He separated the activity into short-latency (< 50 ms) and long-latency (50–100 ms) reflex responses, and a voluntary period (after 100 ms), during which visuomotor responses play a role. He observed that when we move fast, during the first part of a reach, visual information does not contribute significantly; it only matters as the target is approached. Notably, from a control theory standpoint, sensory inputs with different delays, like vision and proprioception, pose a big challenge, because they are hard to integrate. But Scott's group has proposed a way by which the brain may solve this challenge. They have shown that dynamic Bayesian models not only account for error size, but also sensory delays (Crevecoeur et al., 2016). An example of clinical application was given by Sean Dukelow (University of Calgary, Canada), who talked about loss of proprioception after stroke, and the neural mechanisms underlying recovery. Dukelow first presented a method to assess proprioception based on a position matching task that overcomes the lack of accuracy of classic clinical scales (Dukelow et al., 2010). In this method, a robotic exoskeleton moves the patient's affected arm to a location in space, and then the patient has to mirror the position with the unaffected arm. Using this and other robotic tests in a longitudinal study with over a hundred patients, Dukelow and colleagues showed that the time course of motor and sensory recovery is different (Semrau et al., 2015a). This is an important consideration for the design of rehabilitation programs. To further understand recovery after stroke, they studied the relationship between visuospatial and kinesthetic (sense of limb motion, a component of proprioception) deficits (Semrau et al., 2015b). They found that visuospatial deficits are largely predictive of kinesthetic deficits, whereas the opposite is not true: The presence of kinesthetic deficits does not necessarily imply impaired visuospatial function. The work by Dukelow and colleagues provides an example of how basic research on sensory and sensorimotor integration can aid the development of rehabilitation therapies. title: Ispitivanje strojnog dijela FV.18-PI.32
abstract: This paper covers the welding technologies and methods for the examination of welds which are used nowadays. Welding presents an irreplaceable procedure in the construction of both the basic and complex structural parts. Modern welding techniques are based on automated and robotized processes where its quality and flexibility play a key role in meeting high standards of the market. The paper is split into several paragraphs. The basic terminology and types of welded joints are covered at the beginning. The procedure for the preparation of the material to be welded is described together with the importance of the preparation of the joint before welding. After that, the welding techniques and their working principles are discussed, as well as the possible welding errors and their causes. Weld examination techniques that are used for quality control purposes and obtaining the properties of welded joints are explained at the end of the paper. In the experimental part of the paper, the hardness testing of the machine part FV.18-PI.32 is shown.

title: CORR Insights®: Widespread Pain Is Associated with Increased Risk of No Clinical Improvement After TKA in Women
abstract: Where Are We Now? All arthroplasty surgeons have encountered a version of this rare-but-devastating situation: A patient returns for follow-up after TKA by a point in time when (s)he should be fully recovered. Examination reveals that the incision has healed well, ligaments are well-balanced, and radiographs show no evidence of malalignment, fracture, or loosening. But the patient reports substantial pain and says it “just doesn’t feel right”. Workup for infection is negative. The situation is upsetting for patient and surgeon alike. Although TKA is one of the most successful operations orthopaedic surgeons perform [14], persistent knee pain for unclear reasons occurs in as many as 8% to 34% of patients [4]. And while a number of patient factors, surgical technique elements, and implant factors may contribute [3, 8], our fundamental understanding of why some patients have this complication is sorely limited. Pain without objective clinical cause after TKA is the focus of a wide range of clinical studies that point toward an equally broad array of possible etiologies [6]. Some studies suggest pain without objective etiology may be more common in black patients, women, young patients, and patients with lower educational achievement [6, 10, 11]. Other factors that may be associated with persistent pain following TKA include chronic pain remote to the operative knee, fibromyalgia, anxiety, substance use disorders, lack of physical activity in adulthood, and increased acute pain trajectory immediately following TKA [13, 16]. Even genetic polymorphisms are speculated to be associated with persistent post-surgical pain [16]. Widespread pain—a contemporary classification for a number of chronic pain syndromes—encompasses the more-commonly used term of fibromyalgia and includes a broader array of more-nuanced clinical symptoms [18]. The authors of the current study found women (but not men) with widespread pain were more likely not to improve after TKA than were women without widespread pain [17]. Where Do We Need To Go? When it comes to infection or loosening following TKA, modifiable risk factors including diabetes, obesity, and smoking [5, 12] are associated with an increased risk for prosthetic joint infection [2]. Pathways to mitigate these risks have become standard of care [2]. Likewise, we need to classify the risk factors for the less tangible but equally catastrophic outcome of persistent pain following total knee replacement. A framework of modifiable versus non-modifiable risk factors for chronic post-surgical pain after TKA has been proposed [8]. These risks should be addressed prior to surgery as they are for the prevention of PJI or implant loosening. In many other disease states, including diabetes and cardiovascular disease, women experience greater morbidity and mortality than do men with the same diagnosis [7]. Similarly, women with osteoarthritis of the knee have been shown to have increased pain and worse functional outcome scores as measured by Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score at 1 year following TKA [10]. A more-granular understanding of why these disparities exist is needed. Possible causes include gender bias of providers, women seeking care at later stages of disease, biologic differences in inflammation, and variance in hormonal or neural pathways that effect how pain is manifested in women versus men. It remains unclear whether the causes are predominantly external societal barriers versus internal, biologic factors. Solving this puzzle will call upon the overlapping expertise of disciplines including rheumatology, orthopaedic surgery, biomechanical engineering, and pain specialists. As we gain a broader understanding of the patient characteristics that can cause persistent pain after TKA, these factors should be used to develop a predictive model for chronic post-surgical pain that can be universally applied. How Do We Get There? The current data pertaining to the risk factors for having no clinical improvement following TKA should be used to design a robust predictive algorithm to identify at-risk patients pre-surgically. Modifiable risks need to be paired with rigorous, evidence-based treatment strategies. A deeper understanding of these risks will better equip us to formulate pre-operative treatment strategies to reduce the incidence of persistent pain following TKA. Risks including psychological state and widespread pain, may be best addressed with multi-modal treatments including cognitive behavioral treatment, pharmacologic treatment, and modalities of complementary medicine. Innate “unmodifiable” characteristics such as gender, ethnic minority status, and lower level of education need to be uncoupled from other confounding variables (such as poverty, limited access to care) before they are categorically labeled as independent risk factors for chronic post-surgical pain [9]. Barriers of access to care for patients in these under-represented categories should be dismantled. That the disenfranchised have a higher incidence of persistent pain following TKA is a common and unsettling theme in the extant literature. Equitable access to health care and opportunity for higher education is a central issue. A comparative study that evaluates incidence of chronic pain following TKA in societies with universal access to health care and higher education (Sweden, Canada) may prove instructive. Healthcare reform and initiatives that focus on improving health literacy for those with limited access may serve to level the playing field. As we refine our understanding of patient factors that contribute to poor clinical response to TKA we must concurrently investigate the technical pitfalls that may play a role. Innovative concepts such as patient-specific implants, robotics and kinematic alignment may not ultimately prove to be of clinical relevance in the vast majority of patients that continue to have excellent results following TKA [1, 3, 15], but rather may have a focused niche in the minority of patients that are systematically identified via predictive modeling to be disadvantaged from the outset.

title: Synergistic approaches for hexapod mobility: comparative evaluation of structure, navigation, and control strategies on challenging terrains
abstract: The study delivers a cohesive system that combines structural stress investigation, navigational planning evaluation, and adaptive joint control to optimize hexapod effectiveness on hills, stairs, and uneven surfaces. The robot was developed through the iterative drafting technique and designed by assigning in PLA material. Structural examination with Finite Element Analysis (FEA) under 10 N and 20 N forces demonstrated a positive stress allocation and a safety factor of 2.8, combining compact development with durability. In the ROS/Gazebo exploration investigations utilizing global planners like A*, Dijkstra, RRT, and Artificial Potential Field (APF) in combination with a PID-driven local planner, A* as well as Dijkstra developed nearly the best pathways with 100% accuracy. This cut down on route variation by about 17% in comparison to RRT. RRT established confident that the exploration was always the same, but it established paths that were more lengthy and less smooth. APF, on the contrary, made paths that were smooth but less reliable due to the local minima. Adaptive synchronization for joint control quantitatively provided an improvement in joint angle stability, reducing oscillatory deviations by 12% and displacement errors by 15% relative to baseline controllers. The core novelty within this approach is the integrative methodology that will inherently synergize finite element structural analysis, comparative path planning, and Adaptive joint synchronization: presenting a comprehensive optimization strategy, new to hexapod robotics. Together, these advances allow for robust and efficient real-world deployment of hexapods. Future work will extend to hybrid learning-based planning, and sensor-driven dynamic adaptation.

title: Effect of Steel Grades on Technological Properties of Spot Welds
abstract: Because of varying mechanical properties, (e.g. yield point, tensile strength), electric (e.g. electric conductance) and a heat conductivity coefficient, the use of the same welding process parameters leads to the formation of welds having various diameters depending on steels grades subjected to welding The article describes the effect of typical steels used in the automotive industry (e.g. DC 01, DC 600, DC 800) on the weld diameter, i.e. the primary technological parameter of a welded joint. To ensure process repeatability, welded joints were made using a robotic welding station. Afterwards, weld diameters were measured using destructive tests (technological peeling tests and metallographic examination) and non-destructive tests, i.e. ultrasonic tests performed using an RSWA machine provided with a phased-array transducer and acoustic scanning microscopy.

title: Evaluation of Mechanical Properties of S355J2C and HBW450 Materials Joined by MAG Welding Method Using Different Welding Groove Geometries
abstract: In this study, S355J2C and Hardox (HBW450) sheets, which are used extensively in the manufacturing sector, were joined using the robotic MAG welding method by opening the V and X weld groove. Three different variable welding speeds were used in the joints, while other welding parameters were fixed. Microstructural examinations and mechanical tests were carried out on the welded materials produced. The microstructural examinations clearly showed the transition from the base metal to the weld metal and the formation of grains with dendritic structures directed towards the weld centre. The investigations showed that there was a relationship between welding speed and heat input and that hardness and tensile values increased with increasing welding speed. In the microhardness measurements, the lowest hardness values of all the test specimens were measured from the S355J2C base material. It was found that the hardness value of the weld metal was higher than the S355J2C base material and lower than the HBW450 base material, which would be the average of the hardness values of the two materials used. In addition, in the tensile tests, all the specimens failed from the S355J2C base material. As a result of the tests carried out, it was found that the different weld groove geometries did not play a very effective role in the mechanical values of the joints or the resulting microstructure.
