title: Urology in Asia – Malaysia
abstract: Urology in Malaysia had its beginnings in the 1960s, with the endeavors of the late Dato' Sreenevasan. As in other countries, at that time urology was the concern of general surgeons. Ironically, it was hemodialysis that paved the way for urology to develop as its own specialty. Dato' Sreenevasan was instrumental in bringing hemodialysis services to Malaysia. With the development of this service, the public's attention and, more importantly, that of the government was drawn to the importance of urology. With increased public and government attention, Dato' Sreenevasan lobbied for funds and space to develop urology as a specialty. In 1968, the first Urology Unit was started in Malaysia at the General Hospital, Kuala Lumpur (GHKL), which was the biggest hospital in the country at that time. The Institute of Urology and Nephrology (IUN) was started at the GHKL in 1974 and had its own block, consisting of wards, operation theatres, an intensive care unit and a dialysis unit. Since then, urology has grown as specialty in its own right with the development of urology departments in many other hospitals. Currently within the Ministry of Health (MOH) there are urology departments in eight of the 14 states in Malaysia. There are also urology units in the three main university hospitals and urological services are available within many private hospitals in nearly all the states of Malaysia. The Malaysian Urological Association (MUA) had humble beginnings in 1974, within the confines of the new urology block at the GHKL. When the Association was first founded, there were only four members and Dato' Sreenevasan was the founding president. Currently, the MUA has 82 full members, with all practicing urologists in Malaysia being members. Since its inception, the activities of the MUA have grown from journal club sessions to the organization of major international conferences and workshops. The first Malaysian Urological Conference (MUC) was held within the grounds of the General Hospital in 1991. Since then, the MUC has grown to be one of the major medical meetings in the country. In 2011, the MUA will be hosting the 20th MUC in conjunction with the Asia Pacific Society of Uro-oncology meeting in Kuala Lumpur. The MUA has been at the forefront in urologist training in Malaysia. In the beginning, this training was mainly a residency style of training, with the first 3 years in the IUN and a further year in an international center. This was subsequently consolidated with a structured program involving the main urology centers in the MOH and universities. In addition, private urologists contributed to the teaching program. The training was then formalized with the formation of the Board of Urology under the MUA in 2000. The main aim of the board is to coordinate urology training, as well as to provide a comprehensive and structured training program. This was the first board-based training system, for any specialty, in Malaysia. The first board examination was conducted in November 2000 with two candidates. Since then, the board examination has become well established and accepted by the government and medical fraternity. Another milestone was achieved in 2008 when the board examination was held in collaboration with the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Glasgow. This was a joint examination held in Kuala Lumpur with four local examiners and three examiners from Glasgow. The format of the examination is the same as the intercollegiate examinations in the UK. Two of the three candidates were successful and were awarded both the Malaysian Board of Urology certificate and the FRCS (Urol, Glasgow). We have held two further examinations with four overseas candidates taking the joint examination for the first time in 2010. The fourth joint examinations will be held again in November 2011. Urology training in Malaysia has attracted overseas candidates keen to undergo their full training in Malaysia. Currently there is one trainee from Brunei and another from Sudan in the training program. Malaysian urology has close links with Australia and UK for training. Many of the urologists in Malaysia have completed part of their training in one of these countries. The MUA and the Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in 2006 that includes an agreement for two training posts for our trainees in their final year. This cooperation has been very successful and our trainees have benefited greatly from their time spent in the urological centers in Melbourne and Adelaide. Urology in Malaysia had made great strides since its humble start in the late 1960s to its present status, with most of the latest equipment and facilities available here in Malaysia. There are three Da Vinci robots in the Malaysia and many laser machines for the treatment of both stones and prostate diseases. Endourology and the treatment of urinary calculi forms the bulk of the workload of many urologists in the country. Renal transplantations are performed regularly in three main hospitals in Kuala Lumpur, primarily with live related donors. We are seeing a gradual development of subspecialties within Urology and this trend will continue as more urologists are trained. There is a growing trend for research in urology. The MUA recently organized a Malaysian Urology Research Forum with the aim of developing urological research. The ultimate aim is to form a Malaysian Urology Research Group to allow collaborations among the various institutions. This will allow us to pool resources and data to generate meaningful research. The MUA is committed to developing urological services to ensure easy access in all parts of the country. We will also continue to enhance and strengthen the training program to ensure an adequate ratio of urologists per head of population. In this regard, closer links with urological communities within Asia, as well as across the rest of the world, will be strengthened and we will continue to look for opportunities to host international conferences and meetings. We also hope to ensure that research in Urology continues to thrive to ensure further progress in urological services. None declared.

title: Internal representation of external patient dynamics in locomotor rehabilitation
abstract: This research presents a new paradigm of an interactive locomotor simulator (ILS) in order to investigate how humans learn to interact and modify the locomotor pattern of another individual. Manual gait rehabilitation is imperfect at complete restoration of locomotor function in patients with stroke. Physical therapy poses a unique learning challenge, as it involves simultaneous sensorimotor co-adaptation and co-learning between one or more therapists and a patient. While patient motor learning has been extensively investigated, how a therapist adapts and learns to manipulate the gait pattern of a patient has been largely unexplored. Multiple motor learning theories exist that explain various ways this may occur, but confounds resulting from therapist-patient co-adaptation make it difficult to probe therapist learning in a clinical setting. We used the ILS to control for these confounds and hypothesized that therapist learning follows the internal model hypothesis. The internal model hypothesis postulates that through interaction with novel physical dynamics a human develops the ability to predict the behavior of the system and extrapolate to subsequent interactions. In the ILS, a user interacted with a computerized virtual patient (VP) via a robotic manipulandum in order to modify the gait pattern. Manipulandum endpoint impedances transformed from joint-space rigid body dynamics and stiffness create a force field that makes the user feel as if they are holding onto the ankle of a real patient. The user must learn how to apply the correct forces to the leg of the VP to restore a healthy gait pattern. Examination of user responses to random catch trials, the presence of after effects, and the ability of users to generalize were analyzed to assess internal model formation. Results suggest that humans do create internal models of external locomotor dynamics.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Long-Term Care: A Scoping Review
abstract: Population aging is reshaping global health and social service systems at an unprecedented pace. The World Health Organization estimates that the number of people aged 60 and above worldwide will reach 1.4 billion by 2030 and rise to 2.1 billion by 2050. Against this backdrop, long-term care (LTC) — an institutional arrangement under which informal caregivers and professionals deliver continuous daily care and nursing support to people with long-term functional dependencies — has become a core issue for countries tackling aging populations. Long-term care is not a single service but a multifaceted system composed of multiple elements. It covers three service settings: home, community and institutional care, operates relying on financing and payment mechanisms such as long-term care insurance, and is jointly supported by care institutions, professional workforce, and the care workflow of "needs assessment – plan formulation – service delivery – quality supervision". Nevertheless, LTC systems are under mounting structural pressures: there is a persistent shortage of care workforce with growing reliance on migrant labourers; service quality varies widely across different settings and institutions; and the labour-intensive traditional care model fails to meet rapidly expanding demand. Meanwhile, long-term care spending accounts for 1.8% of GDP in Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries and is projected to keep rising, posing challenges to sustainable financing. Artificial intelligence offers a new technical lever to ease the aforementioned pressures. Research indicates that AI has been integrated into multiple links of LTC systems, including health monitoring and anomaly alerts for long-term care recipients based on sensor and wearable data, clinical decision support to assist care planning, long-term care robots and social robots, as well as intelligent applications for institutional operation management, disability assessment under long-term care insurance, and actuarial forecasting. However, there is a lack of comprehensive research that takes the long-term care system as an integral framework and systematically maps cross-setting and cross-link applications of AI. Existing reviews mostly focus on a single technology (robots) or a single dimension (ethics, responsible innovation), with particularly insufficient examination of AI’s role at the institutional level of LTC. In addition, most available evidence remains at the proof-of-concept and prototype stages, lacking sufficient understanding of implementation outcomes in real care settings, cross-link integration, as well as issues including equitable access, privacy protection and governance regulation. In view of the above, this study adopts a scoping review method to systematically outline the research landscape of AI-enabled long-term care systems, clarify the technical forms, functional links and application scenarios of AI, identify governance issues and translation barriers, and provide evidence-based references for technological empowerment, policy design and care practices within LTC systems.

title: CPA Evolution: Curriculum revision for Higher Education
abstract: Recent proposals from the National Association of States Board of Accountancy and the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants aim to modify the CPA license model to reflect the knowledge and abilities that new CPAs will need both now and in the future. The Uniform CPA Examination has recently undergone its most significant modification in many years thanks to the CPA Evolution project. This article discusses the exam's revised structure and content, evaluates the anticipated effects of those changes on accounting education, and explains how colleges will need to modify their curricula to meet the new exam core Plus requirements. Today's accountants and the accounting industry require different technical capabilities than they did even a few years ago. For the accounting profession to advance, proficiency in technology, data analytics, risk management, and IT governance are becoming crucial competencies. The joint CPA Evolution project of the AICPA and NASBA acknowledges the rapidly evolving abilities and competences needed by today's CPAs. The quick development of technical advancements, such as data analytics, robots, and artificial intelligence, among others, is significantly altering the way CPAs do their business. Additionally, this report illustrates the constraints that the COVID-19 placed on the world's environment and economy. The CPA profession is changing, and data from IPEDS and responses from participating U.S. universities and public accounting companies enable us to assess the effects of this change on both the supply and demand of new accounting. The public accounting firms have started to fill the technology and data analytics talent gaps among accounting recruits by hiring non-accounting staff, according to the AICPA's 2021 Accounting Graduate Supply and Demand Report, which includes a survey of the hiring practices of public accounting firms. According to the research, new hires of master's graduates increased by 2% in 2020, despite a 10% decline in the total hiring of new accounting graduates.

title: Experimental Evaluation of Key Welding Process Parameters on the Performance of MIG Welded Mild Steel
abstract: The implementation of innovative techniques and sophisticated procedures in welding enhances efficiency and productivity. Automation, particularly robot assisted automation, is crucial in the development of advanced welding systems. In contrast to traditional Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), contemporary methods enable reduced thermal input, maintaining the workpiece and weld areas at relatively lower temperatures. This reduced heat input not only minimizes thermal distortion but also improves weld precision, reduces spatter, and enables the successful joining of mild steel, galvanized sheets, and dissimilar metals, such as steel and aluminium. In this regard, this current research paper proposes to unearth the effect of the three parameters that are attributed to considerable input of metal and influence on the mechanical performance of Metal Inert Gas (MIG) welded mild steel joints, such as current, voltage, and wire feed speed. Weld strength was assessed by mechanical properties such as tensile strength, hardness, and microstructural characteristics. The techniques employed in underpinning the experiments were drawn using a Taguchi L9 orthogonal array and three uses of three-level input parameters. ANOVA results demonstrated that the strongest influence was made by welding current to tensile strength, with the remaining 2 of the 3 factors being voltage and the wire feed rate. Welding voltage, on the contrary, had the highest impact on hardness, and so did the wire feed rate and the current rate. The best parameter conditions of maximum hardness were determined to be at 30 V, 160 A, and 6 m/min, whereas the optimal conditions of maximum tensile strength were 30 V, 170 A, and 2 m/min. The microstructural examination showed the weld zone to have fine grains of ferrite and pearlite, which meant that the metallurgical standard was high. This paper focuses on the importance of optimizing the process to achieve high-quality welds and also highlights the appropriateness of MIG welding for precision and automated welding.
venue: International Journal of Engineering and Information Management

title: 1610 Don't Let Your Past Determine Your Destiny
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Synovial sarcoma (SS) is a rare mesenchymal soft tissue sarcoma usually involving extremities close to large joints. SS of the GIT is uncommon; SS of the colon is extremely rare. Recognition and management of SS of the GIT can be very challenging. Here we report a rare case of asymptomatic SS of the rectosigmoid diagnosed as a surprising finding of surveillance colonoscopy. CASE DESCRIPTION/METHODS: A 59-year-old asymptomatic lady with past medical history of diabetes mellitus, morbid obesity, colon polyps was referred for surveillance colonoscopy. Prior colonoscopy six years ago revealed two sigmoid colonic tubular adenomas. Examination was unremarkable except for a BMI of 44. Thorough examination of the musculoskeletal system did not reveal any abnormalities. Colonoscopy revealed a large, 5 cm pedunculated and superficially ulcerated round mass in the rectosigmoid colon, filling most of the lumen with the distal end of the lesion being ∼15 cm above the anal verge. Biopsy demonstrated spindle cells with marked nuclear pleomorphism, high mitotic index rate, positive SS18 (SYT) gene rearrangement testing on FISH. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was positive for TLE1, OSCAR, MCK, AE1/AE3, CK7 with Ki-67 of 70% and negative for desmin, CD117, DOG1, p63, CK5, CK6, S100, SMA. Findings were consistent with SS. Staging CT and PET-CT did not demonstrate distant spread. Robotic laparoscopic anterior resection with wide surgical resection margins and lymphadenectomy revealed T1N1 LN 2/20 stage 3 monophasic synovial sarcoma, with negative margins, 20% tumor necrosis and high mitotic rate. The patient was started on adjuvant chemotherapy with 5 cycles of Adriamycin 75 mg/m 2 and Olaratumab on day 1 and day 8 of a 21-day cycle. A repeat PET-CT and a flexible sigmoidoscopy, six months later, did not reveal any tumor recurrence. DISCUSSION: Increasing number of cases of GIT SS are being reported. The majority of GI SS cases involved esophagus and stomach with pain, obstruction and bleeding being the common presenting symptoms; SS of the large intestine is extremely rare. Diagnosis is established by molecular genetics and IHC. Standardized treatment-guidelines are currently lacking. It is of paramount importance to i) consider SS on the list of differentials of colonic neoplasms, ii) report these unusual cases to better understand the pathophysiology, treatment options and success rates. This would facilitate more targeted and effective treatments for SS of the colon.

title: Apprentissage par transfert pour l’analyse des formes 3D
abstract: 3D shape analysis is central to applications such as robotics, autonomous driving, and medical imaging. However, compared to 2D vision and natural language processing, progress in 3D deep learning has been slower. This gap can be attributed to three main factors: significantly smaller labeled datasets, the absence of a unified architectural backbone, and the lack of well-established pre-training strategies that transfer reliably across tasks and domains.This thesis studies transfer learning for 3D shape analysis from three complementary perspectives. It begins with an examination of point cloud transfer learning under uni-modal pre-training, where a layer-wise analysis is conducted to evaluate how learned features behave during linear probing and full fine-tuning on downstream tasks. This analysis reveals specific limitations in feature adaptability, motivating the introduction of a geometric regularization strategy that improves transfer to new datasets.The investigation then extends to cross-modal post-hoc alignment between 3D models and semantic text encoders. Empirical analysis shows that independently trained 3D and text models do not naturally share a common latent space. To address this, a projection-based framework is proposed that identifies a correlated low-dimensional subspace combining geometric and semantic information, enabling zero-shot retrieval without joint training.Finally, the focus shifts from global alignment to dense open-vocabulary understanding. By distilling fine-grained features from large 2D visual foundation models, 3D encoders are trained to support dense shape reasoning. This enables effective part-level zero-shot segmentation in a feed-forward manner, without explicit 3D part supervision.Together, these contributions demonstrate that carefully designed transfer learning strate- gies can substantially improve data efficiency and generalization in 3D shape analysis, particu- larly when they integrate pre-trained visual and semantic priors.

title: Towards online monocular camera calibration: a filtering based approach for intrinsic camera calibration
abstract: Structure-from-motion, visual odometry, SLAM, and many other computer vision technologies rely on the ability to interpret the physical geometry of a scene captured by a camera. To extract accurate geometric information from the captured scene, the camera must be calibrated to establish a robust estimation of the projection function from the scene to the sensor. The calibration is typically a laborious task. If done in the factory, it adds to the cost of manufacturing. If done by the user, it requires expertise and specialised equipment that makes the system less generally useful. Furthermore, calibrations are unstable over time — they change with age, temperature, shock, and vibration. The traditional method of camera calibration, completed offline as a preprocessing step using a predefined calibration pattern, is susceptible to shifts in calibration over time, which can degrade the accuracy of measurements. Our research proposes a novel method for online monocular camera calibration, which utilises data from an IMU and GNSS receiver rigidly attached to the camera to jointly estimate the camera intrinsic parameters, camera pose, and feature positions in real time. This configuration allows for continuous detection and correction of any shifts in the intrinsic parameter calibration. We formulate the calibration as a state-space problem and use high-rate IMU data to predict relative camera and feature motion. GNSS observations and visual data tracking using sparse optical flow serve as the update. The inference is solved using an unscented Kalman filter implementation. Unscented Kalman filtering is a widely used approach in sensor fusion for estimating the state of a dynamic system. It incorporates information from multiple sources, such as visual and inertial sensors, to improve the accuracy and robustness of state and parameter estimation. Our research covers various topics, from 3D geometry and coordinate frames to attitude representations and sensor technologies, including in-depth examinations of cameras, GNSS receivers, and IMUs. We delve into sensor fusion, emphasising the unscented Kalman filter, visual feature detection, and tracking techniques. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method is robust in estimating camera intrinsic parameters in a tightly controlled simulation environment and that our novel approach has the potential to provide accurate and stable calibration in real-world applications. Our approach has potential applications in various fields, including robotics, augmented reality, and remote sensing.

title: Glimpses under the history of medicine
abstract: ANCIENT SYSTEM OF MEDICINE IN INDIA The concepts and techniques of "Healing the Ailing" is as old as life itself from antiquity. India is known as the cradle of this art and Ayurveda the mother of healing that consists of a complete and holistic system integrating the body, mind, and spirit. According to Indian mythology, this is a divine art and science revealed by the creator of this universe, Lord Brahma[1] who passed on this knowledge to some of the learned sages (Rishis) as documented in holy Hindu scriptures viz., Vedas. Out of the four Vedas, Rigveda and Atharvaveda contains detailed descriptions about a spectrum of diseases and their remedies. The first prescription of medicine, "Amruth" is contained in Mrithunjaya Mantra which is a part of Rig Veda - Apart from curative treatment with various herbal medicines, prevention of diseases through life style modulation, yoga,[2] and hygienic living distinguished Ayurveda from other ancient systems of medicine. Ayurveda had also influenced other ancient system of medicine to a considerable extent especially the Tibetian,[3] Chinese, and Greek systems of medicine and this is the reason why Ayurveda was known as the Mother of Healing. The practical text of Ayurveda was divided into 8 branches (Ashtangas) Together, the practice of all these branches was named as Ashtangas of Ayurveda. It is worth mentioning the most important Ayurvedic text which is considered the most valid learning resources in Ayurveda. Even though the exact origin of Ayurveda is a matter of speculations, everybody accepts that the period from 6th century B.C to 7th century A.D was the golden age of the Indian system of medicine, and most of the literary creation in Ayurveda took place during that period. The first literary creation in Ayurveda seems to be Agnivesh Samhitha that consists of all the Ayurveda formulations invented by Arthreya and Agnivesha. Charaka updated and modified Agnivesh Samhitha and brought out a revised edition with his own contribution in the form of Charaka Samhitha against a wide spectrum of disease entities. In fact, there were two schools of medicine during the period of Samhithas, i.e., between 6th century B.C. and 7th century A.D[4] - the Arthreya School of Ayurveda and the Dhanavanthri School of Ayurveda. While Charaka belonged to the Arthreya School of Ayurveda, Shushrutha, the Father of Surgery, belonged to the Dhananvanthri School. Arthreya was the head of the department of Medicine at Nalanda University while Shushrutha independently did his research and surgical work. He used to collect dead bodies from river Ganges and dissect them to learn human anatomy. He also created a treatise called "Shushrutha Samhitha"[56] that contained 84 chapters describing 1120 different disease entities, 700 medicinal plants, and 64 formulations from mineral sources and 57 from animal sources. He also described 300 surgical procedures under 8 categories and 125 surgical instruments. Ashtanga Hridya is another valuable creation in Ayurveda written by VagBhada and is a compilation of relevant portions in Charaka Samhitha and Shushrutha Samhitha with his own original contributions. Ayurvedic knowledge emphasizes the importance of maintaining a harmonious balance between the five components with which the human body is made up of, like any other physical entity, viz, Panchabhuthas that represent the Earth, Air, Sky, Fire, and Water. The diseases are due to the failure to keep healthy balance between these five factors. Any treatment should be aimed at regulating these factors at four levels viz., Body or Sharira, Senses or Indriya, Mind or Manasa, and Soul or Atma. The diagnosis in Ayurveda is based on proper history taking and physical examination. Like the humoral theory of diseases in Greek medicine, Ayurveda believes that the Thridoshas[7] viz, Vada, pitah, and kapha are the three etological factors that predispose to the various disease entities, and the Ayurvedic formulations were prescribed to counteract the imbalance between the Tridoshas. Unani is another system of medicine that had deep roots and royal patronage in India during the Indian Sultanate and Moghul periods. The system was very similar to Ayurveda based on the balance between elements. While Ayurveda followed the Panchabhutha theory of Charvachakas, Unani proposed only four elements viz, Fire, Air, Water, and Earth excluding Sky. ANCIENT SYSTEM OF MEDICINE IN EGYPT[8] Herodotus,[9] a celebrated Alexandrian surgeon, described Egyptians as "healthiest of all men next to Libyans" due to the noble public health system that they possessed. According to him, each physician of the ancient Egypt was a unique specialist in healing only one particular disease and not more. The sources of information is from the famous Edwin Smith Papyrus,[10] which contains the medical formulations of ancient Egypt from 300 B.C. onwards. Father figure of Egyptian medicine, Imhotep is considered to be one of the original authors of Edwin Smith papyrus and claims to have performed the first surgery as early as 2750 B.C. Several authors contributed and finally Edwin Smith Papyrus was compiled into one of the ancient texts of medicine and surgery like Shushrutha Samhitha of India, which is considered to be a more systematic and authentic treatise on surgery. KAUN Gyneugological Papyrus[11] is another ancient Egyptian Papyrus on Obstetrics and Gynaecology dating back to 1800 B.C., which narrates 34 distinct cases of obstetrics and gynaecology including cases with diagnosis and problems of conception and their treatment. Hesey RA, the chief Physician and Dentist of King Djoser, is considered to be one of the earliest physicianin history of Babylonian medicine. Like the Egyptians, the Babylonians also had a rich heritage in healthcare. They also followed a systematic practice of medicine that consisted of detailed history taking, physical examination, diagnosis and treatment, and follow up of prognosis. Their earliest text book was "Diagnostic hand book" written by Esagil-Kin-Apla of Borcippa during the time of KingAdad-Apla-Iddina between 1069-1046 B.C. CHINESE SYSTEM OF MEDICINE[12] China too had a rich tradition in the healing art and the fundamental text of Chinese medicine "HaemidiNeijing" was written between 5th and 3rd century B.C. The Chinese had another text book viz, "Tritisa on cold damage" which gives references from "Haemidi Neijing"[4], "Yellow Emperor's Inner Cannon". They had a third creation of medical literature"Jijyijing" written by HaungfuMitha, the founder of Acu Puncture. During the time of Tang dynasty 'HaemidiNeijing' was revised incorporating all the later inventions and is considered as the authoritative text on Chinese traditional medicine based on herbal therapy, Acu Puncture and massage. GREEK AND ROMAN MEDICINE In 1800 B.C., Homer in his famous poem "Iliad" describes the treatment of the wound on the thigh of one of the two sons of Askla Poas, the healer God of Greece. The patient himself was a renowned physician of that time, and he gives directions to another Dr. Patroclus to remove the foreign body in the wound on his thigh, wash it with hot water, and treat it with herbal medicines. One of the ever living testimony to the in depth knowledge of the Greek in healthcare is the Asklepeon of Epidaurus, which is the installation of three large marbles erected in 350 B.C. with the inscription of the names, history, complaints, and cures of about 70 patients who were treated in their temples. These cases include opening of abdominal abscess, removal of foreign body, etc. under Eukoinesis induced by opium products. The first known medical school in Greece was opened in 700 B.C. in Snidus and Alcaumen,[13] the author of first work on anatomy worked in this school. The Greeks proposed the theory of humors as the basis of health and disease, and the aim of the treatment was to restore the balance of these four humors viz., black bile, yellow bile, phlegm, and blood. The Hippocrates (460-370 B.C.), the father of western medicine,[14] was Greek and compiled a collection of 70 early medical works contributed mainly by the author and his students. The treatise came to be popularly known as the Hippocratic Corpos. He also formulated the famous Hippocrat oath that is still being taken by the medical graduates entering into the medical profession throughout the world. Hippocrates and his students described many diseases and their clinical manifestations. However, the most notable ones are the clubbing of fingers observed in chronic separative lung disease, congenital cynotic heart diseases, infective endocarditis, chronic liver diseases, etc., and the Hippocratic Facies. He only classified the diseases according to the duration into acute and chronic and according to the geographical distribution of diseases into endemic and epidemic. He was the first thoracic surgeon who described the clinical manifestation of emphyemaor, the collection of puss in the pleural cavity. SURGEONS OF ALEXANDRIA Two great anatomists and surgeons of Alexandria viz, Erasistratus of Ceos and Hirophilus of Chalceon controlled bleeding during surgery using ligatures, bringing down the mortality of the patient by a considerable extent. For the first time in history, they used the lithotomy position for various diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. They had performed many standard surgical procedures like herniography, ophthalmic surgery, etc. Herophilus, while working in the medical school of Alexandria, proposed brain as the seat of intelligence and connected central nervous system to the motor and sensory functions of the body. Herophilus for the first time in the history spelt out the distinction between arteries and veins. Cornelius Celsus (30 B.C.-38 A.D.)[15] Cornelius Celsus was a nonmedical scholar who wrote "De Re Medicina" in eight volumes. He was the first to describe the four signs of inflammation viz. rubor, calor, tumor, and dolor. Cadaveric dissection was made illegal in Rome, similar to what the Buddhist did in India; this created a period of stagnation in the progress of medicine during the medieval period. Galen (129-201 A.D.) Galen[16] was born in Pergaunus in Asia minor. He spent considerable time in the rich Alexandrian library and mastered all the existing literature in medicine. He became a follower of Hippocrates and propagated the Greek concepts including the humoral theory through his extensive writings. He described the crab-like growth of cancer and also described the fifth sign of inflammation "loss of function". He had written 500-600 books and treatises including "seat of diseases", "abnormal tumours," and an exhaustive text on anatomy and surgery, which was followed all over the world until the onset of renaissance. title: Power-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks: Optimizing Architectures, Learning Methods, and Hardware Deployment
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are emerging as a powerful class of biologically inspired neural models that offer significant potential for energyefficient and temporally precise computation. Unlike traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) that rely on continuous activation functions and synchronous updates, SNNs communicate through discrete, sparse spike events, mimicking the temporal dynamics of biological neurons. This inherent sparsity and event-driven behavior make SNNs particularly well-suited for deployment in power-constrained environments such as edge computing, robotics, and embedded systems. However, the realization of efficient SNNs entails a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between network architecture, learning algorithms, and hardware deployment strategies. This survey provides an in-depth examination of the core methods and developments enabling efficient SNNs. We begin by analyzing spiking neuron models and their computational properties, emphasizing how design choices in neuron dynamics (e.g., leaky integrate-and-fire, Izhikevich) impact both expressiveness and hardware efficiency. Next, we explore network architectures optimized for energy-aware operation, including sparse connectivity, temporal coding schemes, and biologically inspired design patterns such as lateral inhibition and winner-take-all mechanisms. We then turn to neuromorphic hardware platforms—such as Intel Loihi, IBM TrueNorth, and SpiNNaker—that support asynchronous, event-driven execution, significantly reducing energy consumption by exploiting the temporal sparsity of spikes. A major portion of this work is devoted to learning algorithms for SNNs, covering surrogate gradient methods that approximate backpropagation through time (BPTT), ANN-to-SNN conversion techniques that transfer pretrained models to the spiking domain, and biologically plausible local rules like spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). We discuss how these approaches affect training complexity, inference latency, and overall energy efficiency. Moreover, we investigate energy-aware training objectives and hybrid optimization strategies that jointly minimize task error and hardware cost metrics. Throughout the survey, we present a mathematical framework that unifies different efficiency metrics, from spike count and firing rate to hardwarespecific energy profiles, enabling a rigorous comparison of methods. We also highlight open challenges such as the lack of standardized benchmarks, limitations in scaling to deep architectures, and the trade-offs between biological plausibility and computational performance. In conclusion, efficient SNNs represent a convergence of neuroscienceinspired modeling, algorithmic innovation, and specialized hardware design. As research continues to mature, SNNs are poised to become a cornerstone of next-generation AI systems that demand both intelligence and frugality. This survey aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a comprehensive and mathematically grounded overview of the field, facilitating further advancements in efficient, low-power neural computation.

title: МЕТОД МАРШРУТИЗАЦІЇ ГРУПИ МОБІЛЬНИХ РОБОТІВ НА СТАЦІОНАРНІЙ МЕРЕЖІ ДЛЯ ВИКОНАННЯ ЗАВДАНЬ ПОШУКУ ЗНИКЛИХ ОБ’ЄКТІВ В ЗОНІ ТЕХНОГЕННОЇ АВАРІЇ
abstract: Context. The relevance of the article is determined by the need for further development of models of collective behavior of systems with multi-agent structure construction endowed with intelligence that ensures synchronization of the joint efforts of various agents while achieving the goals set for the system. The method proposed in the article solves the problem of competition between different agents of a multi-agent system, which is important while performing search, rescue, and monitoring tasks in crisis areas of various origins. Objective is to develop a method for determining the sufficient population of a multi-agent system and the optimal routes of movement of its individual elements in a stationary network for the most complete examination of a technological disaster zone (any given zone based on a certain transport network). Method. We implemented the concept of a dynamic programming to search for all possible edge-simple longest paths connecting the directed subsets of vertices-sources and vertices-sinks in the structure of the model weighted directed graph. To this end, the modified Dijkstra method was applied. The modification comprises representing the weights of the arcs of the modeling directed graph with the negative values, which are further used in calculations according to the Dijkstra method. After finding the next edgesimple longest path, the arcs that make up it are fixed in the memory of the computer system (in the route plan) and removed from the graph structure, and the process is iteratively repeated. The search for paths takes place as long as the transitive closure between the vertices that are part of the specified subsets of source vertices and sink vertices is preserved. The developed method makes it possible to find such a set of traffic routes for the elements of the multi-agent system, which maximizes the area examined by them in a technological disaster zone (or the number of checked objects on the traffic routes) in one “wave” of the search and distributes the elements of a multi-agent system by routes that do not have common areas. A derivative of the application of the developed method is the determination of a sufficient population of a multi-agent system for effective search activities within the defined zone. Results. 1) A method of routing a group of mobile robots in a stationary network for searching the missing objects in a technological disaster zone has been developed. 2) The working expression of the Dijkstra method for searching in the structure of a network object (in the structure of a model graph) for the longest paths has been formalized. 3) We have suggested a set of indicators for a comprehensive evaluation of route plans of a multi-agent system. 4) The method has been verified on test problems. Conclusions. Theoretical studies and several experiments confirm the efficiency of the developed method. The solutions made using the developed method are accurate, which allows recommending it for practical use in determining in an automated mode route plans for multi-agent systems, as well as the required number of agents in such systems to perform the required amount of search tasks in a particular crisis area.

title: Rectal cancer surgery: radiology roadmaps
abstract: Based on radiological imaging, a ‘radiology roadmap’ succinctly describes how rectal cancer could be potentially resected with a high probability of histologically clear (R0) margins Radiology roadmaps are increasingly provided as part of a radiology report by specialist gastrointestinal radiologists Radiology roadmaps are created after review of all relevant scans, particularly high-resolution pelvic MRI examinations showing the cancer at its maximal extent, the ‘high-tide mark’, in terms of volume and/or boundary (often before neoadjuvant treatment) Radiology roadmaps can be modified by the surgeon after consideration of clinical and patient-related factors to create a final ‘surgical roadmap’ used to guide the operation in theatre Radiology roadmaps for cancers requiring extended resection are refined in close collaboration with the surgical team, ideally in a dedicated multidisciplinary team and using multimedia aids, such as video vignettes Colorectal surgical trainees should be familiar with the benefits and limitations of imaging; they should be cognisant of the experience of the reporting radiologist when assimilating the information from radiology roadmaps Radiological assessment of rectal cancer has evolved from simple reports of cancer location and exclusion of metastatic disease to detailed anatomical assessments of the cancer in relation to TNM stage, surgical planes, and identification of prognostic factors, such as lymphadenopathy, extramural vascular invasion, and tumour deposits1,2. Increasingly, radiologists are going a step further and using their anatomical understanding of the cancer in vivo to guide surgeons with an operative plan to attain clear pathological margins. This guide is translated into a ‘radiology roadmap’ with an accompanying video vignette (most helpful for extended resections beyond standard total mesorectal excision (TME)) that captures their radiology review in a short, annotated video. When radiology roadmaps are developed in collaboration between local radiology and surgical teams, they can eliminate report ambiguity, highlight discrepancies in disease extent between imaging and clinical assessment, and help the surgeon imagine a dotted line along which they can resect the cancer to achieve complete (R0) excision3,4. Colorectal surgeons should understand which scans to request (and their limitations), the significance of maximal disease extent, and the level of radiology expertise required to construct radiology roadmaps. A thorough discussion of the different imaging modalities used for rectal cancer staging is beyond the scope of this article5,6. In brief, the authors use standard body CT (chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT) for all patients and reserve liver MRI (with a liver-specific contrast agent, such as Primovist™) for patients with cancers with poor prognostic features, according to imaging or histology. PET-CT is generally reserved for patients requiring extended resection, for patients with squamous cell cancers, and/or for patients requiring assessment of enlarged pelvic sidewall (PSW)/extra-pelvic lymph nodes. For cancers with adverse biology (such as signet ring cell adenocarcinoma) with a rapid trajectory to a more advanced stage and with a poor response to neoadjuvant treatment, the authors recommend more frequent imaging with shorter intervals between scans and a lower threshold for use of PET-CT/liver MRI, so that surgical decision-making is based on contemporaneous staging information6, taking into account disease prognosis. Pelvic MRI is the primary modality used in the radiological assessment of rectal cancer. High-quality, high-resolution MRI includes the routine intravenous administration of spasmolytics, typically hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan®), to decrease peristaltic artefact, and the acquisition of high-resolution volume sequences. Small-field-of-view (‘magnified’) T2 sequences acquired in different anatomical planes (sagittal, angled axial, and coronal) mean that radiologists can pinpoint the craniocaudal and radial boundaries of rectal cancer and help assess its relationship to key anatomical landmarks, particularly the anorectal junction, the peritoneal cul-de-sac, and the circumferential resection margin (CRM). Accurate measurement of the distance between the caudal margin of the cancer and the anorectal junction (defined by the cranial margin of the puborectalis sling) will help decide whether to restore luminal continuity. An experienced radiologist can precisely measure the distance between the luminal, mural, and extramural components of the cancer and the cranial surface of the puborectalis (anteriorly, in the midline, or posteriorly, according to the radial location of the cancer). In the authors’ experience, the height of the distal cancer margin above the anorectal junction is particularly relevant when a cancer involves the low rectum, as standard laparoscopic or robotic TME will frequently leave behind a rectal cuff that is 10–20 mm long (typically slightly longer anteriorly due to the angle of anteroposterior surgical stapling). Consequently, the authors recommend that cancers with a distal margin of 20 mm or more above the anorectal junction, particularly those confined to the rectal wall, are generally suitable for standard TME; when 5 to less than 20 mm, TME may be considered, using a handsewn ‘intersphincteric approach’, and, when less than 5 mm, abdominoperineal excision (APE) is usually recommended. MRI review will frequently identify rectal cancer extension into the mesorectum as the invasive component (usually from the centre of the cancer, indicating stage T3) and/or accompanying lymphovascular disease (macroscopic involvement of lymphatics ± blood vessels), perineural, and/or lymph node involvement. Extramural tumour deposits are focal expansions of tumour developing within the mesorectum with no discrete host origin (such as lymphatics, vessels, nerves, or lymph nodes), according to histology. When present, these adverse prognostic features alert the radiologist to further scrutinize staging scans for evidence of metastatic disease (PSW or extra-pelvic disease). Irrespective of feature (primary tumour extension, lymphatics, vessels, or nodes), the colorectal surgeon will need to ensure complete resection of all with a clear margin of healthy tissue to achieve R0 resection. Where the CRM is threatened by or involved by cancer, extended resection should be considered. The surgical resection planes permitting extended resection will depend on the location of the CRM threat; for example, a laterally threatened or involved mesorectal fascia adjacent to the PSW will require a surgical excision plane lateral to the endopelvic fascia, whereas the involvement of PSW structures, by contiguous disease, extramural venous invasion, or discrete deposits, will likely necessitate PSW clearance (excision of internal iliac vessels and lymph nodes, above or below the origin of the superior gluteal artery (SGA) ± ureters ± sciatic nerve roots). Isolated involved or suspicious nodes without extracapsular extension within the PSW can be managed by lymphadenectomy alone. In the context of exenteration surgery, preservation of internal iliac vessels above or below the SGA origin will help the surgeon decide whether closure of the large perineal wound after an extralevator resection can be achieved with an inferior or SGA perforator fasciocutaneous flap. Anterior threat or involvement of the Denonvilliers’ fascia can determine whether a ‘prostatic shave’ or total pelvic exenteration respectively is appropriate. Notably, the gap between the tumour edge and the prostatic urethra is usually small (less than 10 mm) when the Denonvilliers’ fascia ± prostate capsule are involved and so exenteration is generally preferred in this context. A prostatic shave tends to be reserved for select patients, for whom less extensive surgery is preferable due to clinical factors; it is accepted that there will be an increased risk of urological morbidity. In women, anterior involvement of the rectovaginal septum ± vaginal wall will demand that the roadmap help assess the length and the extent of vaginal excision (complete or partial). Endorectal ultrasonography can be particularly helpful with assessment of the anterior margin (and frequently the distal margin) of low rectal cancer for selected patients, as an adjunct to high-quality MRI. Posterior extension of the cancer will help decide whether the coccyx, the distal sacrum (below S2/3), and the high sacrum (above S2/3) are threatened or involved. In general, a threatened presacral fascia requires subperiosteal excision; involvement of the presacral fascia and small areas of cortex requires subcortical sacrectomy (typically not more distal than S2 due to less bone stock and poorer surgical access) and more extensive involvement of the bony cortex or medullary invasion requires sacrectomy7,8. Prior disease (such as Crohn’s disease causing sepsis), previous anastomotic leak, prior resection (such as colonic and prostatic resection), or total abdominal hysterectomy may disrupt standard anatomical borders and their impact can be assessed radiologically. Roadmaps are thus modified to these new boundaries. For example, anterior tumour extension (T3) of a low rectal cancer will be more likely to threaten the bladder and urethra after prior prostatectomy. Previous sepsis often leads to greater complexity and contention, as scarring and fibrosis can mimic the radiological appearance of malignant disease. Abscess cavities can also be considered to be contaminated by tumour and thus their borders should be defined within the roadmap. This can often lead to a more extensive resection, sometimes without an oncological benefit. The radiologist assimilates the size, morphology, signal intensity (mucinous or not), pattern of invasion, adverse prognostic features, and anatomical relationships of the cancer from the MRI and describes them in detail. A helpful acronym developed by the authors is ‘BONVUE’ (Table 1), which helps remind both the radiologist and the surgeon to include all anatomical sites relevant to staging and for creating a radiology roadmap9. The tendency to omit important radiological staging features has been addressed by a national audit with a recommendation for radiologists to provide a template report10. While this can occasionally lead to a ‘dry’ table-like report, use of templates, at least as a memory checklist, results in a report that concludes with TNM classification (eighth version), lists adverse prognostic features, and additionally includes a radiology roadmap as part of the opinion. Components of the ‘BONVUE’ acronym used to assist structured beyond total mesorectal excision rectal cancer reporting Components of the ‘BONVUE’ acronym used to assist structured beyond total mesorectal excision rectal cancer reporting To create a radiology roadmap, the radiologist must understand what the surgeon needs to know from the imaging to help plan their operation. The content of the roadmap will vary between centres and individual surgeons; for example, where a centre does not undertake pelvic exenteration surgery, the authors recommend that the radiology report broadly describes the radiology recommendation for extended surgery and does not include a detailed roadmap. Where standard rectal cancer surgery is recommended from a radiology perspective, the authors recommend that the radiology roadmap suggests the appropriate resection - TME, partial mesenteric excision (PME), APE, or extralevator APE (ELAPE) - that should be considered to achieve R0 excision (Fig. 1). The radiology roadmap for R0 resection recommends consideration of extralevator abdominoperineal excision a Sagittal T2-weighted MRI sequence showing a low rectal tumour (arrows) with the caudal margin at the level of the puborectalis sling (broken line). b Modified axial T2-weighted MRI sequence showing a semi-annular tumour with rolled edges at 12 and 8 o’clock with shallow transmural extension at the leading edge at 4 o’clock within 1 mm of (involving) the fascia over the left levator (arrow). For extended resections, the roadmap should recommend resection planes and detail which structures (bones, organs, nerves, vessels, ureters, and extra sites, including PSW and distant nodes/metastases (‘BONVUE’)) should be sacrificed or retained (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3). The level of detail provided, the terminology, and the assurance of understanding between radiology and surgical teams should be agreed locally and refined over time at regular multidisciplinary team meetings, using a common ‘language’, such as the pelvic exenteration lexicon11. The radiology roadmap for R0 resection recommends consideration of extralevator total pelvic exenteration with a gluteal flap (lexicon code C2 F1) a Sagittal T2-weighted MRI sequence showing an anterior low rectal tumour with the caudal margin at the level of the anorectal junction. The arrows show an anterior leading edge with shallow transmural extension abutting the Denonvilliers’ fascia. b Corresponding axial T2-weighted MRI sequence showing the edge of the tumour (red line) abutting the Denonvilliers’ fascia (white line) at 10–2 o’clock at the prostatic apex without evidence of macroscopic prostatic invasion. No nodes. The radiology roadmap for R0 resection recommends consideration of high sacrectomy at S1/2, angling obliquely to avoid the thecal sac (terminating at the mid-S2 level) and resecting sacral nerve roots S2 and below bilaterally (preserving S1 bilaterally), total pelvic exenteration, and left Extended Lateral Sidewall Excision (ELSiE) with left pelvic sidewall clearance distal to the superior gluteal artery (lexicon code P4 C2 SN3 LSV2) a Sagittal T2-weighted MRI sequence showing a presacral recurrence after anterior resection extending craniocaudally from the proximal S2 level to the coccyx. b Corresponding axial T2-weighted MRI sequence showing tumour contacting the sacral cortex at the proximal S3 level (arrow). It is also invading through the left posterolateral endopelvic fascia and abutting the left piriformis. On the right, it is contained by the endopelvic fascia. The S2 and S3 nerves are threatened or involved on both sides and the left sacral ligamentous and muscle complex is involved (not shown). Video recordings (for example using Microsoft Teams) are routinely provided in St Mark's Hospital for complex cases by radiologists who demonstrate the cancer in vivo and show the pertinent details of a radiology roadmap. A short (2–5 min) video vignette can be a very helpful aide-memoire for surgeons for subsequent surgical planning (for example when creating the surgical roadmap and for educating their team on or before the day of surgery). They can be used for intraoperative reference and rewatched multiple times to consolidate the roadmap in the surgeon’s mind. The radiologist soon becomes familiar with creating vignettes and refines their content over time, according to surgical feedback. A ‘radiology roadmap’ is not a ‘surgical roadmap’, as it is created by a radiologist according to the imaging information available for review and does not take into account critical patient and clinical factors; for example, what the patient is willing to undergo, what the surgeon is willing to undertake, or how the disease trajectory influences the likely risk/benefit ratio of surgery. The radiology roadmap is generally created from scans showing the maximal extent of disease into surrounding structures, usually, but not always, before neoadjuvant treatment. As a tumour regresses in response to neoadjuvant treatment, it does so unevenly, potentially leaving viable islets of tumour cell colonies within the scarring and fibrosis. This concept of a ‘high-tide mark’ takes into account this known viable seeding of cancer within regression sites after a positive response to neoadjuvant treatment12. Therefore, it is of high importance that all relevant imaging scans, from staging scans at diagnosis to the final scans before surgery, are carefully assessed. Although the maximal extent of cancer is often evident in initial staging scans (before neoadjuvant treatment and timely surgery), disease progression can occur at a later date when the cancer is biologically aggressive, unresponsive to treatment, or there are unforeseen delays to surgery. The radiology roadmap is also provided and potentially revised based on the final scans before surgery. Consequently, the longer the time gap between final scans and surgery, the higher the risk of disease progression. To minimize this risk, the authors generally perform such scans a maximum of 4 weeks before surgery, unless specific circumstances extend this to 2 months; for example, for patients with an excellent response to neoadjuvant treatment with stable disease radiologically or clinically over several months6. Radiology roadmaps provide an anatomical step-by-step guide to optimising rectal cancer R0 resection. The approach is helpful for standard rectal cancer resections (both locally advanced and recurrent). Fostering a close working relationship between the surgeon and the radiologist improves the understanding of both disciplines and the use of a common lexicon allows greater accuracy and confidence in creating first the radiology roadmap and then the surgical roadmap. title: ASSESSING USABILITY OF A PROTOTYPE SOFT EXOSKELETON BY INVOLVING PEOPLE WITH GAIT IMPAIRMENTS
abstract: Graf ES1, Bauer CM1, Schülein S2, de Eyto A3, Power V3, Bottenberg E4, Weyermann B5, O'Sullivan L3, Wirz M11Zurich University of Applied Sciences / Institute of Physiotherapy, Winterthur, Switzerland, 2Geriatrics Centre Erlangen, Erlangen, Germany, 3University of Limerick, School of Design, Design Factors Research Group & Health Research Institute, Limerick, Ireland, 4Saxion University of Applied Sciences and Technology, Enschede, Netherlands, 5Geriatrics Centre Erlangen, Physiotherapy, Erlangen, GermanyBackground: Gait impairment is prevalent among many growing clinical populations e.g. people with stroke, incomplete spinal cord injury (iSCI), older adults etc. Such populations may benefit from assistive devices such as exoskeletons to improve their walking ability. XoSoft (www.xosoft.eu) is a soft exoskeleton that is being developed for people with mild to moderate gait impairments to support their mobility by providing physical actuation across joints of the lower extremities. During the design and development of a device like XoSoft, it is crucial that Primary Users (PUs, e.g. patients) are involved and provide insight into their experiences and expectations regarding device usability. However, it is still not standard practice to include PUs in rigorous testing of highly technical exoskeletons. The XoSoft consortium took an iterative design approach to the development of the XoSoft prototypes. Data from usability testing with PUs are informing next iterations of the XoSoft concepts.Purpose: The purpose of this study was to assess the PU experiences of the usability of a XoSoft prototype. This study should also highlight the importance of including PUs during the development of assistive devices.Methods: Eleven participants were recruited (mean age: 73 years, mean height: 166 cm, mean mass: 65 kg). There were three categories of PUs: frail (n=5), stroke (n=1), iSCI (n=5). Participants had no cognitive impairment (Mini Mental State Examination score > 24). The prototype consisted of a leggings-style garment with Velcro straps as anchor points for actuators across the relevant joints (hip, knee, ankle). Actuation and control was provided by a modular pneumatic/sensor controlled system, which was added to the garment in modular fashion based on the PU needs. After independent donning and doffing by the participant, the garment was donned and the Velcro straps placed and secured by a researcher to ensure proper placement. Participants then performed walking tasks with active actuation followed by completion of the System Usability Scale (SUS, Brooke 1996, maximum score = 100).Results: The scores for the SUS ranged from zero to 95 with a median rating of 52.5. The median rating corresponds to an “okay” score. According to the acceptability ranges by Bangor et al. (2008), 3 participants rated the prototype as acceptable, 3 as marginal, and 5 as not acceptable.Conclusion(s): The scores indicate the need for improvement in the design of future XoSoft prototypes. The large variability in SUS scores indicated that the same device may be rated considerably differently by different users. This highlights the importance of including a variety of potential users of assistive devices during development.Implications: Secondary Users (SUs) such as physical therapists are also involved in the development of XoSoft, providing insight into their own needs and the needs of their patients. The therapists also play a key role in motivating their patients to participate in research and development projects. To ensure that such assistive devices can be integrated into users' lives and practices, it is essential to have both PUs and SUs actively involved in the technical development.Keywords: user involvement, assistive device development, exoskeletonFunding acknowledgements: This work has received funding from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under grant agreement No.688175 (XoSoft).Topic: Robotics & technologyEthics approval required: YesInstitution: Canton of Zurich / Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-NürnbergEthics committee: Ethics Committee Canton of Zurich / Clinical Ethics CommitteeEthics number: 2016-01406 / 72_18BAll authors, affiliations and abstracts have been published as submitted.

title: Papers Presented at the Annual Meetings of the Knee Society
abstract: The Papers Presented at Annual Meetings of the Knee Society includes selected papers read at the 2006 Annual Interim Meeting of the Knee Society, held in Alexandria Virginia, and the 2007 Open Scientific Meeting of the Knee Society, held in San Diego. The outstanding depth and breadth of material contained within this symposium can be credited to the organizational skills of the Knee Society education committee and its program chair, Daniel Berry, MD. The quality of manuscripts published in this symposium is excellent and reflects the hard work of the CORR staff in providing clear and consistent guidelines and copyediting that bring clarity, brevity and strength to those manuscripts accepted for publication. The 2007 Ranawat Award paper was authored by Dr. Tad Mabry and colleagues at the Mayo Clinic for their comparative study on the difficult problem of knee arthrodesis for the infected knee replacement. This retrospective review of a large number of patients highlights the clear benefits and drawbacks of two of the established techniques for knee fusion, namely custom intramedullary nailing and external fixation. These data are useful for patient and surgeon alike as they provide definitive information on expected complications, time to fusion and final outcome. The 2007 Coventry Award paper was authored by Dr. William Griffin and colleagues from Charlotte, NC for their report on polyethylene wear-related failures in total knee arthroplasty and the relationship to sterilization methods. This retrospective review provides new information on early and midterm failures due to rapid polyethylene wear and highlights the benefits of periodic follow up examinations of patients after total joint arthroplasty. The 2007 Insall Award paper was authored by Dr. Victoria Brander and colleagues from Chicago and underscores the effects of patient specific characteristics on the midterm outcome of total knee arthroplasty. In this study preoperative pain scores and indicators of depression were predictive of poorer outcomes at five-year followup. This research highlights the importance of pain management in the perioperative care of patients and opens questions about the benefits of addressing psychological and social issues preemptively in an effort to maximize the benefits of surgical interventions such as total knee arthroplasty. The remaining papers in this symposium are grouped to include new information regarding unicompartmental knee arthroplasty technique and results, primary total knee arthroplasty technique and results, computer-assisted surgery, design considerations in knee arthroplasty and topics related to revision total knee arthroplasty. After a strong resurgence of interest at the turn of the millennium, the growth of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) has plateaued over the past few years. There is little doubt UKA represents the best treatment option for a selected subgroup of patients with knee arthritis, but surgeons worldwide continue to debate just what that subgroup looks like. In this symposium there is information on a contemporary surgical technique for UKA, midterm followup looking at contralateral compartment arthritis after UKA and encouraging results of UKA for osteonecrosis, a subgroup of patients for whom many surgeons have historically been uncomfortable in offering UKA. The primary total knee papers address some of the typical concerns faced by every practicing orthopaedic surgeon, including how to maximize flexion, how to address thromboprophylaxis, and when to resurface the patella in primary TKA. One criticism of much of the TKA literature is many of the larger series are from selected high-volume surgeons or academic medical centers where the experience may not reflect that of the typical orthopaedic surgeon. In this issue, two papers address total knee survivorship from a large community based joint registry. Despite the substantial resources being devoted by industry to computer-assisted TKA, relatively few surgeons have found the theoretic advantages of navigation outweigh the practical hurdles and expense to justify its use on a routine basis. Two papers in this issue look at some more esoteric issues related to navigation, namely how to verify tracking protocols and then how to take navigation one step further and couple it with robotics. At the same time surgeons and industry look to improve the surgical process through technique, navigation and robotics, there is also substantial work being invested in implant design with the goal of maximizing knee function. Most surgeons are well aware of the high percentage of total hip patients who largely forget they ever had the hip replaced. Meanwhile we continue to be puzzled as to why we can not get a similar proportion of knee patients to forget about their TKA. This discrepancy highlights the room for improvement in TKA design, technique and perioperative care that continues to exist. Two papers review some of the design considerations that may affect the performance of TKA. Finally, the area of revision TKA is one that will continue to grow in importance over the coming years. The demographic data suggest an increasing need for both primary and revision TKA over the next two decades and the younger age and higher demands of many of today's TKA patients will challenge all of us as surgeons. In this issue there is useful information on rehabilitation techniques for the poorly functioning TKA, outcomes data on isolated tibial insert exchange for wear-related failures, a selected series of bilateral knee revisions, and a review of two-stage reimplantation for infection. The Knee Society remains committed to advancing knowledge of the knee for surgeons and patients alike. The selected scientific papers presented in this issue represent the individual and collective efforts of the Knee Society to improve patient care today and to stimulate the further research that will enhance patient care in the future. Mark W. Pagnano, MD Department of Orthopaedics Mayo Clinic Rochester, MN; and Deputy Editor for the Knee Society Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research Philadelphia, PA
